Reduced multisections and projected jets

A1. A genus bound for multisections of split real line equations

Statement

Let CC be a compact Riemann surface of genus gg, and let N=⨁j=1sLjN=\bigoplus_{j=1}^s L_j be a sum of smooth complex line bundles. Put dj=deg⁡Ljd_j=\deg L_j and d=max⁡jdjd=\max_j d_j. Give each line a smooth real Cauchy–Riemann operator DjD_j. The graph almost-complex structure on NN is the one for which a graph over a holomorphic map ff solves f*Djuj=0f^*D_j u_j=0 in each coordinate; pullback includes the differential of ff on the (0,1)(0,1)-form factor.

Let X0X_0 be a compact connected nodal complex curve and ν:X=∐i=1kXi→X0\nu:X=\coprod_{i=1}^k X_i\to X_0 its normalization. Suppose that

  1. f:X→Cf:X\to C is holomorphic and nonconstant on every component, with total degree mm;
  2. uj∈Γ(X,f*Lj)u_j\in\Gamma(X,f^*L_j) solves f*Djuj=0f^*D_j u_j=0;
  3. the graph F=(f,u1,…,us)F=(f,u_1,\ldots,u_s) matches at the two preimages of every node of X0X_0;
  4. FF is generically one-to-one onto its image, and the images of distinct components of XX are distinct.

The last condition means that the support is reduced and its parametrization has multiplicity one. It excludes a multiple cover of a lower-degree graph. No immersion or transversality assumption at a node is required for the bound.

Proposition. Under these hypotheses, if bb is the number of nodes of X0X_0 and R(f)=∑x∈X(ex(f)−1)R(f)=\sum_{x\in X}(e_x(f)-1) is the total ramification, then

R(f)+2b≤m(m−1)d.R(f)+2b\ \le\ m(m-1)d. \tag{1}

Consequently

pa(X0)≤1+m(g−1)+m(m−1)2d.p_a(X_0)\ \le\ 1+m(g-1)+\frac{m(m-1)}2d. \tag{2}

For balanced split lines, dj=g−1d_j=g-1, this becomes

pa(X0)≤1+m(m+1)2(g−1).p_a(X_0)\ \le\ 1+\frac{m(m+1)}2(g-1). \tag{3}

In particular a genus-two base gives bounds 2,4,7,11,…2,4,7,11,\ldots in degrees 1,2,3,4,…1,2,3,4,\ldots. The degree-two case recovers the bound in the line-operator note, while allowing arbitrary branch profiles and arbitrary numbers of line summands in higher degree.

Proof by differences of sheets

Form the analytic fiber product X×CXX\times_C X, take its reduced structure, and normalize it. Discard the components which are diagonals of components XiX_i. Denote the remaining disjoint union of smooth compact Riemann surfaces by ZZ. There are maps

p1,p2:Z→X,h=fp1=fp2:Z→C.p_1,p_2:Z\longrightarrow X,\qquad h=f p_1=f p_2:Z\longrightarrow C.

All components of ZZ map finitely onto CC: a finite fiber product of the finite maps in question has no component supported over a point. Above a regular value of ff, its points are exactly the ordered pairs of distinct sheets. Therefore

∑Zα⊂Zdeg⁡hα=m(m−1).\sum_{Z_\alpha\subset Z}\deg h_\alpha =m(m-1). \tag{4}

On a connected component ZαZ_\alpha define the difference sections

vαj=p1*uj−p2*uj∈Γ(Zα,hα*Lj).v_{\alpha j}=p_1^*u_j-p_2^*u_j \in\Gamma(Z_\alpha,h_\alpha^*L_j).

The two bundles being subtracted are canonically the same pullback from CC. Functoriality of pullback, including its differential factor, and real linearity give

hα*Djvαj=0.h_\alpha^*D_j v_{\alpha j}=0. \tag{5}

At least one difference is not identically zero on each ZαZ_\alpha. Otherwise the two distinct sheets represented by ZαZ_\alpha would have identical graph values over an open set of regular values. This contradicts generic injectivity, or the distinctness of the images of two components of XX. Choose one such index j(α)j(\alpha), once for each component.

A nonzero solution of a real line Cauchy–Riemann equation has isolated zeros of positive integral order, whose total is the degree of the line. Thus

#zeros⁡(vα,j(α))=dj(α)deg⁡hα≤ddeg⁡hα.\#\operatorname{zeros}(v_{\alpha,j(\alpha)}) = d_{j(\alpha)}\deg h_\alpha \le d\deg h_\alpha. \tag{6}

The zero count includes multiplicities. The coefficients in (5) are smooth even at a branch point of hαh_\alpha; vanishing of the pulled-back zeroth-order coefficient there causes no difficulty. The input is the scalar similarity principle, for example Wendl, Lectures on Symplectic Field Theory, Theorem 2.5.3, printed pp. 52–53. The total-order statement is its usual first-Chern-class consequence.

We next count forced zeros in (6). At a point x∈Xx\in X with ramification index ee, choose holomorphic coordinates in which f(z)=zef(z)=z^e. Near (x,x)(x,x) the fiber product has equation

z1e=z2e.z_1^e=z_2^e.

It has ee distinct smooth branches z2=ζz1z_2=\zeta z_1, with ζe=1\zeta^e=1. One is the discarded diagonal. Each of the other e−1e-1 branches gives a distinct point of the normalization ZZ. At every such point all difference sections vanish. Whichever nonzero coordinate was chosen on its global component therefore has a zero of order at least one. The contribution from these points is at least e−1e-1. Distinct ramification points give distinct points in this count. Summing gives at least R(f)R(f).

Now let a node of X0X_0 have distinct normalization preimages x,yx,y. Matching gives F(x)=F(y)F(x)=F(y), hence f(x)=f(y)f(x)=f(y). The ordered pairs (x,y)(x,y) and (y,x)(y,x) lie off the diagonal. There is at least one point of the normalization over each pair: locally the fiber product has an equation z1ex=z2eyz_1^{e_x}=z_2^{e_y} and has gcd⁡(ex,ey)≥1\gcd(e_x,e_y)\ge1 branches. Each point lies on a component retained in ZZ, and every difference vanishes there. The two ordered pairs thus contribute at least two zeros. They cannot coincide with a point counted over (x,x)(x,x), and different nodes have different pairs of normalization preimages. This contributes at least 2b2b further zeros.

Adding (6) over all components and using (4) proves (1). Riemann–Hurwitz on the components and connectedness of the dual graph give

R(f)=2∑ig(Xi)−2k−m(2g−2),pa(X0)=∑ig(Xi)+b−k+1.\begin{aligned} R(f)&=2\sum_i g(X_i)-2k-m(2g-2),\\ p_a(X_0)&=\sum_i g(X_i)+b-k+1. \end{aligned}

It follows that R(f)+2b=2pa(X0)−2−m(2g−2)R(f)+2b=2p_a(X_0)-2-m(2g-2), which proves (2). Substitution of d=g−1d=g-1 proves (3).

Sharpness and relation to adjunction

The coefficient of m(m−1)dm(m-1)d cannot be lowered in this class. Fix m≥2m\ge2 and take a holomorphic line LL of positive degree dd for which LmL^m has a section ss with a nonempty reduced zero divisor. The spectral curve

wm=sw^m=s

in the total space of LL is smooth and connected. Smoothness follows at a zero of ss from its nonzero derivative; elsewhere the derivative with respect to ww is nonzero. Local monodromy around a simple zero is an mm-cycle, so the cover is connected. Its mdmd branch values each have ramification index mm; hence R(f)=m(m−1)dR(f)=m(m-1)d. Its tautological graph is embedded and attains (2). Such sections exist, for example, whenever md≥2g+1md\ge2g+1, by very ampleness and a general choice of section. Extra line coordinates may be set equal to zero.

For a single line, (2) is also the usual adjunction bound in the four-dimensional total space: the class m[C]m[C] has square m2dm^2d and first Chern number m(2−2g+d)m(2-2g+d). See Wendl, Holomorphic Curves in Low Dimensions, Theorems 2.49 and 2.51 for intersection positivity and adjunction, respectively. The proof above does not project the full graph to a single simple curve. A coordinate projection can be multiply covered; the nonzero coordinate may vary with the component ZαZ_\alpha. This is why the argument applies to a split bundle of any rank without a simplicity hypothesis on any one coordinate projection. No claim of literature priority is made here.

Fiberwise nonlinear equations with independent coordinates

The same bound holds for the following larger class. Fix complex linear Dolbeault operators ∂‾Lj\bar\partial_{L_j} and smooth fiberwise maps

Aj:Lj→Λ0,1T*C⊗LjA_j:L_j\longrightarrow \Lambda^{0,1}T^*C\otimes L_j

covering the identity of CC. The graph equations are

∂‾f*Ljuj+f*Aj(uj)=0.\bar\partial_{f^*L_j}u_j+f^*A_j(u_j)=0. \tag{7}

Here f*Ajf^*A_j again pulls back the form factor. The equation for coordinate jj depends only on that coordinate. The maps AjA_j need not be linear, and need not vanish at the zero section.

On ZαZ_\alpha, put a=p1*uja=p_1^*u_j and b=p2*ujb=p_2^*u_j. The difference of the two equations (7) is a smooth real line Cauchy–Riemann equation for a−ba-b, because

Aj(a)−Aj(b)=Bj(a,b)(a−b),Bj(a,b)=∫01(dfibAj)b+t(a−b)dt.A_j(a)-A_j(b)=B_j(a,b)(a-b),\qquad B_j(a,b)=\int_0^1(d_\mathrm{fib}A_j)_{b+t(a-b)}\,dt. \tag{8}

The integral is a real-linear map on the common fiber LjL_j; the construction is intrinsic under linear changes of bundle frame. Pulling back the form factor gives a smooth zeroth-order coefficient on ZαZ_\alpha. Consequently the same positivity and degree count applies, and the proof of (1)–(2) is unchanged. This extension does not include coupling between different coordinates: in that case the difference in one coordinate need not solve a homogeneous scalar equation.

Compactness for the controlled family

There is a useful compactness consequence with explicit spatial hypotheses. Suppose g≥2g\ge2, d≥0d\ge0, and a compact smooth parameter family of the equations above is realized in a fixed tube in a closed symplectic manifold. Suppose the corresponding ambient almost-complex structures form a compact smooth family tamed by its fixed symplectic form. Fix a compact subset KK of the tube and a degree bound MM. Consider connected reduced nodal graph maps satisfying the proposition, with images in KK, no contracted components, and degree at most MM.

Corollary. Every sequence of these maps has a stable-map convergent subsequence, after reparametrization. Every limiting connected stable map has source arithmetic genus at most

G=1+M(g−1)+M(M−1)2d.G=1+M(g-1)+\frac{M(M-1)}2d.

Proof. The degree and arithmetic genus take only finitely many values by (2); pass to a subsequence on which both are fixed, and on which the parameters converge smoothly. The class in the tube is m[C]m[C], so the symplectic area is m∫Cωm\int_C\omega and is bounded. The nodal graph maps are stable: an automorphism of a nonconstant component preserving a generically injective map is the identity. Gromov compactness for stable maps of fixed genus and bounded area in the closed ambient target now supplies the subsequence. Its image remains in KK, and its arithmetic genus is the fixed source genus, at most GG. Equivalently, to reduce this to smooth-domain compactness, the number of normalization components is at most MM, and (1) bounds the number of nodes. Pass to a fixed labeled dual graph and apply marked Gromov compactness on each normalization component, treating the node preimages as marked points. Continuity of evaluation permits regluing each paired pair of marks in the limit; this preserves the total arithmetic genus. The limit can have contracted components or multiple covers, but their genera are included in this same bound. ▫\square

The compactness theorem used in this corollary is the usual fixed-genus theorem, not a new analytic compactness result. For the marked smooth-domain theorem with varying tame structures and stable nodal limits see Wendl, Holomorphic Curves in Low Dimensions, Theorem 2.35, printed p. 38. The extra input here is that the genus hypothesis has been deduced from the split equations before applying that theorem. The spatial trapping and common tame realization are assumptions, not consequences of (2).

Consequences and limits for the comparison

For fixed m,gm,g and line degrees, the bound is uniform over all smooth operators in the split class, and over all smooth independent fiber equations (7). It bounds ramification and the number of nodal identifications of reduced, multiplicity-one supports, not just the genus of smooth double-cover graphs. Thus it supplies a concrete genus estimate in arbitrary covering multiplicity for this class of local geometries.

It does not by itself supply compactness in a noncompact tube: sections of a linear equation can be scaled without bound. Nor does it bound the arithmetic genus of stable maps with contracted components, or of maps which cover a lower-degree support with higher multiplicity. For example, a contracted curve of arbitrary genus can be attached at a point of any fixed graph.

Finally, arbitrary perturbations used for transversality can couple the line coordinates and destroy (5) or (8). A uniform bound in the split class does not prove a uniform bound for these perturbations. A theorem comparing this controlled class with elementary-cluster factors, including contracted components and the required transverse walls, is still needed before asserting any vanishing of universal exponents. The separate wall comparison investigation examines that obstruction.

A2. An all-genus double-cover comparison for distinct even spin lines

The statement and the existing inputs

Let CC be a smooth compact complex curve of genus two, and let a,ba,b be distinct even theta characteristics. On N=a⊕bN=a\oplus b take the direct sum of their positive-mass real spin operators, with the absolute determinant orientation. Write Lm,kL_{m,k} for the connected local Gromov–Witten degree of covering degree mm and source genus kk. Write nm,hn_{m,h} for the integral exponent of the balanced elementary factor of degree mm and support genus hh, as in Article III, Proposition 3.1. These are different invariants.

Theorem. For the indicated germ,

n2,3=−8,n2,4=2,n2,h=0(h≥5).n_{2,3}=-8,\qquad n_{2,4}=2, \qquad n_{2,h}=0\quad(h\ge5). \tag{1}

Equivalently, with s(t)=2sin⁡(t/2)s(t)=2\sin(t/2),

∑k≥3L2,kt2k−2=−12s(t)4.\sum_{k\ge3}L_{2,k}t^{2k-2}=-\frac12s(t)^4. \tag{2}

Consequently, in every source genus k≥3k\ge3,

L2,k=(−1)k(22k−2−4)(2k−2)!.L_{2,k}=\frac{(-1)^k(2^{2k-2}-4)}{(2k-2)!}. \tag{3}

If Fh(q)F_h(q) denotes the balanced elementary series in the complex cycle algebra, the unique balanced lift of the germ satisfies

P̃a,b(q)=F2(q)F3(q2)−8F4(q2)2(mod⁡q3).\widetilde P_{a,b}(q) =F_2(q)F_3(q^2)^{-8}F_4(q^2)^2\pmod{q^3}. \tag{4}

The entries −8-8 and 22 were already proved by the étale and first-excess calculations in Papers 7–8. The independent genus-five calculation in Calculation B2 also gave n2,5=0n_{2,5}=0. The new assertion here is the uniform vanishing in (1), established by controlling the genera of correction supports.

The proof uses the existing geometric factorization and identification of its exponents with the connected elementary expansion from Article III, Proposition 3.1 and Corollary 3.2. It uses the published cycle compactness and cluster results of Doan–Ionel–Walpuski, abbreviated DIW. It does not assume that Bai–Swaminathan’s all-genus wall invariant has already been identified with elementary exponents, and does not construct a numerical evaluation on arbitrary analytic families.

1. Triangular equations preserve the support bound

Work on fixed smooth degree-one lines L1,L2L_1,L_2 over CC. Fix a positive spin operator D2D_2 on L2L_2 and a reference complex-linear operator ∂‾L1\bar\partial_{L_1}. Consider the equations

∂‾f*L1u1+f*At(u1)=0,f*D2u2+f*Ft(u1)=0.\bar\partial_{f^*L_1}u_1+f^*A_t(u_1)=0,\qquad f^*D_2u_2+f^*F_t(u_1)=0. \tag{5}

Here AtA_t and FtF_t are smooth fiber maps from L1L_1 to the (0,1)(0,1)-form bundles with coefficients in L1L_1 and L2L_2, respectively. The pullbacks include the differential of ff on the form factor. We require At(0)=Ft(0)=0A_t(0)=F_t(0)=0. These equations define a graph almost-complex structure whose projections to CC and to the almost-complex surface L1L_1 are holomorphic. Its fiber complex structure is standard. A compact nonconstant curve cannot lie in one affine fiber.

The spin/Stokes argument in Article III, Lemma 14.1, shows that h*D2h^*D_2 is injective for every smooth connected finite cover hh of CC. It is also injective on connected stable sources: sections vanish on the nonconstant normalized components, and matching propagates their vanishing over the contracted components.

For a reduced graph of total degree mm, use the normalized off-diagonal fiber product of its normalization with itself over CC, as in Calculation A1. On every component, the first-coordinate difference v1v_1 solves a homogeneous scalar real Cauchy–Riemann equation. If it were identically zero, the second-coordinate difference would solve h*D2v2=0h^*D_2v_2=0, and hence vanish. That would identify two generic sheets of the full graph, contrary to reducedness and generic injectivity. Thus v1v_1 is nonzero on every retained component.

The scalar zero count, followed by the ramification and node count of Calculation A1, gives

R(f)+2b≤m(m−1),pa≤1+m(m+1)2.R(f)+2b\le m(m-1),\qquad p_a\le1+\frac{m(m+1)}2. \tag{6}

It also proves that every simple full graph projects to a simple scalar graph in L1L_1, and that distinct full graphs have distinct scalar images. No coordinate is discarded in this argument.

In degree two the scalar image has a particularly rigid description. For the smooth normalization, let ι\iota be the deck involution. The section u1−u1ιu_1-u_1\iota has precisely two zeros. If the cover is branched, its two ramification points exhaust those zeros simply. The scalar graph is then embedded and has genus four. At a branch point with f(w)=w2f(w)=w^2, the equation gives ∂w‾u1(0)=0\partial_{\bar w}u_1(0)=0, and the simple odd zero gives ∂wu1(0)≠0\partial_wu_1(0)\ne0. If the cover is étale, the scalar graph is immersed, has genus three, and has exactly one transverse double point. Degree-one scalar graphs are embedded sections. In particular every simple full graph of degree at most two is immersed before any perturbation is made.

2. A path with regular core

Both even theta characteristics are non-effective. Indeed a line of degree one on a genus-two curve has at most one independent section, and even parity therefore forces h0=0h^0=0.

Keep D2=DbD_2=D_b fixed and join DbD_b to DaD_a on the first smooth line. First lower the positive spin mass on bb to zero. At positive mass the spin norm identity gives injectivity, and at zero mass it follows from h0(b)=0h^0(b)=0. Join the Dolbeault structures of bb and aa inside Pic⁡1(C)\Θ\operatorname{Pic}^1(C)\setminus\Theta, and then restore the positive spin mass on aa. The complement of the theta divisor is path connected: a smooth path in the complex surface Pic⁡1(C)\operatorname{Pic}^1(C) can be perturbed to miss its real-codimension-two divisor. Smooth Dolbeault representatives can be chosen on the fixed underlying line over the interval. All these operators have index zero and zero kernel, so they are invertible.

Denote this smooth base-invertible path by D1,tD_{1,t}. Initially set AtA_t equal to its zeroth-order term and Ft=0F_t=0. Allow arbitrarily small nonlinear perturbations subject to

At(0)=Ft(0)=0,dfibAt|0=D1,t−∂‾L1,dfibFt|0=0.\begin{aligned} A_t(0)&=F_t(0)=0,\\ d_\mathrm{fib}A_t|_0&=D_{1,t}-\bar\partial_{L_1},\qquad d_\mathrm{fib}F_t|_0=0. \tag{7} \end{aligned}

Take the path constant in endpoint collars and keep the complete positive-spin equations fixed there. The spin/Stokes argument ensures that only the zero-section support occurs in those collars. The normal operator of the zero section remains D1,t⊕D2D_{1,t}\oplus D_2 and is invertible throughout. Its determinant sign is positive. Allowing a lower off-diagonal first jet would also preserve this invertibility, but is unnecessary here. The nonlinear freedom away from the zero section will suffice.

The compact-realization construction in the proof of Article III, Proposition 3.1, realizes the entire compact parameter family on one tube VV in a closed symplectic six-torus, with common taming form and primitive class A=[C]A=[C]. The family agrees along the zero section, and compactness of the interval permits one sufficiently small tube for the construction. All local classes have the positive integral degree label mAmA. Take an energy cutoff 2∫Cω≤Λ<3∫Cω2\int_C\omega\le\Lambda<3\int_C\omega.

3. Actual-curve genericity in the triangular class

We require genericity for actual simple curves of degree one or two contained in VV. We do not require a split path to be transverse to every smooth-cover wall, or to satisfy a fixed-genus wall theorem on every compactified stable-map space.

Lemma. There are arbitrarily small smooth triangular perturbations satisfying (7), fixed in the endpoint collars, for which all simple curves of degree at most two in VV are embedded and pairwise disjoint at every parameter. Their fixed-parameter moduli are discrete. A dense set of parameters has every such curve unobstructed.

Proof. The zero section is regular by (7). For a noncore simple graph u:Y→Nu:Y\to N, write u‾:Y→L1\bar u:Y\to L_1 for its scalar projection. Both are immersions by Section 1, so their normal bundles fit into an exact sequence of real Cauchy–Riemann operators

0→(f*L2,f*D2)→(Nu,DuN)→(Nu‾,Qu‾)→0.0\longrightarrow(f^*L_2,f^*D_2) \longrightarrow(N_u,D_u^N) \longrightarrow(N_{\bar u},Q_{\bar u}) \longrightarrow0. \tag{8}

The vertical operator is f*D2f^*D_2 because the second equation in (5) is linear in u2u_2; the quotient is the scalar normal operator of the immersed graph in L1L_1. Thus ker⁡DuN↪ker⁡Qu‾\ker D_u^N\hookrightarrow\ker Q_{\bar u}. The full normal operator has real index zero, since the ambient first Chern number on every local class is zero.

There is an injective unbranched disk of the scalar graph away from the zero section and from the scalar images of any finitely many other distinct curves. Distinct simple scalar curves have isolated intersections; identical scalar images would contradict injectivity of D2D_2 applied to their second-coordinate difference. On this disk, arbitrary values of (Ȧ,Ḟ)(\dot A,\dot F) supply arbitrary normal (0,1)(0,1)-forms. They extend to parameter perturbations supported away from the zero section. The adjoint unique-continuation argument therefore makes the universal normal Fredholm section transverse. At a fixed parameter its projection has Fredholm index zero; for paths the index is one.

Next hold the curve fixed by making the perturbation values zero along its scalar image. First normal derivatives remain arbitrary real maps from the scalar normal line to the rank-two normal output. At a one-dimensional kernel this makes the derivative to Hom⁡(ker⁡DuN,coker⁡DuN)\operatorname{Hom}(\ker D_u^N,\operatorname{coker}D_u^N) surjective. At nullity k≥2k\ge2, choose two independent kernel elements and project them to scalar normal sections q1,q2q_1,q_2. They are real-linearly independent on some disk: otherwise their real ratio would satisfy ∂‾a=0\bar\partial a=0, forcing a constant ratio and global dependence by unique continuation. An annihilator for the variation of these two kernel columns has pointwise expression

q1⊗η1+q2⊗η2=0.q_1\otimes\eta_1+q_2\otimes\eta_2=0.

On the disk of independence this forces both adjoint sections to vanish, and unique continuation makes them zero globally. Hence the derivative on the two columns is onto a space of dimension 2k2k. Finite-dimensional Fredholm reduction puts the nullity-kk locus in a local submanifold of codimension at least 2k≥42k\ge4. This is enough for generic paths to avoid it; no maximal-codimension claim for all kernel strata is needed.

At nullity one, second normal derivatives of (A,F)(A,F) can be varied while their values and first derivatives remain fixed along the scalar curve. A nonzero kernel has a nonzero scalar normal component qq; an adjoint generator η\eta is nonzero on an overlapping disk. A real quadratic fiber map on a fixed nonzero vector has arbitrary output. Thus vanishing of this coefficient imposes one further independent equation. Parametric transversality gives a smooth one-dimensional moduli over the path, with only Morse critical points of its projection: locally t−t0=±x2t-t_0=\pm x^2. Every slice is therefore locally discrete.

The two-point evaluation conditions are transverse with these same restricted parameters. Parameter values on projected injective disks away from the marks kill the adjoint section there; adjoint unique continuation kills it on the punctured domain. An LqL^q section supported at finitely many points is zero. Varying normal values and marked-point positions then kills the point covectors. For distinct curves, disjoint projected disks kill the adjoint sections separately. The same argument works against the fixed core: the other curve has projected injective disks off that core. For applying parametric transversality with moving marks, use sufficiently high Wk,pW^{k,p} and CℓC^\ell charts, with k≥3k\ge3 and ℓ\ell large, so that variable-point evaluation has the required differentiability. The low-regularity surjectivity just proved implies surjectivity there: a finite collection of smooth parameter variations spans the finite-dimensional augmented cokernel, and elliptic regularity upgrades solutions with Wk−1,pW^{k-1,p} right-hand side to Wk,pW^{k,p}. No differentiability of moving evaluation on W1,pW^{1,p} is assumed. The expected dimension of a collision locus in a path is 1+4−6=−11+4-6=-1. Thus there are no self-intersections, intersections between distinct curves, or intersections with the core. Immersion was already known, so there is no unstated critical-point transversality requirement.

These tests apply in countably many Fredholm charts. Each uses perturbations supported off the core and away from endpoint collars; the prescribed jets in (7) do not restrict them. Relative Sard–Smale and a countable smooth local perturbation argument give the asserted path. The critical points of a Morse function on a second-countable one-manifold form a countable set; their values therefore have dense complement. At those parameters every noncore simple curve is regular, and the core is always regular. This proves the final assertion. ▫\square

The scalar zero and unique-continuation inputs are the usual similarity principle; see Wendl, Lectures on Symplectic Field Theory, Theorem 2.5.3. The relevant Fredholm, evaluation, and parametric-transversality framework is described in Wendl, Lectures on Holomorphic Curves, Chapter 4. For the low-to-high Sobolev regularity step, see also Lemma 9.2.9 of the cited SFT lectures. The first-column and second-jet tests above verify the restricted parameter freedom instead of importing genericity from the full ambient almost-complex space. Further detail is recorded in the transversality investigation.

4. Localized cluster transport at degree two

The preceding lemma supplies the local version of DIW Definition 3.13 in VV at energy cutoff Λ\Lambda. We spell out the localization of their Proposition 3.30, so that curves outside VV and arbitrary coupled perturbations do not silently enter the genus estimate.

At each parameter choose Hausdorff neighborhoods of the core whose closures consist of compact sets in a smaller tube V′⋐VV'\Subset V. Every connected cycle in them of degree at most two is a multiplicity-one embedded curve or twice a degree-one curve. Two distinct degree-one components cannot form a connected support, by disjointness. The embedded support spaces of fixed degree are discrete, by the lemma and DIW Propositions 2.21 and 2.24. They are countable. Apply bounded-energy cycle compactness, DIW Theorem 2.11, to all connected cycles supported in a small closed Hausdorff ball, including doubled degree-one curves. Their distances from CC form a countable compact set of radii, including radius zero. Its complement contains arbitrarily small radii with no cycle support on the boundary, as in their Proposition 3.17. All limiting cycles under consideration remain in VV. In particular a sequence of degree-two curves tending to 2C2C has not been omitted from the compact set. No genericity outside VV is used.

Invertibility of the core operator makes CC the unique degree-one support in such a sufficiently small neighborhood. DIW Proposition 3.10 transports its compact open-and-closed cycle insertion over a short interval. The parametrized implicit function theorem retains uniqueness in degree one after shortening the interval. Finitely many intervals cover the path.

On every overlap choose a regular slice from the dense set in the lemma. Refine the two cluster neighborhoods to a common smaller one, as in DIW Proposition 3.19. The difference of the selected cycle sets is compact and open and closed; it contains no degree-one support or double of such a support. Its connected cycles are therefore simple degree-two supports. They form a compact discrete set, hence a finite set. Their cores are regular on the chosen slice. Every one is an actual triangular curve in VV, so its genus is three or four by (6).

Adding the refinement differences along the finite interval cover expresses the difference between the two complete connected local series as a finite signed sum of these degree-two cluster series. Each correction core is primitive at this cutoff: its proper multiples have degree at least four. Its contribution is therefore its sign times Gh(q2,t)G_h(q^2,t) modulo q3q^3. To apply the degree-one base case of DIW Proposition 3.54 with its global genericity hypothesis, first transport a sufficiently small isolating insertion around this regular core to a nearby globally generic ambient structure. DIW Propositions 3.20–3.21 preserve the insertion; the implicit function theorem and openness of the embedded multiplicity-one locus preserve its unique core, genus, and sign. One may also choose this perturbation fixing the core, as in the proof of Proposition 3.54. The primitive base case then applies. This final deformation may leave the triangular class, since all its further proper-multiple corrections are above the cutoff and the genus of the already selected core is fixed.

This argument uses complete support insertions, not only maps with smooth domains. All contracted components and stable-map boundaries over each support remain included. In particular the degree-one part of GhG_h is s(t)2h−2s(t)^{2h-2} and has arbitrarily high source-genus terms. Bounding the genus of the correction core does not remove these terms.

Consequently the endpoint difference has the form

𝖫a,b−𝖫b,b=c3G3(q2,t)+c4G4(q2,t)(mod⁡q3),\mathsf L_{a,b}-\mathsf L_{b,b} =c_3G_3(q^2,t)+c_4G_4(q^2,t)\pmod{q^3}, \tag{9}

The exact check code/all_genus_double_covers.py independently expands the sine products and the cosine expression, compares the previously computed source genera three through five, and performs triangular exponent extraction through genus twenty-four. It checks the formal arithmetic, not the analytic or cluster proof.

The result establishes the degree-two part of the proposed self-conjugate-partition formula for distinct even spins in base genus two. It does not prove that formula in degrees three and higher. The automatic immersion and scalar-image classification used in Section 3 are specific to the present low degree and base genus. Extending the transversality argument beyond this range requires controlling critical points of the scalar projection.

Nor does (9) assign a correction to each singular parameter of the original split linear path. It obtains a finite cluster comparison through a nonlinear triangular path. The precise individual-wall law, general source/base genera, arbitrary multiplicity, and the assembled ten-objective programme remain open.

5. Prime-degree cluster transport

Fix a prime pp and apply the preceding construction with M=pM=p. We use the cycle compactness and cluster results of Doan–Ionel–Walpuski, abbreviated DIW. Only their localization to curves whose supports lie in VV is needed. The argument is the one of Calculation A2, with the following degree filtering made explicit.

At a fixed parameter, all simple local supports through the cutoff are embedded and pairwise disjoint, and their spaces are discrete and countable. Hence all cycles through this cutoff are countable: they are finite sums with positive integral multiplicities. Choose small closed Hausdorff balls about CC whose compact sets lie in V′⋐VV'\Subset V. The cycle space in such a ball is compact by DIW Theorem 2.11. The set of its distances from CC is a countable compact set; it includes every multiple of CC at radius zero. Choose arbitrarily small radii outside it. This selects compact open-and-closed cycle insertions without ignoring disconnected cycles or multiple supports.

Invertibility makes the core the unique degree-one support in a sufficiently small ball. Restrict each boundary-free insertion to DIW’s connected-cycle space. It is relatively open and closed there, so Proposition 3.10 transports its connected Gromov–Witten contribution over a short interval. The stronger all-cycle boundary exclusion also follows from the same properness argument. The parametrized implicit function theorem preserves uniqueness in degree one after shortening the interval. Cover the path by finitely many intervals. At each overlap select a slice from the dense set where all simple curves are regular, and refine the two neighborhoods to a common smaller one, as in DIW Proposition 3.19. The refinement differences are compact and open and closed in the selected cycle spaces. They contain no degree-one support and no multiple of such a support.

Now retain connected degree-pp cycles in a refinement difference. Connectedness is closed under Hausdorff convergence of nonempty compact sets, so this is a compact subset; degree is fixed by the integral class. Disjointness of the embedded supports means any such cycle is rDrD for one support DD. Its projection degree satisfies rdeg⁡(D)=pr\deg(D)=p. Since degree one is excluded, primality gives r=1r=1 and deg⁡(D)=p\deg(D)=p. Thus this compact subset consists of simple degree-pp supports. DIW Propositions 2.21 and 2.24 identify their cycle topology with the embedded-curve topology. It is discrete and therefore finite. Every selected core is an actual triangular curve, so its genus lies in [Hp,Gp][H_p,G_p] by (6).

Each such core is primitive relative to the degree-pp coefficient. Transport a sufficiently small insertion around the regular core to a nearby globally generic ambient almost complex structure, using DIW Propositions 3.20–3.21. The implicit function theorem and openness of the embedded multiplicity-one locus preserve its core genus and sign. The primitive case of DIW Proposition 3.54 then gives its complete degree-pp contribution

σD(2sin⁡(t/2))2h(D)−2.\sigma_D(2\sin(t/2))^{2h(D)-2}. \tag{10}

This final deformation may leave the triangular class: the genus of the selected core is already fixed and any proper multiple of it has degree at least 2p2p. Connected stable maps always have connected image support. They therefore contribute only on the connected subset just considered; no assumption that connectedness is an open condition is needed. The compact clopen insertions are the objects transported, before restricting to connected maps and the coefficient of qpq^p. All stable maps over each selected support, including their contracted components, are retained in (10). The same finite set of supports works coefficientwise for every source genus.

The equal-spin endpoint has elementary series Gg(q,t)G_g(q,t) and only its degree-one elementary factor. The triangular identification in Article III, Proposition 3.1 and Corollary 3.2 therefore gives cp,h=np,hc_{p,h}=n_{p,h}, proving (1). This uses the fixed-target identification of universal exponents; it introduces no numerical evaluation on arbitrary analytic families. Composite degrees below pp do not enter this coefficient.

A4. A zero bound for double covers and real line operators

This calculation concerns reduced graphs on split real lines. A1 proves the extension to every covering degree.

1. Statement

2. A short proof of the inequality upstairs

The scalar similarity principle implies that a nonzero solution of a real Cauchy–Riemann equation on a complex line has isolated zeros of positive integer order. Their total order is the degree of the line bundle: this is the usual winding-number description of its first Chern class. Applied on (Y), the total is [ f^*L=2d. ] Every ramification point is fixed by (), so oddness forces (u=0) there. There are (2r) such points. Therefore (2r2d).

This proof already establishes the genus bound without dividing by the ramification coordinate. In a local coordinate (w) centered at a ramification point, smoothness and the similarity principle give [ u(w)=a wk+o(|w|k),a. ] The equality (u(-w)=-u(w)) makes (k) odd. Zeros away from ramification occur in deck pairs with equal orders. Subtracting one zero at each ramification point, then dividing the remaining total by two, gives (d-r). The next section shows that these are exactly the zeros of a well-defined weak section downstairs.

The analytic input used here, and below, is the author-written source Wendl, Lectures on Symplectic Field Theory, Section 2.5, Theorem 2.5.3, printed pp. 52–53. Its hypothesis allows a zeroth-order coefficient in (L^p), (p>2), and a weak (W^{1,p}) solution. It supplies a continuous invertible complex change of frame taking the solution to a holomorphic function. The local regularity step below is Lemma 2.4.7, printed p. 41: an (L^1) distributional solution of (v=F), with (FL^p), is locally (W^{1,p}).

At an unramified zero of (v), each of the two lifts has order (k). These statements also verify directly the count in Section 2.

4. Genus two and split normal graphs

Now suppose (g=2), (N=L_1L_2), (L_j=1), and [ D=D_1D_2 ] is any pair of smooth real line operators. The operators need not be the special spin endpoint operators. The complex-linear parts may define different holomorphic structures from those initially chosen on the two smooth lines.

For a connected smooth double cover (f:YC), let [ F=(f,u_1,u_2):YN, (D_j)_f u_j=0. ] Decompose each section into its invariant and odd parts using ((1^*)/2). Invariant kernel sections descend to smooth kernel sections on (C): they are bounded near a branch point, solve the base equation off it, and the same distributional removal and elliptic regularity argument applies.

If both odd parts vanish, (F) factors through (f) and a degree-one graph. It is then not a simple degree-two graph. If some odd part is nonzero, the proposition gives (r=0) or (1).

One pair of branch points

If (r=1), choose a nonzero odd component. Its descended section has degree zero and no zeros. It separates the two sheets everywhere off the branch divisor. At each branch point its upstairs expression is (a w+O(|w|^3)), with (a), so the vertical derivative of the graph is nonzero there. The invariant part has zero derivative in the (w)-coordinate at that point. Away from branch points, the base derivative is already nonzero.

It follows that (F) is an injective immersion, hence an embedding, and its domain has genus [ g(Y)=4. ]

An étale double cover

If (r=0), (F) is an immersion because (df) never vanishes. Choose a nonzero odd component. Its descended section has degree one, hence exactly one simple zero. A pair of sheets can coincide under (F) only over this point; coincidence also requires the other odd component to vanish there.

At a zero of a solution of a smooth scalar real Cauchy–Riemann equation, the equation gives (v=0) at that point. A simple zero therefore has a nonzero complex-linear derivative. The difference of the two local graph sections has this nonzero derivative in the chosen component. Thus, if a sheet collision occurs, the two image branches have distinct tangent lines.

The normalization has genus (3). There is at most one ordinary double point in this parametrized sense. Identifying the two preimages of such a collision produces a nodal complex source of arithmetic genus (4); if there is no collision, the image is a smooth embedded genus-three curve. This description does not invoke an algebraic scheme structure on an almost-complex image.

Two degree-one components

For completeness, consider two distinct kernel graphs over (C). Their difference is a section in the kernel of (D_1D_2). Some component is nonzero and, by the ordinary scalar zero theorem, has exactly one simple zero. The two graphs therefore meet at most once, with distinct tangent lines if they meet.

A connected reduced union must have that one intersection. Its nodal source has two genus-two components and one node, hence arithmetic genus (4).

Consequently every reduced connected degree-two nodal curve in this exact split linear graph model, with no contracted components and whose parametrization is generically one-to-one onto its image, has arithmetic genus at most four. For an irreducible curve its smooth normalization is covered by the two cases above. For a reducible curve, the only degree partition is (1+1), covered by the last case.

A5. Split double-cover bounds and the all-genus wall comparison

Let CC have genus g≥2g\ge2, and let N=L1⊕L2N=L_1\oplus L_2 with deg⁡Lj=g−1\deg L_j=g-1. Write D=D1⊕D2D=D_1\oplus D_2 for a real normal Cauchy–Riemann operator. At a super-rigid endpoint, distinguish:

  1. L2,k(D)L_{2,k}(D), the absolute Euler number on the compactified connected stable-map space of degree two and source genus kk.
  2. n2,h(D)n_{2,h}(D), the elementary-factor exponent, recovered from all these Euler numbers by the triangular rule in Article III, Proposition 3.1.
  3. w2,h(D)w_{2,h}(D), Bai–Swaminathan’s linear double-wall invariant.

These have different definitions. In particular, “absence of smooth genus-hh kernels” is not a statement about the compactified Euler number in source genus hh.

The primary-source versions checked were Bai–Swaminathan, arXiv:2106.01206v4 and Doan–Ionel–Walpuski, arXiv:2103.08221v2, the latest versions displayed by arXiv on the investigation date. The former defines ww using generic paths (Definitions 5.14 and 5.17), and constructs a global degree-two invariant (Theorem 1.6). Its identification with elementary-cluster coefficients is explicitly Conjecture 1.10, proved there only in source genus zero (Theorem 6.12). Theorem 6.7 treats a finite smooth-domain degeneracy locus under Definition 6.5. The discussion following Theorem 1.11 identifies removal of these restrictions as the obstacle to the general comparison.

Doan–Ionel–Walpuski Theorem 3.25 gives cluster transport with corrections in proper multiples. Propositions 3.48 and 3.54 give integral elementary coefficients with finite genus support; they do not give the bound four here. Their proof uses generic almost-complex paths, without preserving a normal splitting or a holomorphic projection. These are the numerical inputs used in the proof of Article III, Proposition 3.1.

dim⁡ℝker⁡f*D0=1.\dim_{\mathbb R}\ker f^*D_0=1.

ind⁡ℝ(f*Dj,0)=2(2(g−1)+1−h)=−2r.\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}(f^*D_{j,0}) =2\bigl(2(g-1)+1-h\bigr)=-2r.

dim⁡coker⁡f*D1,0=1+2r,dim⁡coker⁡f*D2,0=2r.\dim\operatorname{coker}f^*D_{1,0}=1+2r, \qquad \dim\operatorname{coker}f^*D_{2,0}=2r. \tag{1}

The base operator is invertible, so the reduced kernel and cokernel agree with the unreduced spaces in this calculation. A deformation of ff and of the split path gives a family of operators still preserving the two pulled-back lines. Extend a kernel generator in the first line. Applying the family of operators, differentiating, and projecting to cokernels produces no component in the second cokernel. The same conclusion is independent of choices of extension and trivialization, since their changes lie in the image of the central operator.

The map required by the simple-wall hypothesis is

Tfℳh(C,2)⊕ℝ→Hom⁡ℝ(ker⁡f*D0,coker⁡f*D0).T_f\mathcal M_h(C,2)\oplus\mathbb R \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R} (\ker f^*D_0,\operatorname{coker}f^*D_0). \tag{2}

Both sides have real dimension 4r+14r+1: the smooth double-cover locus has 2r2r complex branch parameters. But the image of (2) lies in the first cokernel block, of dimension 2r+12r+1. The other block has the strictly positive dimension 2r2r, proving the assertion. The argument also applies if the complex structure of the base varies, because that variation still preserves the direct sum. ▫\square

For g=2g=2 and h=4h=4, the source and target of (2) each have dimension five, while its image has dimension at most three. Thus the first branched wall already fails the published simple-wall hypothesis. If both lines have nonzero kernels, the total kernel has dimension at least two and the simple-wall hypothesis fails earlier.

This does not prove that the split degeneracy locus has its naively expected dimension: additional constraints can make it more singular. It proves the failure of the required linear surjectivity without a dimension heuristic. Off-diagonal operator variations are exactly the directions that can supply the missing block. They leave the setting in which the scalar zero count was proved.

3. Étale crossings and the reference operator

A split étale wall is not an embedded double graph

Suppose now g=2g=2, f:Y→Cf:Y\to C is connected étale of degree two, D=D1⊕D2D=D_1\oplus D_2 is base-invertible, and ker⁡f*D\ker f^*D has real dimension one. Again the kernel lies in one line. Its generator uu is odd: the invariant part descends to a base kernel, which is zero. If α\alpha is the flat sign line of ff, the section uu descends to a solution on Lj⊗αL_j\otimes\alpha, a complex line of degree one. The scalar similarity principle gives exactly one simple zero downstairs.

At the two points of YY over that zero, the graph y↦(f(y),u(y),0)y\mapsto(f(y),u(y),0) has the same image. It is therefore not injective. The simple zero gives distinct tangent lines, so this is the one-double-point case of the line-operator note. The failure is not fixed by demanding that the path be transverse within the split locus.

The exclusion of nonembedded kernel graphs in Bai–Swaminathan’s Definition 5.14, via Definition 5.10, is thus a genuine restriction in this problem. The all-genus kernel-free statement for smooth covers of genus at least five does not put the entire split path into their admissible path space.

h0(C,L2)−h0(C,KC⊗L−2)=g−1>0.h^0(C,L^2)-h^0(C,K_C\otimes L^{-2})=g-1>0.

Choose 0≠s∈H0(C,L2)0\ne s\in H^0(C,L^2) and form the finite spectral curve w2=sw^2=s in LL. Normalize it. If the normalization is connected, its projection is a connected smooth degree-two cover, and the tautological section ww pulls back to a nonzero holomorphic section of f*Lf^*L. The tautological coordinate on either component gives a global square root of ss, hence a nonzero section of LL. ▫\square

For a complex-linear operator on L1⊕L2L_1\oplus L_2 preserving the splitting, the proposition supplies a base or double-cover kernel. Hence the complex-linear double-cover-rigid reference used to normalize ww cannot be chosen in this balanced split locus. Replacing it by the equal-spin real elementary operator is possible as a reference for the local factorization, but requires a comparison of the resulting normalization; it is not Bai–Swaminathan’s defining reference.

4. Contracted components and exact linear transport

There are two different compactness issues.

First, let f:Y→Cf:Y\to C have a nonzero kernel section uu at a wall. Attach a smooth contracted curve TT of genus a≥1a\ge1 at a point p∈Yp\in Y, mapping it constantly to f(p)f(p). Extend uu over TT by the constant value u(p)u(p). On a contracted component the pullback operator is the usual Dolbeault operator with constant vector-space coefficients, so the extension is a kernel section of the nodal map. The source genus is now g(Y)+ag(Y)+a. Varying the attachment and the marked curve TT gives a positive-dimensional degeneracy locus.

Thus a single low-genus wall is simultaneously a non-simple wall in arbitrarily high source genera. This is an actual construction of nodal kernel strata, not just the possibility that ghosts might occur. It does not assert that these strata contribute nonzero Euler numbers or are limits of smooth kernel maps. Their contribution is precisely what an all-genus comparison must compute or cancel.

Second, at a kernel of an exact linear graph equation, every real multiple λu\lambda u is a solution. For an odd nonzero section these give nonconstant degree-two graph curves tending to the zero section. For any disk tube of radius ρ>0\rho>0, scaling to |λ|∥u∥∞=ρ|\lambda|\|u\|_\infty=\rho gives a curve contained in the closed tube and meeting its boundary. Therefore one cannot transport the isolated point insertion 2[C]2[C] through this wall using the boundary-free tubes employed at super-rigid endpoints in Article III, Proposition 15.4.

A nonlinear perturbation or another compact local problem is needed at the wall. Calculation A1 proves the zero estimate for smooth nonlinear equations with independent line coordinates. It does not prove spatial isolation or transversality for such a perturbation, nor does it cover coupling between the coordinates. The required virtual boundary contribution therefore remains to be determined.

The published exclusion of ghosts in limits of embedded curves along a generic path (Bai–Swaminathan Theorem 1.8) does not remove either issue: the split path above violates the genericity conditions, and the compactified Euler integral includes ghost strata independently of whether they are limits of embedded curves in that generic family.

A6. Triangular graph equations and degree-two cluster transport

Conclusion. Once a triangular path has the local isolation properties below, no new all-genus wall formula is needed to obtain the degree-two cutoff. A localized form of DIW Proposition 3.30 gives finitely many correction cores of degree two. Each such core is primitive at this cutoff, so its entire contribution, including contracted components, is its signed elementary series. In genus two the support estimate bounds their genera by four. For distinct even spin endpoints the degree-one core can remain unobstructed throughout the path, avoiding the two-parameter argument of DIW Proposition 3.37.

The substantive outstanding hypothesis is a genericity theorem for actual simple triangular curves, including embeddedness and discreteness at every parameter. Surjectivity for a smooth-cover linear wall alone does not establish this hypothesis. A single tube isolating the entire path is unnecessary for the argument below.

1. The geometric setting

Let CC have genus g≥2g\geq2, let N=L1⊕L2N=L_1\oplus L_2 with deg⁡Lj=g−1\deg L_j=g-1, and consider graph equations

∂‾f*L1u1+f*At(u1)=0,f*D2u2+f*Ft(u1)=0.\bar\partial_{f^*L_1}u_1+f^*A_t(u_1)=0, \qquad f^*D_2u_2+f^*F_t(u_1)=0. \tag{1}

Here AtA_t and FtF_t are smooth fiberwise maps with values in the appropriate (0,1)(0,1)-form bundles; At(0)=Ft(0)=0A_t(0)=F_t(0)=0; and D2D_2 is a fixed positive-mass spin operator. Pullback includes the differential of ff on the form factor. Thus the zero section remains holomorphic. All compact curves have nonconstant projection: a curve lying in an affine fiber is constant because the vertical complex structure is the standard one.

There is a useful strengthening of the support argument in Calculation A1. On a component of the normalized off-diagonal fiber product, write vjv_j for the difference of the two jj-th coordinates. If v1v_1 vanishes identically, then v2v_2 solves the pullback homogeneous equation for D2D_2. Spin super-rigidity forces v2=0v_2=0. For a reduced simple graph this is impossible. Therefore v1v_1 is nonzero on every off-diagonal component. Its scalar difference equation supplies the complete zero count without changing coordinates from component to component:

R(f)+2b≤m(m−1)(g−1),pa≤1+m(m+1)2(g−1).R(f)+2b\leq m(m-1)(g-1),\qquad p_a\leq1+\frac{m(m+1)}2(g-1). \tag{2}

In particular, the projection of a simple full graph to Tot⁡(L1)\operatorname{Tot}(L_1) is also simple. In degree two every embedded full graph has genus at most 3g−23g-2; the bound is four when g=2g=2. The first-coordinate image need not be embedded. The second coordinate can separate its isolated double points.

Use the compact realization in the proof of Article III, Proposition 3.1: a compact smooth family fixing the zero section is realized on one common tube VV in a closed symplectic six-manifold, with a common tame form and a primitive core class A=[C]A=[C]. All the graph structures have the same value along CC, so compactness of the parameter interval gives one tube for the cutoff construction. The six-torus realization makes c1=0c_1=0 and retains the positive integral degree label.

Choose a=∫Cωa=\int_C\omega and 2a≤Λ<3a2a\leq\Lambda<3a. Every curve contained in VV and of energy at most Λ\Lambda has degree one or two. In this note “degree two” always refers to the projection/homology label, not to the multiplicity of the underlying simple support.

2. The precise local hypotheses

DIW’s space 𝒥isol\mathcal J_\mathrm{isol} is defined by four conditions: nonnegative index for simple curves, embeddedness of index-zero simple curves, disjointness of distinct such images, and discreteness of their moduli at a fixed structure. Their 𝒥*\mathcal J_* replaces discreteness by unobstructedness. Proposition 3.30 requires the core path to be unobstructed and the path to lie in 𝒥isol\mathcal J_\mathrm{isol}; it does not require every simple curve along the path to be unobstructed. These are DIW, Definition 3.13 and Proposition 3.30.

The following localized hypotheses suffice here. They concern every curve contained in VV, and not only graphs arbitrarily close to zero.

  1. The normal operator of CC is invertible for every tt.
  2. At every tt, all simple curves in VV of degree one or two are embedded, and the moduli of each such degree is discrete in the Gromov topology.
  3. Distinct degree-one supports in VV are disjoint. It is sufficient, and convenient for genericity, to require all distinct supports of degree at most two to be disjoint. Only pairs whose degrees sum to at most two enter the present connected-cycle argument.
  4. A dense set of parameter values has all these simple curves unobstructed. Equivalently for this argument, every nonempty overlap of the finitely many parameter intervals chosen below contains a slice on which its correction cores are unobstructed.

The index requirement is automatic locally: every class is mAmA and c1(A)=0c_1(A)=0, so the unmarked simple-map index in dimension six is zero. The hypotheses allow ordinary folds of degree-two curves. They do not allow a positive-dimensional family of simple degree-two curves on a fixed slice. An exact linear kernel equation therefore fails condition 2 because nonzero solutions can be scaled.

Embeddedness alone is insufficient; regularity on a dense set alone is also insufficient. The all-parameter discreteness condition is what permits the cluster neighborhoods at the singular parameters. A statement that a path is “generic in degree two” must explicitly imply these conditions or prove a substitute for them.

3. Local degree-two simple isotopy

Proposition. Suppose a path as in (1) has a common compact tame realization and satisfies conditions 1–4. Assume its endpoint germs are super-rigid and contain only the zero-section support in a smaller tube. Let 𝖫0(q,t)\mathsf L_0(q,t) and 𝖫1(q,t)\mathsf L_1(q,t) be their connected local Gromov–Witten series. There are finitely many embedded triangular curves CiC_i, of degree two and genera hi≤3g−2h_i\leq3g-2, and integers cic_i, such that

𝖫1(q,t)−𝖫0(q,t)=∑iciGhi(q2,t)(mod⁡q3).\mathsf L_1(q,t)-\mathsf L_0(q,t) =\sum_i c_iG_{h_i}(q^2,t)\pmod{q^3}. \tag{3}

Here GhG_h is the connected elementary series of DIW Definition 3.45. There is no sign change multiplying the first endpoint series: the core is unobstructed throughout.

Proof. The proof of DIW Proposition 3.30 localizes to these hypotheses as follows.

First choose every Hausdorff neighborhood of CC so small that its closure consists of compact subsets of a smaller tube V′⋐VV'\Subset V. Bounded-energy cycle compactness takes place in the closed ambient manifold. Any limiting cycle belonging to one of these closures is still contained in VV, so its local degree, index, embeddedness and discreteness are controlled. Nothing is assumed about curves elsewhere in the closed manifold.

At a fixed tt, each connected cycle in these neighborhoods is either a multiplicity-one embedded curve of degree one or two, or twice an embedded degree-one curve. A connected sum of two distinct degree-one supports is excluded by disjointness. The support spaces of embedded curves of fixed degree are discrete: use discreteness in the Gromov topology together with DIW Propositions 2.21 and 2.24, which identify the relevant embedded-curve, cycle and support topologies.

The argument of DIW Proposition 3.17 now gives arbitrarily small Hausdorff radii with no cycle on the boundary. The exceptional radii are a countable compact set, obtained from bounded-energy cycle compactness and the discrete support spaces. Invertibility of the degree-one core makes CC the unique nearby degree-one curve. Thus the chosen neighborhoods are clusters at the fixed parameter.

DIW Proposition 3.10 makes each such neighborhood an open-and-closed cycle insertion over a short parameter interval. This step uses closedness of the boundary-cycle locus and properness of the cycle projection. It does not require regularity or genericity of curves outside VV. The parametrized implicit function theorem keeps CC as the unique degree-one support in the neighborhood along that short interval. Choose finitely many such intervals covering [0,1][0,1].

At an overlap, choose a slice allowed by condition 4. Refine the two cluster neighborhoods to a common smaller one, as in DIW Proposition 3.19. The difference between a larger and smaller neighborhood is a compact open-and-closed set of cycles. It contains no degree-one support. Every remaining connected cycle is therefore a simple degree-two support. The remaining support space is both compact and discrete, hence finite. Its cores are unobstructed by the choice of slice. This is the entire finite cluster decomposition required at degree two; no higher-degree induction is involved.

The interval contributions are constant, and the refinement differences add with signs. Summing along the finite cover gives the endpoint difference as a finite signed sum of degree-two cluster contributions. All their cores are actual curves at the selected parameters, inside VV, so (2) bounds their genera.

Finally, a degree-two core is primitive relative to this energy cutoff: its proper multiples have degree at least four. Its cluster contribution is its signed Ghi(q2,t)G_{h_i}(q^2,t) modulo q3q^3. One may use the degree-one case of the elementary comparison, or the base case of DIW Proposition 3.54. The latter deformation may leave the triangular class: every additional correction lies above the cutoff, and the genus hih_i of the existing core is fixed. This proves (3). ▫\square

This is a localization of the published proof, not a claim that DIW state the localized proposition verbatim. Its precise source chain is Theorem 2.11; Propositions 2.21 and 2.24; Lemma 3.8; Propositions 3.10, 3.17, 3.19 and 3.30; and the degree-one base case of Proposition 3.54. The proof above replaces the global cluster decomposition by the compact-discrete degree-two argument. It shows why no uncontrolled perturbation is used when selecting the genera hih_i.

4. Ghosts and the universal exponents

The proposition is an identity of complete connected generating series, not a comparison of smooth-domain Euler numbers. The cycle insertion pulls back along the stable-map-to-cycle map. Therefore it includes every contracted component and every stable-map boundary stratum over the selected support. Contracted components do not create new supports and cannot move a stable map between two open-and-closed support insertions.

For example, the coefficient of qq in the elementary connected series is

[q]Gh(q,t)=(2sin⁡(t/2))2h−2.[q]G_h(q,t)=(2\sin(t/2))^{2h-2}. \tag{4}

It generally has infinitely many source-genus coefficients. Thus bounding the genera hih_i in (3) does not discard higher-genus maps to the degree-two correction cores. Their complete contributions are already present in (4). No assertion of a genus bound on all stable maps is made.

For the endpoint germs, use the existing identification in Article III, Proposition 3.1, between the universal elementary exponents and the coefficients of their connected numerical elementary expansion. Equation (3), uniqueness of that expansion, and constancy of the degree-one core sign imply

n2,h(D1)=n2,h(D0)(h>3g−2).n_{2,h}(D_1)=n_{2,h}(D_0) \quad (h>3g-2). \tag{5}

Equivalently, their balanced lifts satisfy

P̃1P̃0−1=∏h≤3g−2Fh(q2)ch(mod⁡q3).\widetilde P_1\widetilde P_0^{-1} =\prod_{h\leq3g-2}F_h(q^2)^{c_h}\pmod{q^3}. \tag{6}

The passage to (6) uses the already established endpoint factorization and its identification of the same integer exponents. DIW alone is a numerical theorem and does not supply a universal evaluation on arbitrary parameter families. No new such evaluation is being assumed here.

If the initial endpoint is the equal-spin elementary germ, its n2,hn_{2,h} vanish identically. For a path satisfying the proposition, (5) then gives

n2,h=0(h≥3g−1).n_{2,h}=0\qquad(h\geq3g-1). \tag{7}

In genus two this is the desired n2,h=0n_{2,h}=0 for h≥5h\geq5. It remains conditional on constructing the path with conditions 1–4. The conclusion is stronger than the smooth-cover linear wall comparison and does not identify individual wall contributions.

5. An unobstructed core path for the genus-two even-spin endpoints

Let a,ba,b be distinct even theta characteristics on a genus-two curve. They have H0(a)=H0(b)=0H^0(a)=H^0(b)=0: a line of degree one has at most one independent section, whereas even parity forces the dimension to be even. Fix Db=∂‾b+RbD_b=\bar\partial_b+R_b in the second coordinate. On the first underlying smooth line, join DaD_a to an identified copy of DbD_b as follows.

First lower the mass in ∂‾a+sRa\bar\partial_a+sR_a from one to zero. The spin norm identity gives injectivity for s>0s>0, and H0(a)=0H^0(a)=0 gives it at s=0s=0. The real index is zero, so these operators are invertible. Next join the holomorphic line aa to bb inside Pic⁡g−1(C)\Θ\operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}(C)\setminus\Theta, where Θ\Theta is the effective theta divisor. This complement is path connected: the divisor has real codimension two in the connected complex torus and can be avoided by a perturbation of a path. Choose smooth representatives of the resulting Dolbeault operators on the fixed smooth line bundle. Every operator on this segment has zero kernel and index zero. Finally raise the spin mass on bb from zero to one.

The resulting base path is invertible. Arbitrary lower off-diagonal terms preserve base invertibility because the two diagonal base operators are invertible. Small constrained perturbations of the first diagonal term also preserve it. Therefore the ordinary core wall of DIW Proposition 3.37 can be avoided in this even-spin case. There is no need to establish a two-parameter triangular unfolding of that wall before using Proposition 3.30.

This argument uses nonspecial spin endpoints. In higher genus an even theta characteristic can have nonzero even-dimensional section space, so the mass-to-zero segment needs separate attention. For opposite base signs an everywhere invertible base path is impossible.

6. Why a global isolating tube and a projective compactification are different

Article III, Proposition 16.5, requires one compact open-and-closed insertion for the entire selected family. That is a sufficient hypothesis for equality of the endpoint products with no correction factors. It is stronger than what is needed for (3). Here the neighborhoods change along the path, and their differences produce exactly the degree-two correction factors. Linear scaling at a wall obstructs a fixed isolating disk; it does not obstruct this finite refinement argument once nonlinear perturbations give fixed-slice discreteness.

Compactifying the fibers, by itself, would not isolate an affine local contribution. In the ruled surface compactification of a positive line LL, let C0C_0 and C∞C_\infty be its zero and infinity sections and let ff be a fiber class. Then

C0=C∞+(deg⁡L)f,C∞2=−deg⁡L.C_0=C_\infty+(\deg L)f,\qquad C_\infty^2=-\deg L.

An affine class m[C0]m[C_0] can have a boundary configuration containing mC∞mC_\infty and mdeg⁡(L)m\deg(L) fiber components. Its zero intersection with the infinity divisor does not exclude this configuration: the negative self-intersection of the infinity component cancels the positive fiber intersections. Thus positivity of intersections alone cannot prove confinement. A compactification is useful as an ambient space for compactness, but its boundary configurations must not be silently identified with the original local invariant.

The small common tube in the compact realization, together with changing Hausdorff cluster neighborhoods, avoids this extra global problem. Nonlinear confinement may still be useful for a different construction, but it is not a missing hypothesis of the localized Proposition 3.30 argument.

7. Relation to the Bai–Swaminathan comparison

Bai–Swaminathan define their linear double-wall invariant separately from elementary-cluster coefficients; their general identification is Conjecture 1.10. Definition 6.5 and Theorem 6.7 impose a finite smooth-domain degeneracy locus. Attaching contracted components to a low-genus kernel violates that hypothesis in higher source genera. The proposition here does not apply their Euler wall theorem to such nodal loci. It instead uses compact support insertions and the existing elementary comparison at a primitive correction core.

There is therefore no contradiction with the unresolved general comparison in that source. The proposed result concerns a specially controlled family with an a priori support bound and an everywhere unobstructed degree-one core.

A7. Prime-degree cluster comparisons and the first composite-degree obstruction

1. Hypotheses and the invertible core path

Let CC have genus g≥2g\ge2, set c=g−1c=g-1, and fix two non-effective theta characteristics a,ba,b. Thus H0(C,a)=H0(C,b)=0H^0(C,a)=H^0(C,b)=0, and both have even parity. The case a=ba=b is elementary; the interesting case is a≠ba\ne b. Use fixed smooth lines L1,L2L_1,L_2 of degree cc, and the triangular equations

∂‾f*L1u1+f*At(u1)=0,f*Dbu2+f*Ft(u1)=0.\bar\partial_{f^*L_1}u_1+f^*A_t(u_1)=0, \qquad f^*D_bu_2+f^*F_t(u_1)=0. \tag{1}

The pullbacks include dfdf on the form factor. Require At(0)=Ft(0)=0A_t(0)=F_t(0)=0, fix the prescribed normal first jets along the zero section, and keep the positive-spin endpoints fixed in parameter collars. The fixed second operator is injective on every finite cover, including connected stable sources, by the spin/Stokes argument and matching at nodes.

The construction of an invertible first-line path in Calculation A2 works in every genus under the present non-effectivity hypothesis. Lower the spin mass on bb to zero, join bb to aa through Pic⁡g−1(C)\Θ\operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}(C)\setminus\Theta, and restore the mass. The complement is path connected, because a path in the connected complex torus can avoid the real-codimension-two theta divisor, including its lower-dimensional singular strata. All the operators have index zero and no kernel. The core sign consequently stays positive. This argument does not justify replacing non-effectivity by even parity on an arbitrary fixed curve.

Write

Hm=1+mc,Bm=1+(m+12)c.H_m=1+mc,\qquad B_m=1+\binom{m+1}{2}c. \tag{2}

The scalar-difference proof in the degree-two cluster investigation applies in every degree: if the first-coordinate difference vanished on an off-diagonal component, injectivity of the second operator would force the entire difference to vanish. For a reduced simple graph of degree mm this gives

R+2b≤m(m−1)c,Hm≤h≤BmR+2b\le m(m-1)c,\qquad H_m\le h\le B_m \tag{3}

for a smooth embedded support of genus hh. Here RR is the ramification degree and bb counts nodes when a reduced nodal support is considered. The upper bound concerns support genus, not source genera of maps with contracted components.

For a chosen cutoff MM, assume a common compact tame realization and the following properties for all actual simple curves contained in the chosen tube and of degrees at most MM:

  1. Every such curve is embedded, and each fixed-parameter moduli space is discrete in the Gromov topology.
  2. Distinct such supports are disjoint. It suffices to impose this on pairs whose degrees sum to at most MM.
  3. There is a dense set of parameter values on which all these curves are unobstructed.
  4. The zero-section operator is invertible throughout, and the fixed endpoint germs contain only the zero-section support.

These are localized versions of the cluster isolation hypotheses, not merely surjectivity at smooth-cover linear walls. Proving them in the restricted class (1), with the fixed core jets and endpoint collars, is the separate projected-jet problem. A common tube isolating the whole path is not assumed.

2. The degree-three comparison

Let 𝖫a,b\mathsf L_{a,b} and 𝖫b,b\mathsf L_{b,b} be the complete connected local Gromov–Witten series at the endpoints. Let Gh(q,t)G_h(q,t) be the connected elementary series, whose degree-one coefficient is (2sin⁡(t/2))2h−2(2\sin(t/2))^{2h-2}. Assume the hypotheses of Section 1 with M=3M=3. Then there are integers cd,hc_{d,h} such that

𝖫a,b−𝖫b,b=∑h=H2B2c2,hGh(q2,t)+∑h=H3B3c3,hGh(q3,t)(mod⁡q4).\mathsf L_{a,b}-\mathsf L_{b,b} =\sum_{h=H_2}^{B_2}c_{2,h}G_h(q^2,t) +\sum_{h=H_3}^{B_3}c_{3,h}G_h(q^3,t) \pmod{q^4}. \tag{4}

Here is the localized refinement argument. Choose small Hausdorff neighborhoods around the core with closures inside the tube. Bounded-energy cycle compactness, discreteness, and countability of the embedded support spaces give arbitrarily small radii with no cycle on the boundary. The core is the unique nearby degree-one support. Compact open-and-closed cycle insertions transport over short parameter intervals, and finitely many such intervals cover the path. On each overlap choose an unobstructed slice and refine the two neighborhoods to a common smaller one.

The difference contains no degree-one support or any multiple of one. Disjointness excludes connected supports with several distinct irreducible components. A remaining connected cycle of total degree at most three is therefore a simple degree-two or degree-three curve: a multiple of a degree-two curve already has degree at least four. For each of these two degrees the difference is compact and discrete, hence finite. All selected cores are actual curves for the triangular equations, so (3) bounds their genera.

Each correction core is primitive relative to this cutoff. Its complete cluster series is its sign times Gh(qd,t)G_h(q^d,t) modulo q4q^4. For this last step the usual elementary comparison may leave the triangular class, because every further proper-multiple correction is above the cutoff. This proves (4). The compact insertion contains all contracted components and all stable-map boundaries over each support.

The primary cluster inputs are Doan–Ionel–Walpuski, Theorem 2.11, Propositions 3.10, 3.17, 3.19, 3.30, and the primitive case of Proposition 3.54. Equation (4) is our localization and degree filtering of those arguments, not a theorem stated verbatim there. Primary source

The endpoint identification of numerical elementary coefficients with the universal balanced exponents is already supplied by Article III, Proposition 3.1 and Corollary 3.2. It follows that

n2,h=0(h>3g−2),n3,h=0(h>6g−5).n_{2,h}=0\quad(h>3g-2),\qquad n_{3,h}=0\quad(h>6g-5). \tag{5}

No new evaluation on arbitrary analytic families is used. The existing calculations also give, when a≠ba\ne b,

n2,H2=−22g−1,n2,H2+1=c22g−3,n3,H3=−2(62c−22c),n3,H3+1=c6(11⋅62c−3⋅22c).\begin{aligned} n_{2,H_2}&=-2^{2g-1}, & n_{2,H_2+1}&=c\,2^{2g-3},\\ n_{3,H_3}&=-2\left(6^{2c}-2^{2c}\right), & n_{3,H_3+1}&=\frac c6\left(11\cdot6^{2c}-3\cdot2^{2c}\right). \end{aligned} \tag{6}

The cubic entries use the unramified and first-excess results of Article V, §§4–6, independently of the conditional cutoff argument. The positive sign in these formulas is the consequence of the non-effective endpoints.

3. Divisor filtering gives every prime degree

There is a stronger consequence than applying (4) only at cutoff three. Let pp be prime and assume Section 1 through degree pp. Perform the same refinement argument, but retain only the coefficient of qpq^p. On an unobstructed overlap slice, a connected degree-pp cycle has the form rDrD for one embedded support DD, since distinct supports cannot meet. If dd is the degree of DD, then rd=prd=p. The refinement difference has no degree-one support, so d=pd=p and r=1r=1.

Consequently this degree-pp difference is a compact discrete set of simple degree-pp curves, all with genera between HpH_p and BpB_p. Their contributions at this coefficient are primitive. Thus

qp=∑h=HpBpcp,h(2sin⁡(t/2))2h−2,np,h=0(h>Bp).q^p =\sum_{h=H_p}^{B_p}c_{p,h}(2\sin(t/2))^{2h-2}, \qquad n_{p,h}=0\quad(h>B_p). \tag{7}

In the elementary logarithmic expansion, only divisors of pp contribute to degree pp. The degree-one endpoint factors agree, so the coefficients in (7) are exactly np,hn_{p,h}. No unresolved degree-four comparison enters the argument for p=5p=5, for example. Conversely, (7) is not an all-degree statement: the prime-divisor argument is precisely what fails for four.

5. What changes at cutoff four

Assume now the actual-curve hypotheses through degree four. A refinement difference still has no degree-one supports, but it can contain 2D2D where DD is an embedded degree-two curve. Its cluster contribution cannot be replaced, through degree four, by its primitive term alone.

For a regular degree-two correction core DiD_i of genus hih_i, let Ki(q2,t)K_i(q^2,t) denote its full cluster contribution. Existing elementary decomposition gives a finite expansion through this cutoff of the form

Ki(q2,t)=σiGhi(q2,t)+∑rbi,rGr(q4,t)(mod⁡q5).K_i(q^2,t)=\sigma_iG_{h_i}(q^2,t) +\sum_r b_{i,r}G_r(q^4,t)\pmod{q^5}. \tag{15}

The bi,rb_{i,r} describe its own double-cover corrections. They are not the double-cover coefficients of the original split-spin core. The direct degree-four correction cores satisfy h≤B4h\le B_4, but the usual elementary comparison used to obtain (15) may create further degree-four cores outside the triangular class. The original support estimate then supplies no bound for their genera. Qualitative finiteness is already available; the explicit bound B4B_4 is what is missing.

This is also why a prime-degree conclusion does not automatically extend to all degrees by ordinary cluster induction. The general comparison does not retain the local projection data used by (3). The distinct all-genus double-wall invariant of Bai–Swaminathan is related to elementary cluster coefficients by their Conjecture 1.10; it cannot be substituted as an established comparison for these new normal operators.
