6. The inherited normal equations and an exact recursive bound

Suppose a degree-mm embedded correction u:Y→L1⊕L2u:Y\to L_1\oplus L_2 has genus hh, and its scalar projection u‾:Y→L1\bar u:Y\to L_1 is immersed. Then the normal operators have an exact sequence

0→(f*L2,f*Db)→(Nu,DuN)→(Nu‾,Q)→0.0\longrightarrow(f^*L_2,f^*D_b) \longrightarrow(N_u,D_u^N) \longrightarrow(N_{\bar u},Q)\longrightarrow0. \tag{16}

Let R=2(h−1)−2mcR=2(h-1)-2mc be the ramification degree of f:Y→Cf:Y\to C. The degrees and real indices are

degind⁡ℝf*L2mc−RNu‾2(h−1)−mcR.\begin{array}{c|cc} &\deg&\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}\\ \hline f^*L_2&mc&-R\\ N_{\bar u}&2(h-1)-mc& R. \end{array} \tag{17}

The second line degree follows from c1(TL1)[C]=−cc_1(TL_1)[C]=-c and the normal sequence of the immersed scalar curve. The first operator is injective on every cover of YY, since such a cover composes with ff to a cover of CC. For R>0R>0 it is not surjective on YY: its cokernel has real dimension RR. The lower off-diagonal coupling can pair this cokernel with the positive-index kernel of QQ to make the full operator invertible. Removing that coupling is not an innocuous simplification.

After a smooth complex splitting of (16), the homogeneous normal equation is triangular. More generally, consider a deformation of this normal equation that preserves the lower line and its injective operator, with the first equation depending only on the quotient coordinate. The same scalar-difference argument gives, for a reduced relative degree-kk graph of genus h′h',

h′−1≤k(h−1)+(k2)(2(h−1)−mc)=k2(h−1)−mk(k−1)2c.\begin{aligned} h'-1 &\le k(h-1)+\binom{k}{2}\bigl(2(h-1)-mc\bigr)\\ &=k^2(h-1)-\frac{mk(k-1)}2c. \tag{18} \end{aligned}

If h≤Bmh\le B_m, this becomes exactly

h′−1≤mk(mk+1)2c=Bmk−1.h'-1\le\frac{mk(mk+1)}2c=B_{mk}-1. \tag{19}

Thus the quadratic genus estimate is stable under repeated passage to these triangular normal models. No loss in the constant is forced by the arithmetic of the recursion. In the first composite case m=k=2m=k=2,

h′≤4h−3−2c≤1+10c=B4.h'\le4h-3-2c\le1+10c=B_4. \tag{20}

For a genus-two base, the possible degree-two cores have h=3h=3 or 44. Their induced relative-double bounds are respectively 77 and 1111. Calculation A2 proves scalar immersion for both types, so (16)–(20) have no extra projected-immersion hypothesis in this particular first composite case.

In larger degree or base genus, full embeddedness does not alone give scalar immersion. At a critical point of the scalar projection the vertical line can meet the tangent of the full curve; its map to the normal bundle can vanish, and saturation introduces a divisor. The inherited injective operator then cannot be identified with the same line operator without further analysis. Consequently projected immersion, or a substitute controlling this torsion, is an additional hypothesis for the recursive use of (18).

7. Why this recursive estimate is not yet a recursive comparison

For a ramified correction, mc<h−1mc<h-1. Its preserved line in (16) is a pullback spin line satisfying

(f*L2)2=f*KC=KY(−R),(f^*L_2)^2=f^*K_C=K_Y(-R), \tag{21}

not a theta characteristic of YY. In particular it is topologically different from either line of the standard equal-spin elementary model in genus hh.

There is a direct obstruction to ending a deformation at that standard model while keeping a complex invariant line of degree mcmc. Write the equal-spin operator as Dθ⊕DθD_\theta\oplus D_\theta on θ⊗ℂ2\theta\otimes\mathbb C^2, with the same positive mass and metric on the two copies. If a complex line subbundle EE is preserved by this operator, apply it to arbitrary complex multiples of a local generator of EE. Separating the coefficients of the multiplier and its conjugate shows that the projective line E⊗θ−1E\otimes\theta^{-1} is holomorphic and invariant under standard conjugation. It gives a holomorphic map Y→ℙ1Y\to\mathbb P^1 with image in ℝℙ1\mathbb R\mathbb P^1, hence is constant. Therefore

deg⁡E=deg⁡θ=h−1.\deg E=\deg\theta=h-1. \tag{22}

This contradicts deg⁡E=mc\deg E=mc when R>0R>0. The contradiction is invariant under complex bundle identifications. It excludes this particular endpoint while preserving the distinguished line; it does not prove that no other operator in the triangular class can have elementary contribution, nor that cancellations cannot yield the desired final bound by another method.

A useful sufficient theorem would be an elementary comparison for the normal extensions (16), with relative corrections selected inside triangular models retaining the injective lower operator and the degrees in (17), together with a suitable terminal model whose full contribution is known. Subject to projected immersion and the requisite isolation and genericity, (18)–(19) would then propagate nm,h=0n_{m,h}=0 for h>Bmh>B_m through the cluster recursion. Constructing that comparison or an alternative replacing it is genuine additional work. The standard primitive comparison and the existence of the normal sequence alone do not provide it.

A8. First derivatives of scalar projections in triangular families

Conclusion. The first derivative of the scalar projection is transverse to zero in the universal moduli space of marked, simple, noncore triangular graphs with smooth domain. This holds in arbitrary covering degree and base genus, under the parameter freedom specified below. The proof uses a local deformation of the finite covering map, local interpolation for a linear Cauchy–Riemann equation, and perturbations supported on an injective annulus. It does not require the scalar projection to be immersed beforehand.

For balanced line degrees, the marked moduli over a path has Fredholm index three. Its projected critical-point constraint has real codimension four. Consequently generic triangular paths have immersed scalar projections on all their simple noncore graphs. The result addresses the final analytic qualification in Calculation A2. It does not prove an all-degree cluster formula, a statement about stable-map boundaries, or transversality for multiple covers of the core.

1. Setting and the precise perturbation freedom

Let CC be a closed Riemann surface of genus gg, and let L1,L2L_1,L_2 be complex line bundles. Fix a real Cauchy–Riemann operator D2D_2 satisfying

ker⁡h*D2=0\ker h^*D_2=0 \tag{1}

for every nonconstant holomorphic map hh from a smooth closed connected curve to CC. Consider the equations

∂‾f=0,∂‾f*L1u1+f*A(u1)=0,f*D2u2+f*F(u1)=0.\bar\partial f=0,\qquad \bar\partial_{f^*L_1}u_1+f^*A(u_1)=0,\qquad f^*D_2u_2+f^*F(u_1)=0. \tag{2}

Here A,FA,F are smooth maps over CC, with values in Λ0,1T*C⊗L1\Lambda^{0,1}T^*C\otimes L_1 and Λ0,1T*C⊗L2\Lambda^{0,1}T^*C\otimes L_2, respectively. Pullback of each form factor uses dfdf. Write U=(f,u1,u2)U=(f,u_1,u_2) and v=(f,u1)v=(f,u_1). The first equation for u1u_1 defines an almost complex structure JAJ_A on the surface L1L_1; vv is JAJ_A-holomorphic.

Assume A(z,0)=F(z,0)=0A(z,0)=F(z,0)=0. Arbitrarily many prescribed fiber jets of A,FA,F along the zero section may be held fixed. The required parameter space must contain every smooth perturbation (Ȧ,Ḟ)(\dot A,\dot F) with compact support away from that section and inside the region where the triangular equations are valid. It is enough to contain the local perturbations constructed below. For paths, they may additionally be multiplied by a parameter bump supported in the interior of the permitted parameter interval.

Prescribing jets does not mean forbidding perturbations on a fixed open neighborhood of the entire core. The latter stronger restriction need not provide the annuli required for curves lying arbitrarily close to the core. Each perturbation used here vanishes on some neighborhood of the core, but that neighborhood may depend on the curve and the perturbation.

The domain YY is closed, connected and smooth. Its complex structure varies. The map f:Y→Cf:Y\to C has positive degree mm. We restrict to simple full graphs UU whose image is not the core. The covering map ff itself need not be simple as a holomorphic curve into CC and need not have simple ramification.

The scalar-simplicity argument in Proposition 1 of the triangular investigation applies in every degree: a simple full graph has simple scalar projection. Indeed, on a component of the normalized off-diagonal fiber product, equality of the scalar coordinates makes the second-coordinate difference a section in the kernel of a pullback of D2D_2. Equation (1) makes that difference zero, contradicting simplicity of the full graph. Thus no immersion assumption is being inserted at this point.

2. An injective annulus exists even at a cusp

Lemma 1. Let q∈Yq\in Y. For sufficiently small ρ>0\rho>0, every point of the punctured coordinate disk 0<|w|<ρ0<|w|<\rho centered at qq is a globally injective point of vv, is unramified for ff, and has u1(w)≠0u_1(w)\ne0.

Proof. A simple closed pseudoholomorphic curve is embedded away from finitely many critical points and self-intersections. Apply this to vv, and shrink the disk to remove all exceptional domain points other than possibly qq. The ramification points of the nonconstant holomorphic map ff are finite. Finally u1u_1 is nonzero and has isolated zeros: using A(z,0)=0A(z,0)=0, the integral of the fiber derivative of AA along the segment from 00 to u1u_1 rewrites its equation as a homogeneous scalar real Cauchy–Riemann equation. If u1u_1 were identically zero, (1) and the second equation would force u2=0u_2=0, contrary to the noncore assumption. Shrink the disk once more. ▫\square

The finite exceptional-set statement is Wendl, Lectures on Holomorphic Curves, Corollary 2.15.4. Its local factorization input is Theorem 2.14.7. In particular a nontrivial local covering of a branch germ would give infinitely many noninjective points and cannot occur for the simple closed map used here. A primitive cusp is allowed: its derivative may vanish at its center, while its punctured disk supplies the annulus.

For later extension of perturbations, take a compact annulus KK inside a slightly larger annulus V⋐{0<|w|<ρ}V\Subset\{0<|w|<\rho\}. Global injectivity gives

v(K)∩v(Y\V)=⌀.v(K)\cap v(Y\setminus V)=\varnothing.

Lemma 2. Let

4. Moving the covering derivative

Put

R=2h−2−m(2g−2),h=g(Y).R=2h-2-m(2g-2),\qquad h=g(Y).

For e=2e=2, this class is zero in the unmarked normal sheaf: the missing freedom is motion of the marked point, since f″(0)q̇=2q̇f''(0)\dot q=2\dot q. Thus the derivative map on the marked covering space has its expected transverse zero even at a simple branch.

The following concrete realization is useful because it keeps the ensuing forcing local. Choose χ\chi supported in a small coordinate disk and equal to one near 00. For real ss set, in the target coordinate,

fs(w)=f(w)+sαχ(w)w,f_s(w)=f(w)+s\alpha\chi(w)w, \tag{6}

and set fs=ff_s=f outside that disk. On the inner disk fsf_s is holomorphic for the original jj. On the transition annulus, dfdf is invertible, and for small ss, fsf_s is an orientation-preserving local diffeomorphism. Define

js=(dfs)−1jCdfsj_s=(df_s)^{-1}j_Cdf_s

on that annulus, and js=jj_s=j elsewhere. These definitions agree smoothly near its boundary, where fsf_s is holomorphic. Every almost complex structure on a real surface is integrable. Therefore (js,fs)(j_s,f_s) is an actual family of degree-mm holomorphic maps, unchanged off the chosen disk, with js=jj_s=j near qq and ḟw(q)=α\dot f_w(q)=\alpha.

This construction does not keep the local branching order fixed. It must not be used inside a stratum that forbids splitting higher ramification.

5. Surjectivity of the projected first derivative

Proposition 3. At any solution of (2) with simple noncore graph and a marked point qq satisfying dv(q)=0dv(q)=0, the derivative of the scalar holomorphic first derivative is surjective on the tangent space to the universal marked solution space. Its target has complex dimension two. All parameter variations used for this surjectivity preserve the prescribed core jets.

Proof. Since dv(q)=0dv(q)=0, necessarily df(q)=0df(q)=0, so use the coordinates of Section 4. Trivialize both line bundles over the corresponding target disk. In these coordinates the vertical equations have the form

∂w‾u1+a1(f,u1)fw¯=0,∂w‾u2+a2(f,u1,u2)fw¯=0,\partial_{\bar w}u_1+a_1(f,u_1)\overline{f_w}=0, \qquad \partial_{\bar w}u_2+a_2(f,u_1,u_2)\overline{f_w}=0, \tag{7}

where a2a_2 is affine real-linear in u2u_2. The reference line-bundle connection terms are included in a1,a2a_1,a_2.

Specify arbitrary α,β∈ℂ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C. Construct the compactly supported (ḟ,j̇)(\dot f,\dot j) of (6) with ḟw(q)=α\dot f_w(q)=\alpha. Choose its support inside an inner disk. Holding A,FA,F fixed for the moment, the vertical linearization is

Dvertξ+K(ḟ,j̇)=0,D^{\mathrm{vert}}\xi+K(\dot f,\dot j)=0, \tag{8}

where DvertD^{\mathrm{vert}} is a smooth rank-two real Cauchy–Riemann operator, triangular in these trivializations. The smooth forcing KK is supported in the inner disk. Lemma 2 solves (8) on a slightly larger disk with

ξ(q)=0,∂wξ1(q)=β.\xi(q)=0,\qquad \partial_w\xi_1(q)=\beta.

There is no restriction on α\alpha coming from this local equation. For example (7) determines ∂w‾ξ1(q)\partial_{\bar w}\xi_1(q) from α\alpha and the values at qq; it leaves ∂wξ1(q)\partial_w\xi_1(q) free.

Multiply ξ\xi by a second cutoff ρ\rho, equal to one on a neighborhood of the support of (ḟ,j̇)(\dot f,\dot j) and near qq, and supported in the larger disk. Extend ρξ\rho\xi by zero. The residual in (8) is precisely

r=[Dvert,ρ]ξ,r=[D^{\mathrm{vert}},\rho]\xi, \tag{9}

supported in an outer annulus where every point is globally injective for vv, where df≠0df\ne0, and where u1≠0u_1\ne0, by Lemma 1. Along this annulus prescribe

Ȧ(f(w),u1(w))=−r1(w)fw(w)¯,Ḟ(f(w),u1(w))=−r2(w)fw(w)¯.\dot A(f(w),u_1(w))=-\frac{r_1(w)}{\overline{f_w(w)}}, \qquad \dot F(f(w),u_1(w))=-\frac{r_2(w)}{\overline{f_w(w)}}. \tag{10}

The notation suppresses the chosen form and line frames. Since fwf_w does not vanish on this compact support, these are smooth data. Lemma 1 extends them to allowed parameters supported away from the core and meeting the scalar curve only on the annulus. Their pullbacks cancel (9) exactly. The resulting global variation is tangent to the universal solution space and has

(ḟw(q),u̇1,w(q))=(α,β).(\dot f_w(q),\dot u_{1,w}(q))=(\alpha,\beta). \tag{11}

At dv(q)=0dv(q)=0, variations of frames or of the target almost complex structure contribute no additional terms to the linearization of the first derivative. Near qq the chosen jsj_s is fixed. Thus (11) is exactly the required vertical derivative in any local trivialization of the complex rank-two jet bundle.

The construction was written using parametrized maps. To pass to a Hurwitz or Teichmüller slice, subtract the infinitesimal reparametrization generated by a vector field XX and transform the marked point by the same change of parametrization. The derivative contribution −d2v(q)X(q)-d^2v(q)X(q) to the map variation is canceled by d2v(q)X(q)d^2v(q)X(q) from the marked-point variation. Frame changes multiply the derivative by invertible maps and have no inhomogeneous term at its zero. Hence (11) descends to the marked quotient. This explicitly retains the marked-point freedom needed when e=2e=2. ▫\square

If u1(q)=0u_1(q)=0, no parameter is varied at that point. Its zero is isolated, and the outer annulus has positive distance from the zero section. Consequently (10) preserves even the entire formal jet of the parameters along the core. No division by u1(q)u_1(q) occurs. Likewise, higher cusp orders cause no loss: the only denominator is fwf_w on a compact annulus, not at the critical point.

6. Fredholm and regularity details

Fix a compact scalar disk bundle, fix the coefficients on a collar of its outer boundary, and restrict attention to curves whose scalar images lie in the interior of the complement of that collar. For paths, take smooth coefficients on its product with [0,1][0,1], with the prescribed core jets and fixed endpoint collars. These constraints define a closed affine subspace 𝒫∞\mathcal P^\infty of the natural C∞C^\infty Fréchet space, equipped with the seminorms of uniform convergence of all derivatives on that fixed compact domain. Thus 𝒫∞\mathcal P^\infty is a Baire space. The same statement holds if all core jets are prescribed, since this imposes a countable collection of closed linear conditions on the difference from a reference family. Any required open tameness or smallness condition is imposed within this space.

The ambient parameter space is not the union of spaces of perturbations vanishing on unspecified neighborhoods of the core. Such perturbations are only the local directions used in the surjectivity proofs; their vanishing neighborhoods may vary. General elements of 𝒫∞\mathcal P^\infty need satisfy only the stated jet and collar constraints.

The preceding tangent computation is usable because the universal solution space is smooth even before scalar immersion has been proved. Work over a smooth local chart of the finite-cover stack. At fixed ff, the vertical linearization is the elliptic operator

Dvert:W1,p(f*(L1⊕L2))→Lp(Λ0,1T*Y⊗f*(L1⊕L2)).D^{\mathrm{vert}}: W^{1,p}(f^*(L_1\oplus L_2)) \longrightarrow L^p(\Lambda^{0,1}T^*Y\otimes f^*(L_1\oplus L_2)).

An adjoint cokernel section annihilating all parameter variations vanishes on any globally injective, unbranched scalar disk off the core: arbitrary values of Ȧ,Ḟ\dot A,\dot F give both output coordinates there. Adjoint unique continuation then makes the section zero everywhere. The universal vertical equation is therefore split-surjective. A finite collection of smooth parameter variations spans the finite-dimensional cokernel of DvertD^{\mathrm{vert}}.

For derivative evaluation use Wk,pW^{k,p} charts with k≥3k\ge3, p>2p>2, and auxiliary local CℓC^\ell Banach parameter charts, with ℓ\ell sufficiently high for the required Sard–Smale differentiability. One may complete the smooth allowed directions in the CℓC^\ell norm; the perturbations proving surjectivity remain smooth and preserve every prescribed jet. The first-derivative evaluation with a moving mark is then at least continuously differentiable. Increasing kk and the coefficient regularity gives any prescribed finite differentiability. One must not treat derivative evaluation as a bounded functional on W1,pW^{1,p}.

Universal surjectivity at high regularity follows from the preceding W1,p→LpW^{1,p}\to L^p argument and elliptic regularity: use the finite smooth parameter directions spanning the cokernel, solve at low regularity, and upgrade the solution for a Wk−1,pW^{k-1,p} right-hand side. The four real directions in Proposition 3 are themselves smooth and lie in the kernel of the universal equation. Adding them proves surjectivity of the augmented equation-plus-jet map in these high-regularity charts. This avoids a distribution argument involving derivatives of point masses.

For deg⁡L1=deg⁡L2=g−1\deg L_1=\deg L_2=g-1, Riemann–Roch gives

ind⁡ℝDvert=4(1−h)+4m(g−1)=−2R.\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}D^{\mathrm{vert}} =4(1-h)+4m(g-1)=-2R. \tag{12}

The covering chart has real dimension 2R2R. The projection from the universal unmarked graph moduli to the static parameter space therefore has Fredholm index zero. Adding a path parameter and one free marked point gives index three. The complex rank-two projected derivative constraint lowers the index to

0+1+2−4=−1.0+1+2-4=-1. \tag{13}

Relative parametric transversality thus excludes scalar critical points for generic paths on the parameter interval where perturbations are allowed. A fixed endpoint collar must already have the desired property; the positive-spin collars with no noncore graphs meet this condition. Countably many covering degrees, domain genera and local Fredholm charts can be handled by countable smooth local perturbation arguments: in each chart the finite collections of smooth permitted directions above supply transversality, and the resulting open dense local conditions are intersected in 𝒫∞\mathcal P^\infty. This yields a residual subset in its natural C∞C^\infty topology, rather than merely a residual set in one finite-regularity completion. No compactness assertion follows from this countable intersection.

For comparison, the general ambient first-jet transversality theorem is Oh–Zhu, *Embedding property of JJ-holomorphic curves in Calabi–Yau manifolds for generic JJ. The construction above verifies the restricted triangular perturbation freedom directly; genericity in the full space of almost complex structures would not by itself imply this conclusion.

A9. Triangular graph equations and degree-two transversality

Conclusion. A triangular family has more perturbation freedom than the split family in the preceding investigation, while retaining its genus bound. In base genus two, this freedom suffices for the local, degree-at-most-two version of the four conditions in Doan–Ionel–Walpuski Definition 3.13. The argument uses a scalar normal line, rather than an assertion that a generic ambient perturbation preserves the triangular form. It also gives the smooth-domain double-cover transversality tests used by Bai–Swaminathan. These are local analytic assertions. Applying the cluster comparison still requires its ambient compactness and localization hypotheses and the identification of the endpoint contributions.

Throughout, all dimensions and codimensions are real. Claims of residual genericity refer to sufficiently differentiable Banach completions and then to smooth parameters by the usual countable local perturbation argument. The proofs below specify the surjectivity and finite-jet tests needed for that argument.

1. Parameter space and genus bound

Let CC be a compact Riemann surface, let L1,L2L_1,L_2 be complex line bundles of degree g(C)−1g(C)-1, and fix a real Cauchy–Riemann operator D2D_2 on L2L_2 such that

ker⁡h*D2=0\ker h^*D_2=0 \tag{1}

for every nonconstant holomorphic map hh from a smooth compact connected Riemann surface to CC. A positive-mass spin operator has this property; the spin-square/Stokes proof is recalled in Article III, Lemma 14.1. The same conclusion holds for connected stable sources: a kernel section vanishes on every positive-degree component, is constant on every contracted component, and vanishes everywhere by matching and connectedness.

Fix a complex-linear reference ∂‾L1\bar\partial_{L_1}. Consider smooth maps over CC

A:L1→Λ0,1T*C⊗L1,F:L1→Λ0,1T*C⊗L2,A:L_1\longrightarrow\Lambda^{0,1}T^*C\otimes L_1, \qquad F:L_1\longrightarrow\Lambda^{0,1}T^*C\otimes L_2,

and the graph equations

∂‾f*L1u1+f*A(u1)=0,f*D2u2+f*F(u1)=0.\bar\partial_{f^*L_1}u_1+f^*A(u_1)=0, \qquad f^*D_2u_2+f^*F(u_1)=0. \tag{2}

The form factors in A,F,D2A,F,D_2 are pulled back using dfdf. The associated almost-complex structure has holomorphic projections to CC and to the almost-complex surface L1L_1 defined by the first equation. All fibers are standard complex vector spaces. The parameters may be supported in a prescribed disk bundle; the assertions concern curves contained in the region where (2) holds.

Proposition 1. The conclusion of Calculation A1 holds for (2), with d=deg⁡L1d=\deg L_1. Moreover, every reduced simple graph in (2) has a simple projection to L1L_1; distinct full graph components have distinct scalar images.

Proof. Use the normalized off-diagonal fiber product ZZ from Calculation A1. On a connected component of ZZ, the difference v1v_1 of the first coordinates satisfies a homogeneous scalar real Cauchy–Riemann equation, by the integral formula for the fiber derivative of AA. If v1v_1 vanishes identically, the difference of the two second equations is h*D2v2=0h^*D_2v_2=0. Equation (1) gives v2=0v_2=0. This contradicts reducedness and generic injectivity of the full graph. Thus v1v_1 is nonzero on every component of ZZ. Its zero count is (deg⁡h)deg⁡L1(\deg h)\deg L_1.

The forced ramification and nodal zeros are exactly those counted in Calculation A1, so

R(f)+2b≤m(m−1)deg⁡L1,pa≤1+m(g−1)+m(m−1)2deg⁡L1.R(f)+2b\le m(m-1)\deg L_1, \qquad p_a\le1+m(g-1)+\frac{m(m-1)}2\deg L_1. \tag{3}

The same argument excludes a generic identification in the scalar projection, both within a component and between components. ▫\square

The scalar zero theorem used here is the similarity principle and its first-Chern-class consequence; see Wendl, Lectures on Symplectic Field Theory, Theorem 2.5.3. The coupling allowed in (2) is essential: arbitrary dependence of the first equation on u2u_2 does not satisfy this proof.

The special geometry in genus two

Now fix g=2g=2. For a simple degree-two graph with smooth domain, let τ\tau be the deck involution and put v1=u1−u1τv_1=u_1-u_1\tau. It is nonzero and has precisely two zeros, counted with multiplicity. Consequently:

  • A branched graph has source genus four and exactly two ramification points. These exhaust the zeros of v1v_1, both simply. Thus its scalar projection is injective, and its derivative at each ramification point is nonzero. It is an embedding.
  • An étale graph has source genus three. The zeros of v1v_1 are one exchanged pair and are simple. Its scalar projection is an immersion with exactly one transverse double point. Its full graph is embedded precisely when the two second-coordinate values at that pair differ.
  • No simple degree-two graph with smooth domain has genus at least five.

At a ramification point choose a coordinate with f(w)=w2f(w)=w^2. The equation at w=0w=0 gives ∂w‾u1(0)=0\partial_{\bar w}u_1(0)=0, and the simple zero of u1(w)−u1(−w)u_1(w)-u_1(-w) gives ∂wu1(0)≠0\partial_wu_1(0)\ne0. This proves the immersion claim without a transversality assumption. At an étale coincidence the same calculation in base coordinates gives distinct tangent lines. Degree-one graphs are sections and hence embedded.

2. Linear double-cover kernels

Suppose A(z,0)=F(z,0)=0A(z,0)=F(z,0)=0. The normal operator of the zero section has the form

T=(D10BD2),D1=∂‾L1+dfibA|0,B=dfibF|0.T=\begin{pmatrix}D_1&0\\ B&D_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_1=\bar\partial_{L_1}+d_\mathrm{fib}A|_0, \quad B=d_\mathrm{fib}F|_0. \tag{4}

Let f:Y→Cf:Y\to C be a connected smooth double cover of genus h=2g−1+rh=2g-1+r, so there are 2r2r branch points. Write Tf−T_f^- for the operator on the anti-invariant sections. Its index is −4r-4r. The invariant summand has index zero and the index of the full pullback is −4r-4r, as follows by deformation to a complex-linear operator and Riemann–Roch.

If σ=(s,v)∈ker⁡Tf−\sigma=(s,v)\in\ker T_f^- is nonzero, then s≠0s\ne0, by (1). For arbitrary first-column variations,

Ṫfσ=(f*Ȧs,f*Ḃs).\dot T_f\sigma=(f^*\dot A\,s,f^*\dot B\,s). \tag{5}

On an unbranched disk where s≠0s\ne0, the two real bundle maps Ȧ,Ḃ\dot A,\dot B can prescribe both output coordinates arbitrarily. The prescription on the other sheet is forced by oddness and is consistent with descent to the base.

Proposition 2. In the triangular operator space times the smooth double-cover space:

  1. The locus dim⁡ker⁡Tf−=1\dim\ker T_f^-=1 is a submanifold of codimension 4r+14r+1.
  2. Near a point of nullity k≥2k\ge2, the nullity-kk locus is contained in a submanifold of codimension at least 2(k+4r)2(k+4r).

Proof. At nullity one, a cokernel functional annihilating (5) is represented by an anti-invariant adjoint solution. Arbitrary local prescriptions in (5) force that solution to vanish on a disk. Unique continuation makes it zero globally. Thus the normal derivative onto Hom⁡(ker⁡Tf−,coker⁡Tf−)\operatorname{Hom}(\ker T_f^-,\operatorname{coker}T_f^-) is onto.

For the second assertion, choose any independent pair σ1,σ2\sigma_1,\sigma_2 in the kernel and write their first coordinates as s1,s2s_1,s_2. They remain linearly independent, because the second coordinate is uniquely determined by the first. They are pointwise linearly independent over ℝ\mathbb R on some disk. Indeed, if s2=as1s_2=a s_1 with real aa on an open set where s1≠0s_1\ne0, the common scalar equation gives ∂‾a=0\bar\partial a=0; hence aa is constant, and unique continuation would make the sections globally dependent. If they were pointwise dependent everywhere this argument would apply on such an open set.

The dual of the first-column variation map on this pair is

(η1,η2)↦s1⊗ℝη1+s2⊗ℝη2.(\eta_1,\eta_2)\longmapsto s_1\otimes_{\mathbb R}\eta_1+ s_2\otimes_{\mathbb R}\eta_2. \tag{6}

If (6) vanishes, pointwise independence forces both adjoint solutions to vanish on the disk, hence everywhere. The derivative restricted to the two chosen kernel columns is therefore onto Hom⁡ℝ(ℝ2,coker⁡Tf−)\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb R^2, \operatorname{coker}T_f^-), of dimension 2(k+4r)2(k+4r). Finite-dimensional Fredholm reduction and the implicit function theorem give the stated local codimension bound. This does not claim that every higher-kernel stratum is a smooth manifold of its maximal expected codimension. ▫\square

The cover space has dimension 4r4r. Thus generic paths in the triangular operator space meet only simple kernels, and the map

Tfℳh(C,2)⊕ℝt→Hom⁡(ker⁡Tf−,coker⁡Tf−)T_f\mathcal M_h(C,2)\oplus\mathbb R_t \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(\ker T_f^-,\operatorname{coker}T_f^-) \tag{7}

is an isomorphism at each intersection. Higher-kernel loci have codimension at least 4+4r4+4r after allowing the cover to vary, so a one-parameter family avoids them. At a base-invertible operator the anti-invariant spaces in (7) are the full kernel and cokernel spaces.

These statements verify the infinitesimal condition in Bai–Swaminathan, Definition 6.5. They do not by themselves verify that definition’s separate condition on the compactified stable-map space. The distinction is material at an étale wall with attached contracted components.

Removing the étale double point

For g=2g=2 an étale odd scalar kernel ss descends to a section of L1⊗αL_1\otimes\alpha with one simple zero pp, where α\alpha is the nontrivial sign line of the cover. The operator D2⊗αD_2\otimes\alpha is invertible. The second coordinate is

v=−(D2⊗α)−1(Bs).v=-(D_2\otimes\alpha)^{-1}(B s). \tag{8}

Varying BB can prescribe v(p)v(p) arbitrarily while leaving D1,sD_1,s fixed. Here is a direct proof, including the constraint s(p)=0s(p)=0. Choose a local solution ξ\xi of (D2⊗α)ξ=0(D_2\otimes\alpha)\xi=0 with any specified value at pp; local solutions with arbitrary value follow from Wendl, Lemma 2.5.1 and elliptic regularity. Multiply by a cutoff equal to one near pp. The result has (D2⊗α)ξ(D_2\otimes\alpha)\xi supported in an annulus where s≠0s\ne0. There choose a real-linear map Ḃ\dot B with

Ḃs=−(D2⊗α)ξ,\dot B s=-(D_2\otimes\alpha)\xi,

and set it equal to zero elsewhere. Then (s,v+ϵξ)(s,v+\epsilon\xi) is an exact kernel vector for (D1,B+ϵḂ,D2)(D_1,B+\epsilon\dot B,D_2). In particular, the condition v(p)=0v(p)=0 has two additional independent real equations inside the simple-kernel wall. Its projection to operator space has codimension three, so generic paths avoid it. Branched kernel graphs are already embedded by §1.

In genus two there are only fifteen connected étale covers. The two-branch Hurwitz space compactifies by the spectral double covers over branch divisors in Sym⁡2C\operatorname{Sym}^2C. When the branch points coincide, the finite curve has one node. Its normalization is either an étale double cover or two copies of CC. A nonzero odd kernel on the nodal limit would therefore give either an étale kernel vanishing at its exchanged pair or a base kernel. Along a base-invertible path whose étale kernel graphs are embedded, neither occurs. Normalized kernel graphs, scaled into a uniformly tame small tube, satisfy fixed-genus Gromov compactness. Thus simple branched kernel crossings cannot escape through this Hurwitz boundary; the smooth kernel crossings are finite along a compact generic path.

At a genus-four branched crossing with no simultaneous étale kernel, the remaining stable degree-two genus-four strata have no kernel: their positive-degree normalizations have either degree one or are étale. A genus-three étale crossing satisfies the simple-wall condition in genus three. It does not satisfy it in every larger source genus, because contracted tails inherit its kernel.

3. The normal line of a scalar image

The following observation is the additional ingredient needed to control simple curves away from the zero section.

Let u:Y→L1⊕L2u:Y\to L_1\oplus L_2 be a simple solution of (2) of degree one or two over a genus-two base. Let u‾:Y→L1\bar u:Y\to L_1 be its scalar projection. By §1 both maps are immersions, even before generic embeddedness is imposed. Let NuN_u and Nu‾N_{\bar u} be their normal bundles on YY; NuN_u has complex rank two and Nu‾N_{\bar u} has rank one. The holomorphic projection induces an exact sequence of normal Cauchy–Riemann operators

0→(f*L2,f*D2)→(Nu,DuN)→(Nu‾,Qu‾)→0.0\longrightarrow(f^*L_2,f^*D_2) \longrightarrow(N_u,D_u^N) \longrightarrow(N_{\bar u},Q_{\bar u}) \longrightarrow0. \tag{9}

The operator Qu‾Q_{\bar u} is the normal real Cauchy–Riemann operator of the immersed curve in the almost-complex surface L1L_1. The exactness of the bundles follows because du‾d\bar u is injective; compatibility of the operators follows by differentiating the holomorphic projection. The operator on the vertical subbundle is exactly f*D2f^*D_2, since the second equation is linear in u2u_2. After a smooth splitting, (9) is a triangular system; its off-diagonal term has order zero.

In particular,

ker⁡DuN↪ker⁡Qu‾.\ker D_u^N\hookrightarrow\ker Q_{\bar u}. \tag{10}

The index of DuND_u^N is zero: c1(T(L1⊕L2))[C]=2−2g+deg⁡L1+deg⁡L2=0c_1(T(L_1\oplus L_2))[C] =2-2g+\deg L_1+\deg L_2=0, and the unmarked curve index in complex dimension three is twice this Chern number.

Every nonzero kernel element therefore has a nonzero scalar normal component. Any two independent kernel elements project to two independent solutions of the same scalar operator. The independence argument used in (6) applies unchanged to these normal sections.

4. Universal simple-curve transversality with prescribed core jets

Fix a smooth path of operators (4) with D1,tD_{1,t} invertible on CC. Require the nonlinear perturbations to preserve the zero section and its first fiber jet:

At(z,0)=Ft(z,0)=0,dfibAt|0=D1,t−∂‾L1,dfibFt|0=Bt.A_t(z,0)=F_t(z,0)=0, \quad d_\mathrm{fib}A_t|_0=D_{1,t}-\bar\partial_{L_1}, \quad d_\mathrm{fib}F_t|_0=B_t. \tag{11}

One may keep the complete germs fixed in collars of the two endpoint parameters. Perturbations in the interior may have arbitrary higher fiber jets and arbitrary support away from the zero section.

Proposition 3 (local isolation at degree two). Suppose the graph structures are realized in a common tame tube in a closed symplectic six-manifold. Assume the fixed endpoint collars contain only the regular zero-section support; constant positive-spin endpoint germs satisfy this assumption. There is a residual set of arbitrarily small smooth triangular perturbations satisfying (11) and the endpoint constraints such that, among simple closed curves contained in the tube and of degree at most two:

  1. every curve is embedded;
  2. distinct curves are disjoint, including disjointness from the zero section;
  3. for each fixed parameter the moduli space of simple curves is discrete;
  4. away from the zero section the moduli over the parameter interval is a smooth one-dimensional manifold, and its projection to the interval has only nondegenerate critical points.

The zero section is regular throughout. All the curves in this statement have index zero, so this is precisely the four local conditions of Doan–Ionel–Walpuski Definition 3.13 at this degree cutoff.

Proof. The relevant perturbation tests are as follows.

(a) Free values and Fredholm surjectivity. Every noncore curve has an unbranched disk whose scalar image is injective and disjoint from the scalar images of any prescribed finitely many other distinct curves and from the zero section. To see the last assertions, scalar images are simple, and distinct scalar images cannot agree on an open set: if they agreed globally, their second-coordinate difference would be a kernel of f*D2f^*D_2. Distinct scalar images have isolated intersections. The same applies to intersection with the zero section. Choose the disk away from these intersections and from branch points.

On this disk the vertical directions identify with the full normal bundle of the graph, and arbitrary values of (Ȧ,Ḟ)(\dot A,\dot F) prescribe arbitrary normal (0,1)(0,1)-forms. These values extend to smooth perturbations supported in a neighborhood of the scalar disk in L1L_1. They satisfy all of (11). An adjoint cokernel element annihilating these perturbations vanishes on the disk and hence everywhere by unique continuation. The universal normal Fredholm section is therefore transverse. At a fixed tt, the projection of the universal curve space to the space of static perturbations has Fredholm index zero. After including t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], the projection of the universal path-curve space to the space of perturbation paths has Fredholm index one. A regular chosen path consequently has one-dimensional curve moduli; the subsequent projection of this one-manifold to [0,1][0,1] is the map whose critical points are considered below.

(b) Kernel strata. Hold the current curve fixed by requiring the perturbation values to vanish along its scalar image. The first derivative transverse to that scalar image remains an arbitrary real map from the scalar normal line to the two normal output coordinates, supported in the chosen disk. It acts on ker⁡DuN\ker D_u^N through the injection (10). The proof of Proposition 2 now shows that the one-dimensional-kernel locus has codimension one in the universal simple-curve space. At nullity k≥2k\ge2, the derivative on any two kernel columns is onto a space of dimension 2k2k, so the nullity-kk locus is locally contained in a submanifold of codimension at least four. These estimates suffice for avoidance by a one-parameter family.

(c) Nondegenerate quadratic term. At nullity one choose a kernel generator ξ\xi and an adjoint cokernel generator η\eta. Its scalar normal component ξ‾\bar\xi is nonzero on an open set. Vary the second normal derivative of (A,F)(A,F) on a smaller disk there, while holding their values and first derivatives fixed along the scalar curve. Such a perturbation changes the scalar quadratic Kuranishi coefficient by a nonzero constant multiple of

∫Y⟨η,Ṗ(2)(ξ‾,ξ‾)⟩.\int_Y\left\langle\eta, \dot P^{(2)}(\bar\xi,\bar\xi)\right\rangle. \tag{12}

Because η\eta satisfies unique continuation, the disk can be chosen where both factors are nonzero. A real quadratic map evaluated on a fixed nonzero real vector can take any prescribed output value. Thus (12) can be varied arbitrarily, without changing the curve or its linearized operator. Vanishing of this coefficient imposes one additional independent equation inside the nullity-one locus.

Relative parametric transversality therefore makes the curve moduli over the path a one-manifold, avoids nullity at least two and the vanishing-quadratic locus, and meets the nullity-one locus transversely. The local equation for the projection is t−t0=±x2t-t_0=\pm x^2 at a critical point. In particular its fiber at every fixed tt is locally discrete. At the zero section regularity follows directly from (11) and the invertibility of both diagonal base operators.

(d) Evaluation constraints. For an immersed simple graph, the universal normal equation together with evaluation at two distinct marked points is transverse to the coincidence condition. The same holds for a pair of distinct curves, and for intersection with the fixed zero section. We first prove a bounded linear statement at fixed smooth maps and fixed marked points, and only then allow the marks to move in higher-regularity charts.

Fix p>2p>2 and distinct marks z1,z2z_1,z_2. On W1,p(Nu)W^{1,p}(N_u), evaluation at these fixed points is bounded. Consider the augmented linear map

(ξ,Ṗ)↦(DuNξ+Ṗu,ξ(z1),ξ(z2))∈Lp(Λ0,1⊗Nu)⊕Nu,z1⊕Nu,z2,(\xi,\dot P)\longmapsto \left(D_u^N\xi+\dot P_u,\xi(z_1),\xi(z_2)\right) \in L^p(\Lambda^{0,1}\otimes N_u) \oplus N_{u,z_1}\oplus N_{u,z_2},

where Ṗ=(Ȧ,Ḟ)\dot P=(\dot A,\dot F) ranges over smooth permitted perturbations. The operator on ξ\xi alone is Fredholm, since the evaluation terms are finite-dimensional. Its image has finite codimension, so adding parameter directions still gives a closed image. An annihilator is therefore an LqL^q adjoint section, with 1/p+1/q=11/p+1/q=1, together with covectors at the fixed marks. The adjoint equation has point sources at the marks and is homogeneous elsewhere. Perturbations supported on projected injective disks away from the marks force the adjoint section to vanish on those disks. Elliptic regularity and unique continuation make it zero on each punctured domain. An LqL^q section supported at finitely many points is zero. Arbitrary fixed-point normal values of smooth ξ\xi then force the remaining point covectors to vanish. The augmented linear map is surjective. For distinct curves one chooses disjoint projected disks and applies the same argument to their direct-sum normal operator, killing the adjoint sections independently.

Because the cokernel of the augmented operator on ξ\xi is finite dimensional, finitely many smooth parameter variations suffice for this surjectivity. Keep this finite-dimensional parameter space and replace W1,p→LpW^{1,p}\to L^p by Wk,p→Wk−1,pW^{k,p}\to W^{k-1,p}. Given a Wk−1,pW^{k-1,p} right-hand side and prescribed evaluation values, solve using the W1,pW^{1,p} result. The parameter term is smooth, and elliptic regularity upgrades the resulting section to Wk,pW^{k,p}, with the same values at the marks. This is the regularity upgrade used in Wendl, Lectures on Symplectic Field Theory, Lemma 9.2.9, now with the fixed-point evaluation factors retained.

Take k≥3k\ge3 sufficiently large and parameter regularity ℓ\ell sufficiently larger than kk for the required differentiability. The nonlinear evaluation maps with moving marks are then defined in these Wk,pW^{k,p} and CℓC^\ell charts with the differentiability needed for Sard–Smale. Their derivative adds du(zi)żidu(z_i)\dot z_i to the fixed-point variations. Since each map is immersed, these tangent directions together with the arbitrary normal values span the full target tangent spaces. Thus the coincidence constraint is transverse in the moving-mark problem. For the fixed core, the variable curve already supplies arbitrary full evaluation variations. The multi-evaluation setup is the one in Wendl, Lectures on Holomorphic Curves, version 3.3, Section 4.6. No differentiability of moving-point evaluation on W1,pW^{1,p}, or LqL^q description of a higher-Sobolev dual, is used.

In a path the two-marked self-intersection locus, and likewise the intersection locus for two distinct curves, has expected dimension

1+4−6=−1.1+4-6=-1. \tag{13}

The index for intersection with the fixed core is the same: the two marks are one on the moving curve and one on the core. Hence all these loci are empty for generic paths. Immersion was already proved in §1, so no missing jet condition for critical points of the maps is being suppressed.

Apply these statements in countably many normal/Fredholm charts and in an exhaustion of the punctured tube. On each chart the required perturbations are supported a positive distance from the core and from the endpoint collars. The conditions (11) therefore do not restrict any of the value or jet variations used above. Parametric Sard–Smale and the Baire theorem give a simultaneous residual choice. Elliptic regularity and smooth local perturbations give the smooth version. ▫\square

There is a dense set of parameters at which all these simple curves are regular. Indeed, for each of the finitely many degree/genus possibilities, the path moduli is a second-countable one-manifold and the projection has only isolated critical points. The union of their critical values is countable and has measure zero; its complement is dense. This statement does not assert that the entire path moduli is compact or that there are only finitely many simple-curve folds.

For the underlying Banach/Floer-space and smooth Baire argument, see Wendl, Sections 9.1–9.2 and Remark 9.2.6. That argument is used only after verifying (a)–(d) for the restricted parameter space; ambient genericity alone would not imply them.

The normal-bundle formulation also explains why prescribing the core’s first jet is compatible with this assertion. At a noncore curve, its projected injective disk lies away from the locus on which the jet was prescribed. Keeping the zero section fixed would obstruct a generic fold argument at a singular zero section; that issue is absent here because its operator is invertible for the entire path.

5. Endpoint paths and optional cover bifurcation jets

For distinct even theta characteristics on a genus-two curve, both holomorphic line operators are invertible: a degree-one line has at most one independent holomorphic section, so even parity means none. One can therefore connect their positive spin operators through base-invertible scalar real operators. First lower the positive spin mass to zero. The spin norm identity preserves injectivity at every positive mass, and the zero-mass endpoint is invertible. Next join the holomorphic lines through Pic⁡1(C)\Θ\operatorname{Pic}^1(C)\setminus\Theta, lifting the path to Dolbeault operators on a fixed smooth complex line. This complement is path-connected: the theta divisor is a complex curve in the connected complex surface Pic⁡1(C)\operatorname{Pic}^1(C), and a general path avoids its real codimension-two locus. Finally restore the other spin mass.

The resulting compact path has a uniform bounded inverse on the base. It can be perturbed slightly to satisfy the double-cover conditions of §2 without losing base invertibility. The lower term BB does not affect base invertibility, since D2D_2 is invertible there. Choose B=0B=0 in endpoint collars. The higher-order perturbations of Proposition 3 can then be made with exactly these prescribed first jets.

If a detailed double-cover bifurcation model is also desired, its nonlinear coefficient is accessible inside the same triangular family. At a simple cover kernel (s,v)(s,v), choose a disk where s≠0s\ne0. A real cubic fiber map from L1L_1 to either output line can take an arbitrary prescribed value at ss; on the other sheet it takes the negative value. Thus cubic perturbations, vanishing through second order at the core, can vary the anti-invariant cubic obstruction in any cokernel direction. Combining this with the isomorphism (7) gives a local reduced equation

x(L(δf,t−t0)+x2c+higher terms)=0.x\bigl(L(\delta f,t-t_0)+x^2c+\text{higher terms}\bigr)=0. \tag{14}

The deck action is x↦−xx\mapsto-x. Solve the bracket using the invertible map LL; the coefficient of x2x^2 in t−t0t-t_0 can be made nonzero. This is the required nondegenerate pitchfork coefficient. It is an additional finite-jet condition, not a consequence of (7) alone. Multiplying all perturbations by an interior time cutoff preserves every endpoint jet. Proposition 3 does not require this extra condition for local isolation of the simple curves.

6. Precise interface with the cluster argument

The verified primary-source conditions are Doan–Ionel–Walpuski, Definition 3.13 and Proposition 3.30: their simple-isotopy argument uses isolated embedded disjoint curves and an unobstructed core; its Hausdorff neighborhoods may change along the path. It does not require one fixed disk tube with no curves on its boundary for every parameter. This removes the particular objection based on scaling solutions of a linear equation through a fixed tube boundary.

Proposition 3 supplies the local isolation conditions at degree at most two for a nonlinear triangular path with the specified base-invertible core. The genus bound supplies the only possible genera of simple degree-two correction cores, namely three and four. In a compact realization, one must still justify that the localized cycle neighborhoods and all the correction cores in the chosen application remain inside the triangular region. Curves outside that region are not covered by Proposition 3. One may perturb the ambient structure away from a smaller closed tube, but no global 𝒥isol\mathcal J_\mathrm{isol} assertion in arbitrary degrees is proved here.

The compactness statement needed locally is the bounded-degree, bounded-region version of Calculation A1, now with (3). It bounds reduced supports before applying compactness. It does not assert an arithmetic genus bound for all stable maps with contracted components. The cluster series includes those maps; they must be retained in the cluster comparison and in the multiplicity-one elementary factor.

Accordingly, the local transversality obstacle identified for split operators has been removed in degree two. If the separate localized cluster comparison applies along this path, its correction cores have degree two and genus at most four. At a degree-two cutoff those cores occur only with multiplicity one. This is the precise input needed to infer an elementary-exponent cutoff after identifying their complete local series. The present note does not replace those localization and series-identification arguments with a count of smooth kernels.

A10. The degree-one class for two line bundles of unequal degrees

Let CC be a smooth compact complex curve of genus g≥2g\ge2, let AB=KCA B=K_C be a pair of holomorphic lines with deg⁡A=g−1+c\deg A=g-1+c and c≥0c\ge0, and give the two summands weights r,s∈ℤ\{0}r,s\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}, respectively. For the equivariant insertion, see the antidiagonal local-curve construction, §2.

The virtual cycle at second excess

B1. The components of the second-excess double-cover integral

Let CC be a smooth compact curve of genus g≥2g\ge2, let a,ba,b be theta characteristics, and use the direct sum of their positive real spin operators as the normal operator DD. Write Va,VbV_a,V_b for the oriented real cokernel bundles on stable maps, with determinant orientations continued from the complex Dolbeault operators. The connected degree-two local invariant in source genus 2g+12g+1 is

L2,2g+1(D)=∫[ℳ¯2g+1(C,2)]vire(Va)e(Vb).L_{2,2g+1}(D)=\int_{[\overline{\mathcal M}_{2g+1}(C,2)]^\mathrm{vir}} e(V_a)e(V_b).

The genus 2g−12g-1 is the unramified minimum, so this is excess two. Let MM be the reduced closure of the locus of smooth double covers with four simple branch points, and set

Ig(a,b)=∫[M]e(Va)e(Vb).I_g(a,b)=\int_{[M]}e(V_a)e(V_b).

This integral is over a proper stable-map component. It is not an integral over the open finite-map locus. The spin obstruction bundle is the one constructed by Lee–Parker, restricted from the full stable-map space. Lee–Parker, Theorem 8.1 and §§11–12

Component reduction

Put s(t)=2sin⁡(t/2)s(t)=2\sin(t/2), let c2(D)c_2(D) be the signed stack count of connected étale double covers, and let F2(D)F_2(D) be the finite-map integral at first excess, on the compact surface of source genus 2g2g. Then

L2,2g+1(D)=Ig(a,b)−g−16F2(D)+c2(D)[t4g]s(t)4g−4.\boxed{L_{2,2g+1}(D)=I_g(a,b)-\frac{g-1}{6}F_2(D) +c_2(D)[t^{4g}]s(t)^{4g-4}.} \tag{1}

n2,2g+1=Ig(a,b)−ϵ22g−6(g−1)(g−2).\boxed{n_{2,2g+1}=I_g(a,b) -\epsilon\,2^{2g-6}(g-1)(g-2).} \tag{2}

In particular, for a genus-two positive distinct-spin core,

L2,5=I2(a,b)−1160,n2,5=I2(a,b).L_{2,5}=I_2(a,b)-\frac1{160},\qquad n_{2,5}=I_2(a,b). \tag{3}

The remaining integer is an Euler integral on the compactified four-branch component. Equations (1)–(3) do not assert its vanishing.

The stable-map strata

Normalize the nonconstant components of a stable map. Let 2r2r be their total ramification, tt the number of direct nodes between nonconstant branches, and let GiG_i be the maximal connected contracted subcurves. Write qi=pa(Gi)q_i=p_a(G_i) and aia_i for their numbers of attachments. Since the total degree is two, ai≤2a_i\le2: distinct attachments use distinct points of the normalized cover over one target point. Stability gives 2qi−2+ai>02q_i-2+a_i>0, hence qi≥1q_i\ge1. Riemann–Hurwitz and the dual-graph genus formula give

r+t+∑i(qi+ai−1)=2.r+t+\sum_i(q_i+a_i-1)=2. \tag{4}

Thus finite maps have (r,t)=(2,0),(1,1),(0,2)(r,t)=(2,0),(1,1),(0,2). The other possibilities are an elliptic tail on a two-branched cover; an elliptic tail on a one-node finite cover; two elliptic tails on a connected étale cover; a genus-two tail on a connected étale cover; or an elliptic bridge joining the two sheets of an étale normalization. The last normalization may be connected or two copies of CC. Contracted blocks include their nodal stable limits. This convention includes rational components carrying several positive-genus branches.

The image of the source fundamental group in π1(C)\pi_1(C) is locally constant in stable-map families. Consequently the stack is the disjoint union of its open and closed étale-lift summands and its primitive summand, where primitive means surjective on π1(C)\pi_1(C). This is the decomposition of Bryan–Pandharipande, not primitivity in homology or in the cycle algebra. In degree two, a nontrivial étale lift has degree one upstairs. Only the two-elliptic-tail and genus-two-tail types belong to these summands. A bridge joining conjugate sheets does not lift: its constant value upstairs would have to be two different points. Bryan–Pandharipande, Definition 2.2 and Proposition 2.3

Let ℱ2\mathcal F_2 be the proper finite-map surface at first excess and π:𝒰→ℱ2\pi:\mathcal U\to\mathcal F_2 its universal curve, viewed as the stack of one-pointed stable maps. A marking at a node is carried by an inserted rational component. Gluing a pointed elliptic curve defines a proper map

γ:𝒰×ℳ¯1,1→ℳ¯2g+1(C,2).\gamma:\mathcal U\times\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1} \longrightarrow\overline{\mathcal M}_{2g+1}(C,2).

Its image GG is the elliptic-tail component, and its generic stack degree is one. Every primitive map lies in M∪GM\cup G. Pair collisions produce the finite nodal maps. A three-branch collision replaces a cusp by an elliptic tail at ramification, and a four-branch collision replaces a tacnode by an elliptic bridge. These limits follow by introducing a rational target bubble and taking its degree-two cover. Conversely |2p||2p| on a pointed elliptic curve and |p+q||p+q| on a twice-pointed one produce the required admissible covers. Smoothing their nodes with stabilized target CC gives every smooth bridge in MM; nodal bridges follow by degeneration. Tails on nodal finite cores lie in GG.

Both components have dimension four, the expected dimension, and are generically unobstructed. The smooth-cover deformation complex has finite-length cohomology at the ramification points. At a generic elliptic tail the attachment is unramified, and its smoothing line maps isomorphically to the tail obstruction by df⊗δdf\otimes\delta, where δ:TpE→H1(E,𝒪E)\delta:T_pE\to H^1(E,\mathcal O_E) is the principal-part map. The four remaining dimensions are those of the first-excess cover, attachment point and pointed elliptic curve. Equation (4) leaves no other component. A four-dimensional virtual cycle on this pure four-dimensional stack is determined by its generic multiplicities; these are one. Thus

[ℳ¯2g+1(C,2)prim]vir=[M]+γ*[𝒰×ℳ¯1,1].[\overline{\mathcal M}_{2g+1}(C,2)^\mathrm{prim}]^\mathrm{vir} =[M]+\gamma_*[\mathcal U\times\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1}]. \tag{5}

This top-cycle statement does not require global smoothness of MM or separation of the components at their intersection. At a smooth ramification-attached elliptic tail the local equation is uv=0uv=0: the obstruction is divisible by the node-smoothing parameter, and its quotient has nonzero derivative in the attachment coordinate transverse to simple ramification.

The two contributions outside the main component

On the source of γ\gamma, normalizing the attaching node cancels the constant sections of the tail against the matching fiber. The normal cokernel has the core cokernel and 𝔼∨⊗ev⁡*(a⊕b)\mathbb E^\vee\otimes\operatorname{ev}^*(a\oplus b) as its two successive factors, with complex orientation on the latter. This continues to a marked node: the inserted rational component has no H1H^1, and its matching sequence recovers the original nodal core. With λ=c1(𝔼)\lambda=c_1(\mathbb E) and κ=c1(KC)\kappa=c_1(K_C),

c2(𝔼∨⊗ev⁡*(a⊕b))=−λev⁡*κ.c_2(\mathbb E^\vee\otimes\operatorname{ev}^*(a\oplus b)) =-\lambda\operatorname{ev}^*\kappa.

Here λ2=0\lambda^2=0 on ℳ¯1,1\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1} and both normal Chern roots come from CC. The two pushforwards are ∫λ=1/24\int\lambda=1/24 and π*ev⁡*κ=4(g−1)\pi_*\operatorname{ev}^*\kappa=4(g-1). The ghost component therefore contributes −(g−1)F2(D)/6-(g-1)F_2(D)/6. All automorphism factors are retained by the universal curve and the pointed elliptic stack; there is no additional uniform factor of two.

For a connected étale double cover p:Y→Cp:Y\to C, the other summand is [ℳ¯2g+1(Y,1)/Aut⁡C(p)][\overline{\mathcal M}_{2g+1}(Y,1)/\operatorname{Aut}_C(p)]. B2. The genus-five contribution of two distinct spin lines

The complete holomorphic-kernel locus

Write ι\iota for the hyperelliptic involution and WW for the six Weierstrass points. The kernel locus for an even θ\theta has the following surface components.

To see exhaustiveness, use the strata in Calculation B1. On a finite arithmetic-genus-five double cover the anti-invariant spin line has degree minus one. On a smooth genus-four normalization it has degree zero, and a section forces its root to equal θ\theta. A direct node on this normalization would require that section to vanish at two distinct points of one unramified fiber, which it does not. On an étale double normalization the anti-invariant line is θξ\theta\xi, of degree one. Matching across a direct node or a bridge requires its section to vanish at the image of that node or bridge. A tail on a one-node finite core lies in the main component only in its marked-node limit; that limit belongs to the intersection of the displayed surfaces. Finally, two degree-one components have no sections since H0(C,θ)=0H^0(C,\theta)=0.

These arguments also show that the kernel is one-dimensional on the entire locus and that the kernel loci for two distinct even theta characteristics are disjoint. In particular an elliptic bridge supplies one theta characteristic, determined by its character and target point. Put

Zθ=[Aθ]+∑p∈W[Bθ,p].Z_\theta=[A_\theta]+\sum_{p\in W}[B_{\theta,p}]. \tag{2}

The classes in (2) mean the Thom classes of the surface components in their smooth ambient neighborhoods, extended to MM.

Deformation charts at their compact boundaries

The finite first-excess double-cover surface FF is the root gerbe over the blow-up of Pic⁡1(C)\operatorname{Pic}^1(C) at the sixteen theta characteristics. Let Dθ≃ℙ1D_\theta\simeq\mathbb P^1 be its exceptional curve. Its coarse normal line is 𝒪(−1)\mathcal O(-1). The ramification-marked cover of DθD_\theta is C→ℙ1C\to\mathbb P^1, the canonical double cover. The exceptional curve meets each relevant nodal diagonal transversely: it is the exceptional divisor of the blow-up, whereas the diagonal is the strict transform of the smooth Abel curve through that theta point.

At a smooth ramification-attached tail, the tangential deformation space has the four node-preserving parameters and one smoothing parameter τ\tau, with one obstruction line. The obstruction is divisible by τ\tau and its quotient vanishes simply with dfdf at the attaching point. Thus the two components have equation τu=0\tau u=0; the main branch is smooth. Its tail divisor is Cartier and its normal is the attaching-node smoothing line.

The only additional boundary relevant to the surface intersections is a rational bridge carrying an elliptic tail. The one-pointed finite cover has a smooth universal-curve chart in which its map near the marked point z=1z=1 of that rational bridge is

f(z)=ν+uz+v/z.f(z)=\nu+u z+v/z. \tag{3}

The old finite node has smoothing parameter uvuv. The two bridge-node smoothings are u,vu,v, and ν\nu moves their image in CC. Normalization of the tangential deformation complex cancels the unobstructed finite core and the constant matching terms; it leaves exactly H1(E,𝒪E)⊗TνCH^1(E,\mathcal O_E)\otimes T_\nu C as obstruction. Thus a versal analytic chart has one equation FF in these five parameters.

The family with τ=0\tau=0 exists identically. The family with u=v=0u=v=0 also exists identically for every τ\tau: the whole bridge remains contracted. The principal-part smoothing map is the derivative u−vu-v at z=1z=1, multiplied by the nonzero elliptic connecting map. Therefore

with analytic units. Replacing u,vu,v by uU,vVuU,vV gives a smooth main branch u=vu=v. The bridge divisor on it is u=0u=0, and the tail divisor is τ=0\tau=0. The root condition DθD_\theta is transverse to the finite nodal diagonal, so the surface equations take the form

Aθ:τ=0,ν=h(u2),Bθ,p:u=0,ν=0,A_\theta:\ \tau=0,\ \nu=h(u^2),\qquad B_{\theta,p}:\ u=0,\ \nu=0, \tag{5}

after choosing the local target origin at pp. Thus both surfaces are regularly embedded and meet cleanly along ℳ¯1,1\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1}. The common normal direction at this intersection is the fixed target/root direction.

For a smooth elliptic bridge, the two smoothing lines map surjectively onto its single elliptic obstruction; the main component is smooth there as well. The same statement holds on the nonseparating boundary: for an irreducible nodal elliptic bridge, or for a cycle of two rational components with one attaching mark on each, the dualizing differential is nonzero at each smooth attaching point. On each rational component of the latter cycle the dualizing line has degree zero and the differential has opposite nonzero residues at its two nodes. The separating boundary is the rational bridge with an elliptic tail already treated by (3)–(5), including a nodal elliptic tail. These exhaust the stable genus-one dual graphs with two markings. The calculations hold on orbifold charts and retain all automorphisms. They establish the required smooth neighborhoods of the compact kernel surfaces; global smoothness of MM is not needed.

The oriented Euler correction

We first specify the local family comparison at nodal maps. This is stronger than the existence of the positive-mass cokernel bundle alone. For a versal nodal family and L=f*θL=f^*\theta, use Siebert’s Banach realization of the Dolbeault family: Corollary 4.7 identifies its kernel and cokernel with sheaf cohomology, Corollary 4.11 identifies the family complex with the holomorphic Cech complex, and Proposition 4.15(1),(3) gives uniform sup-norm control on input sections and norm-continuity of the operators in Banach-bundle trivializations. Siebert, version 2, §4 Zinger explicitly records this stronger Fredholm-family statement for flat stratified nodal families in §2.4 of his comparison theorem. Zinger, §2.4

The real zeroth-order term R=A(df)R=A(df) is continuous in these realizations as well. Locally write the source plumbing as xy=sxy=s and the holomorphic map in a target coordinate as f=F(x,y,b)f=F(x,y,b). On the half-neck |x|≥|s||x|\ge\sqrt{|s|} its derivative is

df=(Fx−sx−2Fy)dx.df=(F_x-sx^{-2}F_y)\,dx.

The coefficient is uniformly bounded, and the other half-neck has the same estimate with x,yx,y exchanged. Consequently ∂‾+tR\bar\partial+tR, including t=0t=0, is a continuous local family of Fredholm operators.

Choose a finite complex space of obstruction forms supported away from the nodes spanning the central Dolbeault cokernel. Stabilization stays surjective on a small product of the base and mass interval. It gives a finite-dimensional family, whose complex at t=0t=0 represents Rπ*LR\pi_*L by the cited Cech comparison. The initial complex obstruction space has real dimension six; at a positive-mass point a real four-dimensional complement to its relation space gives a rank-four cokernel chart. Relations among these forms in either realization are exactly solutions of the same equation on the normalized components, with matching values. Sobolev embedding, elliptic regularity and removal of bounded punctures identify these solutions. Thus the quotient charts and their overlap maps agree, rather than merely having isomorphic individual fibers. Both determinant orientations come from the same homotopy to t=0t=0. Finite stabilizer groups are retained by equivariant stabilization.

At a general point of either surface, a finite-dimensional reduction of the Dolbeault operator has a one-dimensional kernel and three-dimensional cokernel. Its variation has rank two transverse to the kernel locus. B3. The second genus excess in every covering degree

Let CC be a smooth curve of genus g≥2g\ge2, let a,ba,b be theta characteristics, and use their positive real spin operators. Set c=g−1c=g-1 and Hm=1+mcH_m=1+mc. [ℳ¯Hm+2(Y,1)/Aut⁡C(p)].\left[\overline{\mathcal M}_{H_m+2}(Y,1) /\operatorname{Aut}_C(p)\right]. \tag{4}

For composite mm, 𝒳m∘\mathcal X_m^\circ still contains maps factoring through étale covers of smaller degree. It must not be called the primitive summand. At prime mm it is that summand.

A degree-one map to the smooth curve YY has a unique nonconstant component, mapping isomorphically, and every connected contracted block attaches to it just once. Distinct points cannot be identified over the same target point of YY. This characterizes (4) among maps whose nonconstant normalization is an étale degree-mm cover of CC.

3. The finite, bridge and tripod loci lie in the main closure

We use admissible covers only to produce smoothings; no isomorphism between their compactification and the stable-map compactification is assumed. The balanced equations at a target node are uv=τuv=\tau, xy=τexy=\tau^e, x=uex=u^e, y=vey=v^e. Connectedness of the constructed admissible source ensures connected nearby smooth sources.

For a rational tripod choose the three simple poles 0,1,∞0,1,\infty of

ϕ(z)=z+z−1+(z−1)−1.\phi(z)=z+z^{-1}+(z-1)^{-1}. \tag{7}

z+z−1,z2+z−1,z3+z−1,z2+z+z−2.z+z^{-1},\quad z^2+z^{-1},\quad z^3+z^{-1},\quad z^2+z+z^{-2}. \tag{9}

4. The virtual four-cycle

Let ℱm\mathcal F_m be the proper first-excess finite-map surface from Article V, §§4–6 and let 𝒰m→ℱm\mathcal U_m\to\mathcal F_m be its universal one-pointed stable curve. A marking at a finite node is carried by an inserted rational component. Gluing a pointed elliptic curve gives a proper map

Sections 2–3 show that the support of 𝒳m∘\mathcal X_m^\circ is Mm∪GmM_m\cup G_m. Both are pure four-dimensional closures. B4. Four branch points and the spin obstruction in genus two

test. The target curve CC has genus two. Unless specified otherwise, θ\theta is an even theta characteristic; thus H0(C,θ)=0H^0(C,\theta)=0. The two spin lines in the mixed calculation can both be chosen even and distinct. The results below distinguish a compact spectral parameter space from the stable-map compactification. In particular, the first zero computed below is not the local Gromov–Witten invariant.

The finite-cover calculation

Let J=Pic⁡2(C)J=\operatorname{Pic}^2(C), let ℳ\mathcal M be the Poincaré line on C×JC\times J normalized at a fixed point of CC, and let PP be the principal polarization class on JJ. Put

V=π*ℳ2,Eθ=R1π*(θℳ−1),B=ℙJ(V),ζ=c1(𝒪B(1)).V=\pi_*\mathcal M^2,\qquad E_\theta=R^1\pi_*(\theta\mathcal M^{-1}),\qquad B=\mathbb P_J(V),\qquad \zeta=c_1(\mathcal O_B(1)).

The ranks are three and two: every degree-four line on CC has three sections and no first cohomology, whereas θM−1\theta M^{-1} has degree minus one and no sections. The point (M,[s])(M,[s]) of BB gives the double-cover algebra 𝒪C⊕M−1\mathcal O_C\oplus M^{-1} with equation w2=sw^2=s.

The stack of these spectral curves is the gerbe on which a line TT with T2=𝒪B(1)T^2=\mathcal O_B(1) exists. The universal root is ℳ⊗T\mathcal M\otimes T. On the open subset BnodB^{\mathrm{nod}} where the zeros of ss have multiplicity at most two, the source is nodal. The finite-cover normal cokernel is, as an oriented real bundle, the underlying real bundle of Eθ⊗T−1E_\theta\otimes T^{-1}. Indeed, the invariant Dolbeault cohomology is zero, the anti-invariant kernel vanishes, and the positive spin mass gives the complex cokernel projection of Lee–Parker, Proposition 12.2. This statement includes finite nodal domains by the normalization sequence.

Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch gives

ch⁡(V)=3−4P,ch⁡(Eθ)=2+P.\operatorname{ch}(V)=3-4P,\qquad \operatorname{ch}(E_\theta)=2+P.

c=P22−Pζ2+ζ24.c=\frac{P^2}{2}-\frac{P\zeta}{2}+\frac{\zeta^2}{4}. \tag{1}

p*ζ2=1,p*ζ3=4P,p*ζ4=8P2.p_*\zeta^2=1,\qquad p_*\zeta^3=4P,\qquad p_*\zeta^4=8P^2.

∫Bc2=∫J(12P2−P2+12P2)=0.\int_B c^2= \int_J\left(\frac12P^2-P^2+\frac12P^2\right)=0. \tag{2}

The gerbe multiplies this zero by 1/21/2. Equation (2) is an intersection calculation on the spectral compactification. At a triple zero the source has a cusp, and at a quadruple zero it has a tacnode. These are not stable nodal domains. The corresponding stable limits contain contracted elliptic tails or bridges. Thus (2) cannot be substituted for an Euler integral on ℳ¯5(C,2)\overline{\mathcal M}_5(C,2).

The holomorphic kernel on the main component

Consider the closure of the smooth-source double covers inside the stable-map stack, called the main component here. For even θ\theta, the holomorphic pullback acquires a section only in the following two kinds of codimension-two loci.

First, a degree-two genus-four finite cover with root M1=θM_1=\theta has one anti-invariant section. Attach an elliptic tail at a ramification point. The section extends over the tail by its attaching value, which is zero. The resulting surface is denoted AθA_\theta. Its compact parameter curve for the pointed finite cover is CC: the branch divisor is x+ι(x)x+\iota(x), where ι\iota is the hyperelliptic involution, and the chosen ramification point lies above xx. The tail parameter is ℳ¯1,1\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1}. There is an additional generic stack factor 1/21/2 from the double-cover involution, which fixes the ramification point. At a Weierstrass point the pointed finite cover is stabilized by inserting a rational bridge at its node before attaching the elliptic tail.

Second, let pp be one of the six Weierstrass points and put ξ=θ(−p)∈Pic⁡0(C)[2]\xi=\theta(-p)\in\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)[2]. This is nontrivial because θ\theta is even. Take the étale double cover with character ξ\xi and join its two points over pp by a contracted two-pointed elliptic curve. The anti-invariant section corresponds to the unique section of θξ=𝒪C(p)\theta\xi=\mathcal O_C(p); it vanishes at both attaching points. These maps form a surface Bθ,pB_{\theta,p}. It meets AθA_\theta along the boundary where the two attaching points lie on a rational component with an elliptic tail. This common curve has parameter ℳ¯1,1\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1}. The bridge retains the simultaneous core deck transformation and elliptic involution exchanging the two attaching points. An elementary quotient of a sheet-labelled product can lose this stabilizer, so it should not be substituted for the bridge stack without a separate comparison. The vanishing intersections below use its constant target normal line and do not require such a global presentation.

The elementary kernel argument is useful independently of intersection theory. With four simple branch points the anti-invariant line has degree minus one. With two branch points it has degree zero, and a section forces M1=θM_1=\theta. On an étale normalization it is a theta characteristic; matching the two sheets across a bridge forces its zero to be the bridge image. A genus-two effective theta characteristic is 𝒪C(p)\mathcal O_C(p) for a Weierstrass point pp. Two degree-one positive components have no sections because H0(C,θ)=0H^0(C,\theta)=0. These observations also show that the kernel loci for two distinct even theta characteristics are disjoint. The bridge surfaces cannot be omitted from the compact kernel locus.

At the central map the nonconstant normalization is étale. The contracted subcurve is a rational bridge with an elliptic tail. A complete assembled proof should spell out the Kuranishi construction and verify its compatibility with the stack charts at every boundary point.

The local Euler correction

There is a simple finite-dimensional model for a transverse codimension-two jump of a one-dimensional Dolbeault kernel. After discarding invertible summands it is

Dz(u)=(z1u,z2u,u¯):ℂ→ℂ3.D_z(u)=(z_1u,z_2u,\overline u):\mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb C^3. \tag{6}

The real cokernel has rank four. Its quotient identification with the first two complex coordinates has the negative of their complex orientation, since conjugation reverses the orientation of the one-dimensional kernel. The section induced by the third coordinate has local zero degree minus one. Replacing the last coordinate of (6) by εu\varepsilon u, ε≠0\varepsilon\ne0, gives the corresponding complex index representative, for which this zero degree is plus one. Their difference is therefore minus two times the complex orientation of the kernel locus.

The two required transverse directions are visible geometrically. On AθA_\theta they are variation of the root away from θ\theta and smoothing the elliptic attachment: the anti-invariant section has a simple zero at the ramification point. On a generic bridge surface, moving its image away from pp violates matching to first order. If τ1,τ2\tau_1,\tau_2 are the node smoothings and δ1,δ2\delta_1,\delta_2 the elliptic principal-part maps, the tangential equation is τ1δ1+τ2δ2=0\tau_1\delta_1+\tau_2\delta_2=0. The anti-invariant section has opposite derivatives on the two sheets, so its equation is τ1δ1−τ2δ2=0\tau_1\delta_1-\tau_2\delta_2=0. Restricted to the tangential smoothing line, the latter is nonzero. Both surface components therefore have generic multiplicity one in the kernel degeneracy cycle.

If these charts are used to identify the global real Euler correction, the resulting formula is

e(Vθ)=c2(−Rπ*f*θ)−2Zθ,Zθ=[Aθ]+∑pmWeierstrass[Bθ,p].e(V_\theta)=c_2(-R\pi_*f^*\theta)-2Z_\theta, \qquad Z_\theta=[A_\theta]+\sum_{p\ { m Weierstrass}}[B_{\theta,p}]. \tag{7}

For a full proof one must use the compact-support/Thom sequence to exclude any additional codimension-two contribution. Equation (6) determines the generic coefficients; strata of complex codimension at least three cannot support a degree-four correction on a smooth ambient chart. The common rational Chern class in (7) is independent of θ\theta, by Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch and the torsion difference between theta characteristics. This Chern class is on the stable-map main component, and should not be confused with the particular extension (1) on BB.

Equations (7)–(9), together with a justified decomposition of the primitive virtual class and its equal-spin calibration, would imply vanishing of the mixed main-component integral. At this stage the assembled virtual-class argument and a fresh independent check of the compact charts remain necessary. No value of n2,5n_{2,5} is asserted by this investigation alone.
