Primary-source comparison

  • Lee–Parker, An obstruction bundle relating Gromov–Witten invariants of curves and Kähler surfaces, §12, gives the constant-rank quotient and orientation used above. Its construction gives the stable real obstruction bundle; it does not give the mixed-spin integral here. Primary PDF.
  • Kiem–Li, Low degree GW invariants of spin surfaces, Theorem 1.1 and §4, treats the analogous obstruction-theoretic comparison and analyzes corrections where Dolbeault cohomology fails to be locally free. It concerns one spin class. It is not a theorem about products of two distinct spin Euler classes. An earlier manuscript contains the related calculation in §4: arXiv:0707.2986.
  • Nesterov–Schimpf, Admissible covers and stable maps, Theorem 2.7 and §7, gives a cycle-valued comparison with explicit contracted-curve corrections, including a fixed-target formulation. The spin Euler classes would require a compatible pullback comparison before applying that theorem here. arXiv:2505.03487.

Common spin sections and their excess intersection

C1. Triple covers with two holomorphic spin sections

Let CC be a smooth curve of genus two, with hyperelliptic involution ι\iota, and let a,ba,b be distinct even theta characteristics. They are non-effective. Fix their square isomorphisms with KCK_C and let Sθ(x,p)S_\theta(x,p) be the Szegő kernel of θ\theta, normalized to have diagonal residue one. The difference of their squares is the symmetric holomorphic bidifferential

𝒟(x,p)=Sa(x,p)2−Sb(x,p)2∈H0(C×C,KC⊠KC).\mathscr D(x,p)=S_a(x,p)^2-S_b(x,p)^2 \in H^0(C\times C,K_C\boxtimes K_C).

Write Q(p)=𝒟(p,p)∈H0(C,KC2)Q(p)=\mathscr D(p,p)\in H^0(C,K_C^2).

Theorem. Smooth connected degree-three covers f:Y→Cf:Y\to C with g(Y)=5g(Y)=5 and

H0(Y,f*a)≠0,H0(Y,f*b)≠0H^0(Y,f^*a)\ne0,\qquad H^0(Y,f^*b)\ne0 \tag{1}

are classified, up to isomorphism over CC, by the distinct zeros of QQ. The cover indexed by pp has exactly one ramification point, of index three, over ιp\iota p. Both spaces in (1) have dimension one. The monodromy is S3S_3 and the cover has no nontrivial automorphism over CC.

The section QQ is the pullback of a nondegenerate binary quadratic under the canonical double cover C→ℙ1C\to\mathbb P^1. Consequently there are four such covers generically and between two and four distinct covers for every fixed pair. A zero at a Weierstrass point has order two in QQ, but still gives one smooth cover; it is not discarded. The statement classifies geometric points and their ordinary stack stabilizers, not intersection multiplicities of the kernel loci.

For every resulting cover, attaching a pointed elliptic curve at its triple ramification point gives a complete curve of simultaneous holomorphic kernels inside the reduced main genus-six locus M3M_3 of Calculation B3. Thus the common kernel locus there is nonempty even after the full étale-lift summands have been removed. This is a geometric boundary obstruction to a disjoint-kernel argument. Calculation C2 evaluates the common-kernel intersection, and Article V, Corollary 1.2 computes the elementary cubic exponents.

1. The trace-free bundle determines an elementary modification

Put f*𝒪Y=𝒪C⊕Tf_*\mathcal O_Y=\mathcal O_C\oplus T. Its trace-free bundle has rank two and degree 4−g(Y)=−14-g(Y)=-1. Since a,ba,b have no base sections, any sections in (1) give a map

a−1⊕b−1→T.a^{-1}\oplus b^{-1}\longrightarrow T. \tag{2}

It has generic rank two. Otherwise the joint graph would lie in a line subbundle M⊂a⊕bM\subset a\oplus b with both projections nonzero. Then deg⁡M≤0\deg M\le0: degree one would identify aa and bb. The graph has degree three over CC, since the field extension has prime degree and a degree-one graph would give base sections. Its monic spectral equation has arithmetic genus 4+3deg⁡M≤44+3\deg M\le4. Its normalization cannot have genus five, a contradiction.

Thus (2) has a torsion cokernel of length one, at a point pp. For E=T*E=T^* it gives

0→E→a⊕b→ℂp→0.0\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow a\oplus b \longrightarrow\mathbb C_p\longrightarrow0. \tag{3}

The quotient uses both summands. If, for example, E=a(−p)⊕bE=a(-p)\oplus b, the four summands of Sym⁡3E⊗(det⁡E)−1\operatorname{Sym}^3E\otimes(\det E)^{-1} are b(−2p),a(−p),b,a(p)b(-2p),a(-p),b,a(p). Only the last has a section, so every nonzero cubic datum is a pure cube with identically zero discriminant. It cannot define the generic algebra of a smooth connected cover. The other axis is the same with a,ba,b interchanged.

We use the cubic-algebra convention in which EE is the dual trace-free bundle, so cubic data lie in H0(Sym⁡3E⊗(det⁡E)−1)H^0(\operatorname{Sym}^3E\otimes(\det E)^{-1}). This is the dual of the trace-free-bundle convention in Miranda, Theorem 3.6.

2. The Szegő extension condition

Choose a coordinate zz centered at pp and local frames X,YX,Y of a,ba,b whose squares are dzdz. Normalize the meromorphic sections A=Sa(⋅,p)A=S_a(\cdot,p) and B=Sb(⋅,p)B=S_b(\cdot,p) using the corresponding fiber frames. Their scalar expansions are

A=z−1+caz+eaz2+O(z3),B=z−1+cbz+ebz2+O(z3).A=z^{-1}+c_a z+e_a z^2+O(z^3),\qquad B=z^{-1}+c_b z+e_b z^2+O(z^3). \tag{4}

The constant term vanishes by antisymmetry of the even-spin Szegő kernel in compatible coordinate frames. Each space H0(θ(p))H^0(\theta(p)) has dimension one, and the residue determines its meromorphic section. These are standard consequences of the prime-form expression for the Szegő kernel; a primary account is Matone–Volpato, §1, p. 741. Their prime-form convention gives residue −1-1; multiplying by the constant sign −1-1 gives the normalization used here and does not change any squared kernel.

Write the nonaxial kernel in (3) at pp as X−rYX-rY, r≠0r\ne0. A local frame of EE is k=X−rYk=X-rY, l=zYl=zY. A global cubic on EE maps to meromorphic cubic data on a⊕ba\oplus b with at most a simple pole at pp. Its coefficient spaces are, in order, H0(b(p)),H0(a(p)),H0(b(p)),H0(a(p))H^0(b(p)),H^0(a(p)),H^0(b(p)),H^0(a(p)). The residue must be a multiple of (X−rY)3(X-rY)^3. If the residue vanished, all coefficients would be holomorphic and hence zero. Thus every nonzero possibility is a scalar multiple of

Φr=BX3−3rAX2Y+3r2BXY2−r3AY3.\Phi_r=BX^3-3rAX^2Y+3r^2BXY^2-r^3AY^3. \tag{5}

Since k∧l=zX∧Yk\wedge l=zX\wedge Y, the determinant correction multiplies the cubic by zz. In the modified frame it is

zBk3+3r(B−A)k2l+6r2B−Azkl2+4r3B−Az2l3.zB k^3+3r(B-A)k^2l +6r^2\frac{B-A}{z}kl^2+4r^3\frac{B-A}{z^2}l^3. \tag{6}

Its extension condition is exactly ca(p)=cb(p)c_a(p)=c_b(p). The difference dp=A2−B2d_p=A^2-B^2 is a holomorphic one-form: its double pole cancels and (4) has no simple pole in either square. Its value at pp is 2(ca−cb)2(c_a-c_b) in these frames. Thus (6) extends if and only if Q(p)=0Q(p)=0.

The one-form dpd_p is never identically zero. Equality A2=B2A^2=B^2 would make their nonzero meromorphic sections have the same divisor, and their quotient would trivialize a⊗b−1a\otimes b^{-1}. This would contradict a≠ba\ne b.

3. The actual algebra is smooth

The discriminant of (5), normalized to r=1r=1, is −108(A2−B2)2-108(A^2-B^2)^2. After modification it is −108z−2dp2-108z^{-2}d_p^2. Its zero divisor is consequently 2div⁡(dp)−2p2\operatorname{div}(d_p)-2p. To verify smoothness one must also inspect the algebra, rather than just this discriminant divisor.

In Miranda’s convention write a binary cubic as −βX3+3αX2Y−3δXY2+γY3-\beta X^3+3\alpha X^2Y-3\delta XY^2+\gamma Y^3. Where β\beta is invertible, his multiplication formulas eliminate one trace-free generator and give

U3+3(βδ−α2)U+3αβδ−2α3−β2γ=0.U^3+3(\beta\delta-\alpha^2)U +3\alpha\beta\delta-2\alpha^3-\beta^2\gamma=0.

Substituting (5), or (6) near pp, reduces this to

U3−3dpU+2Adp=0.U^3-3d_pU+2Ad_p=0. \tag{7}

Near pp the modified coefficient β=−zB\beta=-zB is a unit. Although AA has a pole, AdpAd_p is holomorphic when Q(p)=0Q(p)=0.

If pp is not Weierstrass, the divisor of dpd_p is p+qp+q with q=ιp≠pq=\iota p\ne p, both simple. At pp, write dp=d1z+O(z2)d_p=d_1z+O(z^2), d1≠0d_1\ne0. The special fiber of (7) is U3+2d1U^3+2d_1, with three distinct roots. The cover is étale there. At qq, neither AA nor BB vanishes: otherwise dpd_p would have a double zero at qq as well as a zero at pp. The unmodified β=−B\beta=-B is therefore a unit near qq. For a coordinate tt at qq, write dp=μt+O(t2)d_p=\mu t+O(t^2). The derivative in tt of (7) at its triple root is 2A(q)μ≠02A(q)\mu\ne0. This proves that the source is smooth and the map has ramification index three.

If pp is Weierstrass, then div⁡(dp)=2p\operatorname{div}(d_p)=2p. For dp=d2z2+O(z3)d_p=d_2z^2+O(z^3), d2≠0d_2\ne0, equation (7) has the form

U3+2d2z+O(z2)+O(z2U)=0.U^3+2d_2z+O(z^2)+O(z^2U)=0. \tag{8}

It again defines a smooth source with index-three ramification, now over p=ιpp=\iota p. Away from the indicated point the discriminant is nonzero. No zero-cubic fiber occurs: its leading modified coefficient at pp is one, and at q≠pq\ne p it is a nonzero cube. A component containing a point of local degree three already has the full degree of the cover, so the source is connected. Finally deg⁡T=−1\deg T=-1 gives genus five by Riemann–Roch.

4. Uniqueness, number of covers and monodromy

The parameters rr and the nonzero scalar in (5) are absorbed by diagonal automorphisms of a⊕ba\oplus b in the cubic-algebra correspondence. They do not give additional covers.

To show that pp is intrinsic, use T⊂a−1(p)⊕b−1(p)T\subset a^{-1}(p)\oplus b^{-1}(p), whose permitted polar parts form a line with both coordinates nonzero. After tensoring by aa, the first coordinate of a global section lies in H0(𝒪C(p))=ℂH^0(\mathcal O_C(p))=\mathbb C and has no pole. The residue condition then kills the other polar part; its remaining holomorphic section lies in H0(a⊗b−1)=0H^0(a\otimes b^{-1})=0. Hence h0(T⊗a)=1h^0(T\otimes a)=1, and similarly h0(T⊗b)=1h^0(T\otimes b)=1. The two sections therefore recover (2) up to their individual scalars and recover its determinant zero pp. This proves the bijection.

Write 𝒟=∑Mijωi⊠ωj\mathscr D=\sum M_{ij}\omega_i\boxtimes\omega_j in a basis of H0(KC)H^0(K_C), with MM symmetric. The matrix is nonsingular. Otherwise a kernel direction is the canonical evaluation direction at some pp, since C→ℙ1C\to\mathbb P^1 is surjective. Then dpd_p would be identically zero, contradicting Section 2. The nondegenerate quadratic v𝖳Mvv^{\mathsf T}Mv has two distinct roots on ℙ1\mathbb P^1. Their inverse images give the stated two, three or four distinct zeros of QQ. This also proves existence for every fixed pair, without a genericity assumption.

The discriminant divisor is 2q2q, while det⁡E=ab(−p)\det E=ab(-p). Its sign local system is therefore

det⁡E(−q)=ab⊗KC−1=a⊗b−1.\det E(-q)=ab\otimes K_C^{-1}=a\otimes b^{-1}.

This nontrivial two-torsion character makes the transitive monodromy S3S_3, rather than its cyclic subgroup. Its centralizer in the permutation group on three sheets is trivial. Each cover consequently has ordinary stack weight one. No local intersection or virtual multiplicity follows from this stabilizer calculation.

5. Simultaneous kernels on the main genus-six boundary

Let f:Y→Cf:Y\to C be one of these covers, with triple ramification point rr over qq. Attach any pointed smooth elliptic curve (E,e)(E,e) at rr. Both sections in (1) extend over the tail by their matching constant value. The resulting genus-six stable map has both kernels.

It lies in M3M_3, the closure of smooth four-simple-branch triple covers. Expand the target at qq and use a degree-three function on EE with sole pole 3e3e and four distinct simple finite branch points. Such a function exists: the embedding by |3e||3e| realizes EE as a smooth plane cubic with flex tangent 3e3e; projection from a general point of that tangent line has the required pencil. Avoiding the other finitely many flex tangents gives simple finite branching. A line cannot be tangent to a smooth plane cubic at two distinct points, so their branch values are distinct. Attach its pole to rr, with matching index three. Fixed-target admissible-cover smoothing as in Calculation B3 gives the desired smooth covers. The stabilized limit is exactly the given tail map.

Properness of the gluing map includes the nodal elliptic tail. For each cover this gives a closed copy of ℳ¯1,1\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1} in the simultaneous-kernel locus inside M3M_3. The core cover and its attachment are intrinsic, and its deck group is trivial, so there is no additional covering gerbe. Different core covers give disjoint such substacks.

These maps are in the fundamental-group-surjective summand: at degree three a nontrivial étale factorization would have degree one upstairs, incompatible with the ramified core. Thus the common-kernel boundary persists after the complete étale reduction in Calculation B3. Its positive-dimensional intersections are exactly why smooth finite-cover kernel exclusion cannot by itself evaluate the main mixed Euler integral. The theorem makes no claim that these elliptic-tail curves exhaust every contracted-boundary common-kernel locus.

6. An exact example and scope

For C:y2=∏j=16(x−j)C:y^2=\prod_{j=1}^6(x-j), take the even theta partitions 123∣456123\mid456 and 124∣356124\mid356. The hyperelliptic Szegő-square formula gives

𝒟(x,t)=2xt−7x−7t+17y(x)y(t)dxdt.\mathscr D(x,t)=\frac{2xt-7x-7t+17}{y(x)y(t)}\,dx\,dt.

Its diagonal zeros have coordinates

t=7±152.t=\frac{7\pm\sqrt{15}}2.

Neither is a branch value, and each has two lifts to CC. Thus this example has four covers and four corresponding elliptic-tail boundary curves. The formula follows by subtracting the partition numerators in D’Hoker–Schlotterer, Appendix C, (C.3)–(C.4). It is an exact algebraic calculation, not a numerical theta-function approximation.

The exact identities are reproduced by code/cubic_szego_construction.py, using uv run --no-project --with sympy==1.14.0 python code/cubic_szego_construction.py. The check verifies the frame change, discriminant, actual algebra coefficients and explicit bidifferential; it does not assign any kernel-locus intersection multiplicity.

C2. The common spin-kernel intersection on the cubic main locus

1. Statement and notation

Let CC be a smooth genus-two curve and let a,ba,b be distinct even theta characteristics. They are noneffective. Write ℱ\mathcal F for the proper surface of connected finite cubic maps of arithmetic genus five, with its reduced nodal boundary, and let M=M3M=M_3 be the reduced closure of smooth connected cubic covers with four distinct simple branch points in ℳ¯6(C,3)\overline{\mathcal M}_6(C,3). Thus MM is the proper four-cycle of Calculation B3, with all of its components retained. It lies in the primitive summand; the full degree-one-upstairs étale summands are separate.

For the universal map ff and curve π\pi over MM, put

Wθ=−Rπ*f*θ,c=c2(Wθ),Δθ=c−e(Vθ)2∈H4(M;ℚ),θ=a,b.W_\theta=-R\pi_*f^*\theta,\qquad c=c_2(W_\theta),\qquad \Delta_\theta=\frac{c-e(V_\theta)}2\in H^4(M;\mathbb Q), \qquad\theta=a,b. \tag{1}

Here VθV_\theta is the oriented real rank-four positive-spin-mass cokernel bundle. Rational Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch makes cc independent of the theta characteristic. The virtual complex bundle WθW_\theta has rank two; this does not assert that its higher Chern classes vanish. The classes in (1) are defined before making any identification with holomorphic kernel cycles.

Let SθS_\theta be the residue-one Szegő kernel and set

Q=(Sa2−Sb2)|Δ∈H0(C,KC2).Q=\left.(S_a^2-S_b^2)\right|_\Delta\in H^0(C,K_C^2). \tag{2}

Theorem. The determinantal kernel loci Ka,KbK_a,K_b on ℱ\mathcal F have scheme-theoretic intersection isomorphic to the zero scheme of QQ. Its length is four. Every common finite map is smooth and is one of the covers fp:Yp→Cf_p:Y_p\to C of Calculation C1. On MM, the common holomorphic-kernel support consists exactly of the disjoint closed curves

Ep={fp:Yp→C with a contracted pointed genus-one tail at its unique triple ramification point rp}≃ℳ¯1,1,p∈Z(Q)red.E_p=\{f_p:Y_p\to C\text{ with a contracted pointed genus-one tail at its unique triple ramification point }r_p\} \simeq\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1}, \qquad p\in Z(Q)_{\mathrm{red}}. \tag{3}

If QQ has four simple zeros, then

∫[M]ΔaΔb=−13.\boxed{\displaystyle \int_{[M]}\Delta_a\Delta_b=-\frac13.} \tag{4}

Each of the four curves in (3) contributes −1/12-1/12. This includes the nodal elliptic endpoint and its stabilizer. The numerical assertion is stated under the simple-zero hypothesis; no specialization argument at colliding zeros is needed here.

Define Saself=∫[M]Δa2S_a^{\mathrm{self}}=\int_{[M]}\Delta_a^2 and Sbself=∫[M]Δb2S_b^{\mathrm{self}}=\int_{[M]}\Delta_b^2. The equal-spin calibration and component reduction of Calculation B3 give the following consequence:

I3(a,b)=512−2(Saself+Sbself),n3,6=4−2(Saself+Sbself).\begin{aligned} I_3(a,b)&=\frac{51}{2}-2(S_a^{\mathrm{self}}+S_b^{\mathrm{self}}),\\ n_{3,6}&=4-2(S_a^{\mathrm{self}}+S_b^{\mathrm{self}}). \end{aligned} \tag{5}

2. The finite-cover intersection as a scheme

This section records the new local argument; the construction of the individual covers remains that of Calculation C1. Near any common cover, the surface ℱ\mathcal F is smooth. For L=f*θL=f^*\theta, choose a large relative reduced divisor DD away from the ramification and resolve Rπ*LR\pi_*L by

π*L(D)→π*(L(D)|D).\pi_*L(D)\longrightarrow\pi_*(L(D)|_D).

Cancel an invertible block. Since h0(L)=1h^0(L)=1 and χ(L)=−1\chi(L)=-1, the residual complex is a column r:𝒪→𝒪2r:\mathcal O\to\mathcal O^2. Its domain generator lifts to a family of meromorphic sections ss. At the divisor sections write s=αi/xi+βi+⋯s=\alpha_i/x_i+\beta_i+\cdots and σ=df=qi(xi)dxi\sigma=df=q_i(x_i)\,dx_i in local spin frames. The residue theorem gives an identity on the whole neighborhood, before imposing r=0r=0:

0=∑iRes⁡(σs2)=∑i(2qi(0)βi+qi′(0)αi)αi.0=\sum_i\operatorname{Res}(\sigma s^2) =\sum_i\bigl(2q_i(0)\beta_i+q_i'(0)\alpha_i\bigr)\alpha_i. \tag{6}

The principal-parts vector is a holomorphic linear image of rr. Thus (6) gives a holomorphic row annihilating rr. At the central kernel section uu it is twice the Serre-duality functional of σu≠0\sigma u\ne0. The row is nonzero, so the residual complex becomes 𝒪→(gθ,0)𝒪2\mathcal O\xrightarrow{(g_\theta,0)}\mathcal O^2. The determinantal ideal is exactly (gθ)(g_\theta). On its zero scheme the kernel is a free line, including after Artin base change.

For an Artin deformation with both kernels, the two lifted sections give a trace-free map a−1⊕b−1→Ta^{-1}\oplus b^{-1}\to T, where f*𝒪Y=𝒪C⊕Tf_*\mathcal O_Y=\mathcal O_C\oplus T. Its determinant has a simple zero on the central curve. The implicit-function theorem over the Artin base therefore identifies its divisor with a unique relative point pp. Dualizing gives

0→E=T*→a⊕b→𝒪p→0.0\longrightarrow E=T^*\longrightarrow a\oplus b \longrightarrow\mathcal O_p\longrightarrow0. \tag{7}

Both quotient coordinates are units. The polynomial cubic-algebra construction of Miranda, applied over the same Artin ring, gives the unique possible nonzero datum up to the two diagonal changes of frame:

λ(BX3−3rAX2Y+3r2BXY2−r3AY3),A=Sa(⋅,p),B=Sb(⋅,p),r,λ∈R*.\lambda\bigl(BX^3-3rAX^2Y+3r^2BXY^2-r^3AY^3\bigr), \quad A=S_a(\cdot,p),\quad B=S_b(\cdot,p),\quad r,\lambda\in R^*. \tag{8}

The residue-one kernels have zero constant term. Consequently the only extension condition is Q(p)=0Q(p)=0 in the Artin ring, with its actual nilpotents. The diagonal action on (r,λ)(r,\lambda) is free and transitive, so no extra parameter or infinitesimal stabilizer remains. The inverse construction recovers pp as the determinant divisor. Hence

𝒪̂ℱ,fp/(ga,gb)≃𝒪̂C,p/(Q).\widehat{\mathcal O}_{\mathcal F,f_p}/(g_a,g_b) \simeq\widehat{\mathcal O}_{C,p}/(Q). \tag{9}

Finite colength in a regular surface makes each gθg_\theta a nonzero Cartier equation near the common points. At a simple zero of QQ, their differentials are independent. The local multiplicity is ord⁡pQ\operatorname{ord}_pQ, and the total is four. Calculation C1 gives trivial deck groups, so no additional weight modifies this length.

We also need transversality to the triple-ramification divisor 𝒯⊂ℱ\mathcal T\subset\mathcal F. On this divisor the discriminant line is η=ab−1\eta=ab^{-1}. At its branch point qq, the trace pairing on TT, in the algebra w=z3w=z^3, has matrix (03w3w0)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&3w\\3w&0\end{smallmatrix}\right). After division by qq it is nondegenerate. Since det⁡T=η𝒪(−q)\det T=\eta\mathcal O(-q), this identifies TT with T⊗ηT\otimes\eta in families on 𝒯\mathcal T. It identifies the two cohomology-jump ideals restricted to 𝒯\mathcal T. At a simple common point their common restriction must have order one: otherwise both independent differentials in (9) would annihilate T𝒯T\mathcal T. Thus each KθK_\theta meets 𝒯\mathcal T transversely.

The relative deformation calculation immediately below establishes the local scheme structure. The global single-spin dimension bound is proved in C3. No global reduced-divisor formula for the individual KθK_\theta is being inferred from their behavior at the common points.

3. Exhaustion of the compact common support

The smooth classification extends to finite reduced sources as follows. For a connected reduced finite cubic u:Z→Cu:Z\to C, u*𝒪Z=𝒪C⊕Tu_*\mathcal O_Z=\mathcal O_C\oplus T and deg⁡T=4−pa(Z)\deg T=4-p_a(Z). Suppose both spin sections are nonzero. If a−1⊕b−1→Ta^{-1}\oplus b^{-1}\to T has rank one, its joint graph lies in a line N⊂a⊕bN\subset a\oplus b of degree at most zero. The graph is a reduced monic spectral cubic, and ZZ maps finitely and birationally to it. This remains true for normalization degrees 2+12+1: the generic section values are s,−s,0s,-s,0, whereas three degree-one components have no sections. Therefore

pa(Z)≤4+3deg⁡N≤4.p_a(Z)\le4+3\deg N\le4. \tag{10}

This is an arithmetic-genus inequality, not merely a bound on the normalization. In the rank-two case, genus six forces T=a−1⊕b−1T=a^{-1}\oplus b^{-1}, whose Miranda cubic coefficient space is H0(b⊕a⊕b⊕a)=0H^0(b\oplus a\oplus b\oplus a)=0. Genus five gives (7). An axial quotient permits only a pure cube, incompatible with a generically reduced algebra. A nonaxial quotient gives (8), and the actual multiplication algebra in Calculation C1 is smooth. These arguments also cover reducible and non-Gorenstein finite sources: the trace-zero rank-three multiplication identities are polynomial and do not require irreducibility. Thus every finite common-kernel genus-five source is smooth, and no finite genus-six source has both kernels.

For a stable map X→CX\to C of genus six, contract each maximal connected ghost block to obtain the finite reduced curve Z=Spec⁡Cf*𝒪XZ=\operatorname{Spec}_C f_*\mathcal O_X. If the blocks have genera qiq_i and attachment numbers aia_i, then

r+t+∑i(qi+ai−1)=2,pa(Z)=6−∑iqi,H0(X,f*θ)=H0(Z,u*θ),r+t+\sum_i(q_i+a_i-1)=2,\qquad p_a(Z)=6-\sum_iq_i, \qquad H^0(X,f^*\theta)=H^0(Z,u^*\theta), \tag{11}

where 2r2r is total ramification and tt counts direct nodes on the nonconstant normalization. Stability allows only (1,1),(2,1),(1,2)(1,1),(2,1),(1,2) and (0,3)(0,3). The finite genus-six exclusion removes rational tripods as well as finite maps. An elliptic bridge becomes a genus-five node, which the smoothness conclusion removes. The same argument removes a nodal core with an elliptic tail, including the rational insertion when its marking reaches a node. Two elliptic tails or one genus-two tail force a connected étale core and belong to the removed full étale summands. The only primitive common kernels are therefore YpY_p with a genus-one tail attached at an arbitrary point.

For membership in the main locus the attachment must be ramified. Indeed, the necessary smoothing condition of Rezaee–Swaminathan, Theorem 1.7 applies to a nodal ghost as well. For a one-pointed stable genus-one curve (E,e)(E,e) the connecting map δ:TE,e→H1(E,𝒪E)\delta:T_{E,e}\to H^1(E,\mathcal O_E) is an isomorphism, by Serre duality and the nonvanishing dualizing differential at ee. The theorem then forces dfdf at the attachment to vanish. This rules out higher-order smoothings at an unramified point, not merely their first-order tangent vectors. Each YpY_p has exactly one ramification point, of index three. Calculation C1 proves sufficiency by a fixed-target admissible-cover smoothing and includes the nodal tail by properness. This proves (3).

4. The main chart and the two kernel surfaces

Assume henceforth that QQ has simple zeros and fix fpf_p. The finite-cover deformation has the local A2A_2 form w3+tw+vw^3+tw+v at its triple point. B|τ=0=t+3x2,∂B∂t≠0.B|_{\tau=0}=t+3x^2,\qquad \frac{\partial B}{\partial t}\ne0. \tag{12}

D=R×ℳ¯1,1,R:t=−3x2,R→ℱ has degree 2.D=R\times\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1},\qquad R:\ t=-3x^2,\qquad R\longrightarrow\mathcal F\text{ has degree }2. \tag{13}

ND/M|Ep=TrpYp⊗𝕃e∨,c1(ND/M|Ep)=−ψe=−λ.N_{D/M}|_{E_p}=T_{r_p}Y_p\otimes\mathbb L_e^\vee, \qquad c_1(N_{D/M}|_{E_p})=-\psi_e=-\lambda. \tag{14}

5. The supported Euler correction

The comparison needed here is a comparison of families, not just of individual cokernel fibers. Use the nodal Fredholm construction in Calculation B2. It applies unchanged to degree three: Siebert’s cohomology realization, norm-continuity and uniform sup estimates identify the Dolbeault family with its finite cohomology complex; the plumbing estimate for the zeroth-order spin term makes ∂‾+sA(df)\bar\partial+sA(df) continuous also at s=0s=0. Stabilization by forms supported away from nodes identifies the positive-mass quotient charts and their determinant orientations with those of the actual real obstruction bundle. The construction retains finite stabilizers. The relevant sources are Siebert, §4, Zinger, §2.4, and Lee–Parker, §§8, 11–12.

We specify the supported class to avoid a possible ambiguity. The mass homotopy gives a stable oriented real identification between VθV_\theta and the realification of WθW_\theta. Classify this datum by the homotopy pullback

P=BU×BSOhBSO(4),P=BU\times^h_{BSO}BSO(4), \tag{16}

where BUBU is the virtual-rank-two component. Over the kernel-free complement, the same homotopy gives a reduction to BU(2)BU(2): the Dolbeault cokernel is an actual complex rank-two bundle. On this subspace c2−e=0c_2-e=0. Since H3(BU(2);ℚ)=0H^3(BU(2);\mathbb Q)=0, the relative cohomology exact sequence gives a unique universal lift of c2−ec_2-e to H4(P,BU(2);ℚ)H^4(P,BU(2);\mathbb Q). where 𝒦θ\mathcal K_\theta is the full holomorphic-kernel support. The specified homotopy is part of this construction. Equality of absolute characteristic classes away from the kernel, by itself, would not determine a supported lift.

At every point of (15), the transverse complex variations have rank two. The spin mass pairs nontrivially with σu\sigma u, while (6) makes the two complex variations orthogonal to that functional. After cancellation the real reduction is homotopic to

u↦(z1u,z2u,u¯):ℂ→ℂ3.u\longmapsto(z_1u,z_2u,\overline u): \mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb C^3.\tag{18}

Its quotient has the opposite orientation to the first two complex coordinates at the central point. The projected last-coordinate section has local Euler degree −1-1, compared with +1+1 for the complex reduction replacing u¯\overline u by uu. The relative Euler difference is −2-2 times the complex Thom class. Therefore Δ̃θ\widetilde\Delta_\theta is the Thom class of ZθZ_\theta near the whole of EpE_p, with coefficient +1+1. The nodal elliptic point cannot carry an additional degree-four correction: it has complex codimension at least three in this smooth neighborhood, so such supported degree-four cohomology vanishes. Equivalently (18) itself holds on its uniformizing chart.

The product of the two supported lifts is supported on the common locus (3). Excision therefore computes its pairing with [M][M] entirely in the smooth neighborhoods just described. No assertion that every individual kernel component elsewhere is a smooth surface, or that it has coefficient one, is used.

A global one-dimensional-kernel bound

For every finite connected nodal cubic map of arithmetic genus five and every noneffective theta characteristic θ\theta on CC,

h0(Y,f*θ)≤1.h^0(Y,f^*\theta)\le1. \tag{13}

Every line subbundle of f*𝒪Yf_*\mathcal O_Y has degree at most zero: a positive-degree subbundle would, by adjunction, give a nonzero section of f*N−1f^*N^{-1}, which has negative degree on every positive-degree component of the finite source. Hence deg⁡(Nθ)≤1\deg(N\theta)\le1, and on a genus-two curve it has at most one independent section, a contradiction.

If the generic rank is two, its determinant has degree one, so dualizing gives an elementary modification of θ⊕θ\theta\oplus\theta at one point pp. The constant GL2\mathrm{GL}_2-action makes its quotient axial, and

E≃θ⊕θ(−p).E\simeq\theta\oplus\theta(-p).

The four cubic coefficient spaces are, in some order, H0(θ(p))H^0(\theta(p)), H0(θ)H^0(\theta), H0(θ(−p))H^0(\theta(-p)), and H0(θ(−2p))H^0(\theta(-2p)). Only the first is nonzero. Every cubic datum is therefore a pure cube, with identically zero discriminant, whereas the source is reduced and the generic algebra is a product of separable field extensions. This contradiction proves (13).

The proof covers reducible and irreducible finite nodal sources. It is a bound on the fiber dimensions. It does not alone prove that every individual global kernel component is a generically reduced divisor, or that no entire connected component of ℱ\mathcal F has persistent kernel.

[I]=(2ξ+2h)(3ξ+3h)(3ξ+5h)=18ξ3+66hξ2.[I]=(2\xi+2h)(3\xi+3h)(3\xi+5h) =18\xi^3+66h\xi^2. \tag{9}

Two nodes on a general discriminant member would give proportional normals, contradicting the embedding by the two pencils. A cubic cannot have two distinct singular roots over the same base point. The reducible locus B=0B=0 is proper as well. Thus a dense open subset of II parametrizes integral one-node spectra and their smooth genus-six normalizations. The node’s distinct branches make normalization commute with Artin deformations preserving the node. Conversely the determinant of the spectral-algebra inclusion for a deformed section recovers its unique node. This identifies the ordinary-node incidence locally with the determinantal kernel scheme, not just with its closed points. It is a regular surface there, with local coefficient +1+1 in the supported correction Δθ\Delta_\theta.

4. The global divisor on the finite genus-five surface

A genus-five finite kernel source maps birationally to (5) with algebra colength two. Its spectrum therefore lies outside the one-node open subset just proved. Properness of the incidence makes that complement a closed subset of the discriminant of dimension at most one.

There are finitely many nodal intermediate sources over a fixed reduced spectrum. Normalize the spectrum once. Every such source identifies disjoint pairs of distinct points of this normalization lying over the finite singular set. Its subalgebra consists exactly of functions whose residue values agree at each selected pair. There are no gluing scalars or jet parameters in a unital nodal algebra. Thus only finitely many choices occur. General nonnodal intermediate algebras would not obey this assertion. Since the kernel is one-dimensional, its projectivization adds no parameter. The entire genus-five kernel locus has dimension at most one; no component of ℱ\mathcal F has persistent kernel.

At any of its points, cancellation in a divisor resolution of Rπ*f*θR\pi_*f^*\theta gives a column r:𝒪→𝒪2r:\mathcal O\to\mathcal O^2. The exact residue identity from Calculation C2 is valid also at finite nodes. Locally xy=sxy=s and df=(xFx−yFy)dx/xdf=(xF_x-yF_y)dx/x is dualizing; its branch residues cancel. The identity supplies a holomorphic row annihilating rr, nonzero at the kernel because its Serre-duality functional is 2dfu2df\,u. The column becomes (g,0)(g,0). The dimension bound makes gg a nonzero germ in the regular surface ring. Therefore the global determinantal ideal defines an effective Cartier divisor DθD_\theta.

5. Ramification derivatives and the tail cycle

Every component of DθD_\theta is generically a smooth-source cover, by the no-total-ramification statement of §2 and the component reduction. Its section gives a finite birational map to an integral spectral curve of arithmetic genus seven. For a smooth source of genus five this is its normalization, and the total delta invariant of the spectrum is two.

If df(r)=ds(r)=0df(r)=ds(r)=0, the normalization map to the smooth surface Tot⁡θ\operatorname{Tot}\theta is not immersive at rr. Its image singularity is not an ordinary node, so the marked spectrum belongs to the nonnodal singular incidence. Sections 3–4 show that only finitely many such spectra have delta invariant two. Each has a unique normalization, and the section is unique up to scale. Thus only finitely many smooth kernel covers can fail the derivative condition. The finite ramification marking preserves this finiteness. It cannot contain a component of R×ℱDθR\times_{\mathcal F}D_\theta. This proves the proposition.

For completeness, the imported local tail comparison uses a node smoothing parameter τ\tau and the pulled-back determinantal equation gRg_R. Its two kernel equations reduce generically to (gR,τh)(g_R,\tau h), where the restriction of hh is the nonzero derivative ds(r)ds(r) times the elliptic principal-part isomorphism. Thus the ideal is (gR,τ)(g_R,\tau) and retains every power in gRg_R. The supported oriented multiplicity is positive, and gluing has generic stack degree one. The actual tail cycle is consequently j*[(R×ℱDθ)×ℳ¯1,1]j_*[(R\times_{\mathcal F}D_\theta)\times \overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1}]. Its pairing with Δθ\Delta_\theta is 11 by Calculation C3. Together with the compact bridge vanishing, this proves (2) using the component calculation in §7.

6. Consequence for stable replacement and its remaining gap

On these explicit spin curves the residual spectral family of Calculation C3 is nodal away from finitely many points of II. A spectrum with a unique ordinary node or cusp gives a smooth partial normalization after blowing up its marked singular point. Any nonnodal residual fiber therefore requires either a more singular marked point or an additional nonnodal unmarked point. Such a spectrum has total delta at least two and lies in the finite set of §§3–4. Reducible spectra cause no exception: two simple zeros of their canonical coefficient give ordinary nodes, and a double zero at a Weierstrass point gives the retained nodal rational tripod.

An integral residual fiber has arithmetic genus six and normalization genus at least four. Its total delta is at most two. If that delta is two, the normalization is an étale cubic, so all its graph branches are immersed. Thus the only possible nonnodal singularity in that case is an ordinary tacnode. If the delta is one, the only nonnodal possibility is an ordinary cusp. This reduces the remaining stable replacement problem to cusp and tacnode fibers over finitely many incidence points.

This finiteness does not establish equality of compact characteristic degrees. Stable reduction changes cohomology lattices on exceptional divisors, and tacnode replacement can itself acquire a cuspidal elliptic component. A comparison must control the actual index sheaf and any successive modifications, including their intersections. Article V, §7 instead obtains the smooth-source degree 5 by subtracting the ramification-tail degree from the individual square.

7. Components of the kernel cycle and the elliptic-tail multiplicity

Write MM for the reduced main four-cycle and W=−Rπ*f*θW=-R\pi_*f^*\theta. The constant-kernel formula of Calculation C3, §6 gives j*Δθ=c2(j*W)−ξc1(j*W)+ξ2,ξ=−c1(ker⁡∂‾).j^*\Delta_\theta=c_2(j^*W)-\xi c_1(j^*W)+\xi^2,\qquad \xi=-c_1(\ker\bar\partial). Unramified normalizations. On a cyclic cubic the two trace-free summands of the space of spin sections are the sections of θη±1\theta\eta^{\pm1} for a nontrivial line η\eta of order three. They have equal dimensions by Serre duality. Any nonzero section gives θη=𝒪C(p)\theta\eta=\mathcal O_C(p), contrary to the pencil condition. On a non-Galois unramified cubic let π:D→C\pi:D\to C be its discriminant double. The trace-free summand of the direct image is π*L\pi_*L for an order-three line LL on DD, by induction of a nontrivial character of the cyclic subgroup in S3S_3. The degree-two bundle π*θ⊗L\pi^*\theta\otimes L on DD has at most one section. Indeed, two sections would give a hyperelliptic pencil, whose square on this genus-three curve is KDK_D. Squaring the displayed line would give L2=1L^2=1, a contradiction. In partition 2+12+1 the double contributes at most one section of θη\theta\eta for a two-torsion line η\eta and the identity contributes none. In partition 1+1+11+1+1 there are no sections.

Matching on a finite nodal source. On a connected smooth cubic a nonzero section is primitive over the function field, since the covering degree is prime and θ\theta has no sections on CC. Its three values are generically distinct. On a 2+12+1 normalization they are s,−s,0s,-s,0. Thus a fixed kernel section matches two distinct sheets over only finitely many points. In genus five a finite nodal source has one node and unramified normalization. There are finitely many such normalizations, each with at most one projective section and finitely many matching pairs. No component of DθD_\theta lies in the nodal boundary. In genus six a finite nodal source has one node and half-ramification one, or two nodes and unramified normalization. In the former case, the connected smooth genus-five cores form at most a divisor in the Hurwitz surface by C3. On a disconnected 2+12+1 normalization a branched double with trace-free summand A−1A^{-1}, deg⁡A=1\deg A=1, can have a section only for A=θA=\theta. Its branch section varies in ℙH0(KC)\mathbb P H^0(K_C) of dimension one. Finite matching therefore bounds the finite nodal kernel locus by dimension one.

Contracted blocks. If rr is half the total ramification of the nonconstant normalization, tt the number of direct nodes, and qi,aiq_i,a_i the genus and number of external attachments of each connected contracted block, the genus budget is r+t+∑i(qi+ai−1)=2.r+t+\sum_i(q_i+a_i-1)=2 . A rational tripod has three attachments and an unramified normalization. The possible kernel maps are finite by matching and ℳ¯0,3\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,3} is a point. A genus-two contracted block with one attachment, or two one-pointed elliptic tails, leaves a connected unramified cubic. Its full unramified summand has already been removed from the main cycle, as in Calculation C2. A single elliptic tail with one attachment lies over the ramification scheme of a genus-five core. Its surface components have generically smooth core by the preceding paragraph.

For an elliptic bridge, r=t=0r=t=0 and the two sheets have equal section values at the attachments. There are finitely many choices of normalization and attachment pair. Order the attachments and rigidify that normalization. The compact bridge family is then ℳ¯1,2\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,2}, with fixed image q∈Cq\in C and constant kernel line. Normalization at the two external nodes gives j*W=Wnorm+θq⊗(𝒪+𝔼∨).j^*W=W_\mathrm{norm}+\theta_q\otimes(\mathcal O+\mathbb E^\vee). Here WnormW_\mathrm{norm} is a constant virtual vector space of rank zero and 𝔼\mathbb E is the elliptic Hodge line. Thus ξ=0\xi=0 and c2(j*W)=0c_2(j^*W)=0, even when the two markings lie on a rational bubble. Finite push-pull descends the vanishing of j*Δθj^*\Delta_\theta to the unordered family. Its contribution to the square vanishes regardless of the multiplicity of this bridge surface in the supported cycle.

Tail multiplicity. At a generic ramification-marked genus-five core, let gRg_R be the pulled-back local determinantal equation of DθD_\theta, and τ\tau the smoothing of the elliptic attachment. The one-tail chart of C2 gives kernel equations restricting at τ=0\tau=0 to (gR,0)(g_R,0). The second equation is τh\tau h with h|τ=gR=0=ds(r)δh|_{\tau=g_R=0}=ds(r)\,\delta, where δ:TeE→H1(E,𝒪E)\delta:T_eE\to H^1(E,\mathcal O_E) is the principal-part isomorphism at the elliptic attaching point. The derivative proposition above makes hh a unit generically on every reduced component. The kernel ideal is therefore (τ,gR)(\tau,g_R), including any multiplicity in gRg_R. The complex determinantal orientation has positive sign by C2 and C3. The smooth tail map recovers the core, marked ramification point and elliptic tail, so the generic gluing degree as stacks is one. The supported tail cycle thus has the multiplicities of the compact test family of C3, §7, whose pairing is 11. Only the smooth-source closure remains. This proves (2).

Relative spin operators and gluing

D1. Spin matching at one contact of order two

We compute the orientation sign on a finite contact chart for the nonseparating cut of Article V, §2. The orientation character belongs to the orthogonal normal bundle of the target curve. In a split representative the two spin lines are θ\theta and θη\theta\eta, where η\eta is the flat real sign line complexified. We choose the cut dual to w1(ηℝ)w_1(\eta_{\mathbb R}) and a parallel unit of η\eta on its complement. Changing the identification across this cut by a minus sign changes the spin gluing. In the two isotropic normal coordinates this interchanges the lines. That exchange on a pair of complex lines preserves their joint real orientation. The sign computed below concerns the oriented real cokernel on the source.

Proposition

Let BB be a smooth connected compact complex curve of genus at least one with distinct points p,qp,q, and let f0:Y→Bf_0:Y\to B be a smooth connected double cover with a single preimage P,QP,Q of each respective point. Form the nodal target by identifying pp with qq and the nodal source by identifying PP with QQ. Plumb the cover in coordinates xy=t,uv=s,x=u2,y=v2,t=s2.xy=t,\qquad uv=s,\qquad x=u^2,\qquad y=v^2,\qquad t=s^2. Keep the complement of the plumbing discs fixed. Let RR be the ramification divisor away from P,QP,Q, of even degree 2r2r. Fix either root ss of a small nonzero tt. Compare the two target spin structures θ+,θ−\theta_+,\theta_- agreeing off the cut and differing in the gluing sign. For either target spin type described below, the canonical orientations of the two real spin cokernels on this same smoothed cover are opposite under the common orthogonal identification of their ramification residue spaces. At r=0r=0 this compares the signs of the index-zero determinants.

In particular the ordered mixed pair (θ+,θ−)(\theta_+,\theta_-) differs in orientation from the equal pair (θ+,θ+)(\theta_+,\theta_+) by −1-1. If ee is the sign of this mixed pair on the identity cover, the degree-two normalization divides by e2=1e^2=1. The comparison holds on charts with the indicated complement identification and on either smoothing branch. The following proof extends the algebraic orientation test across the finite nodal cover.

1. The two spin plumbings

Write D=P+QD=P+Q. The two types over an irreducible one-node target occur in Cornalba’s description of stable spin curves. Cornalba, §6, Example (6.2)

  • Locally free target spin (Ramond). Choose AA on BB with A2=KB(p+q)A^2=K_B(p+q). Take frames squaring to dx/xdx/x and dy/ydy/y. The logarithmic differential sends the squares of the two pulled-back frames to 2du/u2du/u and 2dv/v2dv/v. The source gluing has the same two choices for either ss. The two target gluings have opposite spin parity.
  • Exceptional target spin (Neveu–Schwarz). Choose A02=KBA_0^2=K_B and frames ℓx2=dx\ell_x^2=dx, ℓy2=dy\ell_y^2=dy. Choose δ\delta with δ2=t\delta^2=t. Their transition is ny=εi(δ/s)nx.n_y=\varepsilon i(\delta/s)n_x. Thus on either branch s=±δs=\pm\delta the two source identifications differ by sign. The relative dualizing sheaf there has generator du/u=−dv/vdu/u=-dv/v. The resulting square map is a unit at the node and agrees with the usual differential off the neck. Evaluation of 𝒪(1)\mathcal O(1) at the two attaching points is an isomorphism, so their common parity is that of A0A_0. In particular an even A0A_0 gives a pair of even target spins.

In each case H2=KY(D)(−R)H^2=K_Y(D)(-R) and the resulting source line HεH_\varepsilon on the nodal curve X=Y/(P∼Q)X=Y/(P\sim Q) is locally free. Write Mε=ωXHε−1M_\varepsilon=\omega_X H_\varepsilon^{-1}. The differential defines σ:Hε→Mε\sigma:H_\varepsilon\to M_\varepsilon, invertible at the node with divisor RR. On the smooth fibers the pair is the usual pulled-back spin and differential. At fixed choice of s/δs/\delta the two matching conditions at the node differ by a sign. On YY put M=KY(D)H−1M=K_Y(D)H^{-1}, E=H0(M/σH)E=H^0(M/\sigma H) and F=MP⊕MQF=M_P\oplus M_Q. Here EE is the same space for both gluings. 3. Transport to smooth fibers and the determinant sign

The complement identification identifies the two orthogonal residue spaces throughout the plumbings. Extend UU there (it may be held fixed for the chosen family). To compare dd through jumps of cohomology, choose a divisor GG of sufficiently many smooth, distinct auxiliary sections away from the neck and RR. Together with UU they give a second maximal isotropic. Their intersection dimension is dsd_s since regular jets enforce absence of poles at GG. This proves that the central parity of dεd_\varepsilon persists on its smoothing.

On a smooth fiber set S=im⁡(H0(Ms)→E)S=\operatorname{im}(H^0(M_s)\to E) and k=h0(Hs)k=h^0(H_s). The residue theorem for the spin operator in Article V, §§4–6 identifies its real cokernel with a positive real form V⊂EV\subset E. With the orientation continued from the complex Dolbeault operator, the real projection V→E/SV\to E/S has sign (−1)k(-1)^k. Both spins are compared with the same complex orientation on E/UE/U. Section 2 gives opposite signs. This calculation requires the Fredholm identification only on smooth fibers. The comparison on the singular fiber used dualizing sheaves, the residue theorem and the two matching conditions.

4. Smoothing roots, automorphisms and the scope of the test

For each nonzero tt the framed plumbing has two roots. The simultaneous deck involution sends (u,v)(u,v) to (−u,−v)(-u,-v), preserving ss and both graphs. It acts by +1+1 on the two pulled-back Ramond frames and by −1-1 on both modified exceptional frames. On the smooth spin determinant its action preserves the continued complex orientation, by equivariance along the mass homotopy using an invariant metric. Changing one coordinate sign can relabel the two roots and need not extend to a deck transformation of the connected normalization. The comparison is made separately at each root with the same automorphism weight for both spin choices. There is no extra orientation sign from enumerating the roots. Reversing the chosen unit of η\eta on the connected cut complement changes the common residue identification by −1-1 on every summand, of total even dimension, hence preserves the comparison.

For a concrete positive-rank case take BB elliptic and A0A_0 a nontrivial two-torsion line. Form a connected double cover branched simply at p,qp,q and two other distinct points, using a square root of their divisor line bundle. This root exists because multiplication by two on Pic⁡0(B)\operatorname{Pic}^0(B) is onto. The smoothed target has genus two and both target spins are even. The residual rank is two. Both projection orientations can be compared even though the rational Euler class on the smooth profile stratum vanishes. Indeed every branch point of a smooth double cover is simple, and the vanishing for an even ramification index follows from the odd-rank orthogonal summand in Article V, §§4–6. When R=0R=0 the sign recovers the determinant sign of a transposition in the unramified model of Article III, Appendix F.

Lee and Parker pair different smoothing choices at fixed spin data in their cancellation formula for spin Hurwitz numbers. The comparison here varies the target spin at a fixed smoothing of a finite cover and also treats residual simple ramification. Lee–Parker, §§5 and 10

The calculation yields the predicted factor −1-1 on the finite contact chart. A compact relative gluing formula must also treat degenerations of this chart, identify its real normal determinant with that of the expanded or contracted stable map, and pair the obstruction class with the relative virtual class with its stack multiplicities. In particular, on a contracted component dfdf vanishes identically, so the sheaf quotient in §2 no longer has finite support. No integrated boundary coefficient or partition trace follows from the present sign. Calculations D6 and D7 extend the comparison to the compact boundary and evaluate the resulting trace.

D2. A contracted elliptic tail at a contact of order two

In the étale smoothing of Calculation D1, move the attaching point of a contracted elliptic tail into the nonseparating neck. Write g≥2g\ge2 for the genus of the smooth target. Its normalization BB at the node has genus g−1g-1. The connected double cover Y→BY\to B branches just at P,QP,Q over the two ends of the neck. Fix the target, its spin data, the identification on the complement of the neck and a choice of smoothing root as in Calculation D1.

There are three conclusions. A separating contracted component contributes a hyperbolic Hodge summand to the spin complex, also in nodal families. On the balanced expansion of this particular contact the pullback of the exceptional target spin has one complex bridge kernel per spin. The corresponding defect on the untailed family has length one in each of two cohomological degrees. Its first obstruction to smoothing singles out one of the two null lines of the residue plane. Changing the target spin exchanges them. Finally, the signed Euler integral of the smooth elliptic-tail component specializes on the compact parameter space of attaching points. In the exceptional target-spin extension its bridge part has magnitude 1/121/12 per smoothing root. That part depends on the extension. Below we distinguish this specialization of an explicit bundle from a relative virtual contribution.

1. Moving the attachment through the node

The smooth cover has plumbing uv=suv=s, xy=t=s2xy=t=s^2, (x,y)=(u2,v2)(x,y)=(u^2,v^2). Write (a,b)(a,b) for the point of attachment, so ab=sab=s. At a=b=0a=b=0 the normalization YY joins the bridge at its two ends and the pointed tail FF attaches at 11. Contracting the target bridge collapses the entire source bridge to the node. Relative expansions and their automorphisms provide the ambient local model for these equations. Jun Li, expanded degenerations

Over the fixed target with labeled branches, a bridge scaling preserving the attaching point is the identity, which also fixes the target scaling by W=Z2W=Z^2. The involution on YY fixes P,QP,Q and acts on (a,b)(a,b) by (−a,−b)(-a,-b) while fixing the marked bridge in the central expanded chart. The pointed tail has its ordinary stack stabilizer. At smooth parameters the deck group acts freely on the moving point of an étale cover. The quotient by the deck group is taken once on the whole parameter space. The chart is over the specified smoothing root ss. The equation t=(ab)2t=(ab)^2 accounts separately for the two roots.

The first-order obstruction to smoothing the tail attachment, in the tangent direction of the expanded target, is the map T1ℙZ1⊗TeF→T1ℙW1⊗H1(F,𝒪F),d(Z2)1⊗∂e.T_1\mathbb P^1_Z\otimes T_eF\longrightarrow T_1\mathbb P^1_W\otimes H^1(F,\mathcal O_F),\qquad d(Z^2)_1\otimes\partial_e. Here ee is the attaching point on FF and ∂e\partial_e is the principal-part connecting map for 𝒪F(e)\mathcal O_F(e). In the chosen coordinates the derivative is two. For a stable one-pointed curve of arithmetic genus one, ∂e\partial_e is an isomorphism, including on the irreducible nodal tail. This follows from H1(𝒪F(e))=0H^1(\mathcal O_F(e))=0 and H0(𝒪F(e))=ℂH^0(\mathcal O_F(e))=\mathbb C. This identifies the attachment smoothing with its tangent obstruction on the expanded chart. On contraction the bridge map is constant, so the same tangent calculation cannot be used there. The other two nodes of the expanded cover have contact order two.

2. Separating a contracted component in the spin complex

Here is a family statement independent of the covering degree. Let Z=S∪FZ=S\cup F over a base TT be obtained by gluing proper flat families of connected nodal curves along smooth sections, with a single separating node between SS and FF. For HH the core complex is acyclic on the whole disk. Equation (1) gives the corresponding correction for a family with a persistent contracted tail. At genus one it adds two dimensions in degree one per spin. The two torsion lengths refer to the parameter dd of this semistable family.

The singular-fiber kernel can also be seen directly. The target-pulled LL restricts to f0*A0f_0^*A_0 on YY and to 𝒪(2)\mathcal O(2) on T0T_0. The square map of the exceptional spin is zero on the target bridge. On the source bridge the ordinary component operator is ∂‾𝒪(2)\bar\partial_{\mathcal O(2)}. On YY it is the smooth spin operator for the branched double cover Y→BY\to B with ordinary differential. It is injective and its real cokernel has rank two by the spin-residue calculation in Article V, §§4–6. Evaluation of H0(𝒪(2))H^0(\mathcal O(2)) at both ends is onto; its kernel H0(𝒪(2)(−0−∞))H^0(\mathcal O(2)(-0-\infty)) is a complex line. Normalization thus gives this line as the matched core kernel and the real plane on YY as its cokernel. At the third point on the bridge a constant tail section takes precisely the required value. Adding the tail preserves the kernel and adds H1(F,𝒪F)⊗L|1H^1(F,\mathcal O_F)\otimes L|_1 to the cokernel, as a quotient or direct summand after a splitting. On each smooth étale core the kernel vanished. This is an explicit failure of constant rank for the componentwise target-pulled operator; transport of an ordinary cokernel bundle of that operator across the seam is impossible. The derived calculation specifies the jump without making an identification of real small-eigenvalue spaces during the smoothing.

Consequences for gluing

The attachment equation, hyperbolic splitting and rank jump distinguish the tangential and normal parts of the problem. The derivative at the tail mark is invertible in the smoothing obstruction even while the target-pulled normal operator has a kernel on the bridge. Twisting by +T0+T_0 restores the dualizing spin complex on the untailed core; (1) tracks the accompanying change of the evaluation line on every separating tail. Equation (3) fixes the compact total while the two extensions assign different integrals to the bridge. A relative degeneration theorem must account for the real orientation of the disappearing kernel and cokernel and identify the resulting relative obstruction class with the absolute one under gluing. The algebraic length-one complexes and the attachment-space integral give explicit data for that comparison. Its real determinant gluing and the relative virtual pairing remain open. Lee and Parker’s localization of small modes concerns spin Hurwitz parity for different smoothings; their analysis supplies a precedent for investigating this comparison. Lee–Parker, §§7–10

D3. Real spin operators at finite contacts

We compute a finite-dimensional reduction of the actual real spin operator through a nonseparating degeneration of the target. We use the exceptional target spin of Calculation D1. Its two gluings include the two distinct even target spins. The expansion of Calculation D2 is the case of one contact of order two.

Finite-cover theorem

Let f:Y→Bf:Y\to B be a finite map of smooth connected compact complex curves. Let BB have genus at least one. Choose two distinct target points and pair their preimages with the same contact orders m1,…,mnm_1,\ldots,m_n, including the contacts of order one. Write m=∑imim=\sum_i m_i, M=m−nM=m-n. Keep all other ramification, of total degree 2r2r, in a fixed complement of the plumbing discs. Fix branch coordinates, smoothing roots, and an isometry of the two spin data on the complement. The target plumbing is xy=txy=t. Choose the semistable spin target with parameter δ2=t\delta^2=t, with exceptional spin of degree one on its rational component and square root A02=KBA_0^2=K_B on BB. Write LL for its pullback to the expanded source. Choose smooth positive Hermitian metrics on these line bundles on the family, with common restriction on YY. For a deck quotient take deck-invariant metrics, obtained by averaging over the finite group. The operator on smooth fibers is D=∂‾+cσD=\bar\partial+c\sigma, where σ\sigma is the spin square map followed by the cover differential and cc is metric conjugation. Orient its determinant by continuation from ∂‾\bar\partial.

Work on a framed disk with simi=ts_i^{m_i}=t, si=di2s_i=d_i^2. We may take t=q2Nt=q^{2N}, N=lcm⁡(mi)N=\operatorname{lcm}(m_i), and di=γiqN/mid_i=\gamma_i q^{N/m_i} for fixed compatible roots. The normalized source acquires a two-pointed rational bridge at each pair. The real space VV represents the cokernel on the normalization, of rank 2M+2r2M+2r. The map b0b_0 is, up to the common stabilization isomorphism, real projection of a specified isotropic subspace of the ramification residue space. We calculate it below. In particular, on an étale smoothing (r=0r=0) the absolute real determinant of this finite block is a continuous positive unit times ∏i|di|2⌊mi2/4⌋.\prod_i |d_i|^{2\lfloor m_i^2/4\rfloor}. \tag{2} This exponent uses the displayed coordinates, the stated trivializations of the finite-dimensional reduction, and the balanced parameters did_i. It describes the vanishing of the determinant of that map, as distinct from singular values in a degenerating L2L^2 metric.

This compares oriented spaces even when their Euler classes vanish.

The class of each limiting force in the cokernel on YY has a direct description. Write aa for its meromorphic polar section with the branch coefficients given below. 5. A compact attachment calculation in every even degree

For a single full contact of even order mm there are examples in every target genus g≥2g\ge 2. The finite-cover theorem computes the predicted sign and the disappearing bridge modes for every partition on the stated chart. Neither root counts nor virtual multiplicities are supplied by the orders in (2).

This realizes the insertion of (1) by a real normal problem with paired endpoints. On a quotient that permutes spin branches, the rational insertion in (1) is invariant. We make no assertion of an individually equivariant spin line for a deck transformation that changes the branch data.

For a cyclic cover with a single full even contact kk, the main deck group has order kk, with inverse characters on the two branches. It preserves the gluing and the descended operator. Such examples exist for every even kk by the cyclic construction of Calculation D3. Here σ=−1\sigma=-1. The cut relative normal pairing is +(g−1)/12+(g-1)/12, and the glued ordinary-target contribution is +k(g−1)/12+k(g-1)/12 for that matched core. In genus two and degree two these are +1/12+1/12 and +1/6+1/6. The resolved spin-target evaluation in Calculation D2 puts +1/12+1/12 on its exceptional curve per smooth root. The intrinsic unbalanced model uses (4) and the target dualizing insertion. An extra seam contribution added to (1) would count part of the same smooth specialization twice.

This proves a virtual pairing with nonzero contact data on the one-elliptic-tail sector. The finite ramified component of the same excess, strata with several ghosts or nonseparating contracted components, and a gluing theorem for the entire split-spin theory still require separate arguments. The result concerns a numerical local theory of a fixed degeneration and does not construct a universal evaluation on arbitrary analytic parameter families.

D5. Collision divisors in the relative first-excess formula

Let a smooth genus-gg target degenerate to an irreducible curve with one ordinary node, g≥2g\ge2. Its normalization is (B,p,q)(B,p,q). In degree m≥2m\ge2 and source genus 2+m(g−1)2+m(g-1), the normal Euler integral for a pair of spin lines splits into a finite-map term and an elliptic-tail term. We compute the specialization of the signed collision divisors representing the finite-map term. For double covers the coefficient on each nodal divisor also has a real-operator interpretation on a neighborhood of the compact divisor. The smooth-target divisor theorem and its numerical evaluations are in Article V, §§4–6.

The cut formula

Choose a projective one-parameter smoothing over R=ℂ[[t]]R=\mathbb C[[t]] transverse to the nodal boundary. Use ordered target branches xy=txy=t and ordinary expanded maps. The two exceptional spin gluings of Calculation D1 agree off the neck and differ by the class dual to its vanishing circle. For this pair set χ(μ)=(−1)m−ℓ(μ)\chi(\mu)=(-1)^{m-\ell(\mu)} on a seam profile μ=(k1,…,kn)\mu=(k_1,\ldots,k_n). For a repeated spin set χ=1\chi=1. Write Cμ=∏ikiC_\mu=\prod_i k_i and κ=c1(KB(p+q))\kappa=c_1(K_B(p+q)).

Cut the target node. Include in the cut data a matching of the fibers over p,qp,q with the same prescribed profile μ\mu. Take the quotient by all automorphisms preserving the matching. Keep all cut sources for which the paired source is connected. In the cut relative stack let JJ range over the components of the following two reduced collision curves, completed by closure, with their matching data.

  • On the nodal curve NN of the Hurwitz surface, identify an unordered pair of distinct unramified sheets over one ordinary target value. The normalized cover is unramified away from the two relative fibers. It can be disconnected.
  • On the triple curve TT of that surface, one point over an ordinary target value has ramification index three. All other ramification is prescribed at the two relative fibers.

Write eJ:J→Be_J:J\to B for the contracted image of the collision and hJ=1h_J=1 on NN, hJ=3h_J=3 on TT. Let Φ\Phi denote the gluing map, including the inclusion of the indicated collision cycle. Then the specialization of the smooth signed-divisor representative of the finite-map Euler product is the following rational zero-cycle class: −18∑μCμχ(μ)∑J with profile μ1hJΦ*(eJ*κ∩[J]).-\frac18\sum_{\mu} C_\mu\chi(\mu) \sum_{J\text{ with profile }\mu}\frac{1}{h_J}\, \Phi_*\big(e_J^*\kappa\cap[J]\big). \tag{1} One may push from the normalizations of the components. At a point where several branches of the same type meet, the normal line used in (1) belongs to the total reduced collision divisor of that type. The formula is for the ordinary target parameter. On a splitting spin or root disk use its actual degree over the chosen parameter as in Calculation D4. There is no further factor for permutations of indices on an already matched cover.

In particular the proper cut geometry determines separately the nodal and triple contributions. In the first ramified source genus these exhaust the smooth finite-map integral. Together with the one-tail term of §5 this gives a numerical degeneration formula for this entire genus in every degree. At the level of rational Chow groups (1) specializes a specified algebraic representative. The real smooth Euler class is identified with it in rational cohomology. We do not assume a Chow-valued real Euler class or an all-profile compact real obstruction bundle.

1. Collision curves on a smooth target

On a smooth target CC, the proper finite-map locus is a smooth surface of the expected dimension. Its nodal and triple curves and the curves where two distinct simple ramification points have equal image are smooth and pairwise disjoint. Article V, §§4–6 identifies the spin Euler class with −1/4-1/4 times the sum of the nodal and triple divisor classes, weighted by the respective single-spin signs. The two-simple-point collision carries zero coefficient. Let DD run through the nodal and triple curves and νD\nu_D be the corresponding normal line on the surface. A rational algebraic representative for the product of the two smooth Euler classes is Zη=116∑Dsa(D)sb(D)iD*(c1(νD)∩[D]).Z_\eta=\frac1{16}\sum_D s_a(D)s_b(D)\,i_{D*} \big(c_1(\nu_D)\cap[D]\big). \tag{2} Take the formula on the generic fiber of the algebraic family after a finite extension splitting the component and spin labels. It determines a rational class on the generic fiber before splitting by transfer of the invariant weighted sum. Its cycle class on smooth complex fibers is the actual Euler product by the cited theorem. The normal-line computation below also constructs (2) by evaluating the target cotangent on the collision curve.

For a nodal map the signs come from the étale cover obtained by normalizing the ordinary node. The product is the sign of its permutation around the vanishing circle for the mixed pair. This includes disconnected normalizations by direct sum. For a triple ramification point rr the signs are the spin parities of f*a(r)f^*a(r) and f*b(r)f^*b(r). The orthogonal direct image f*𝒪(r)f_*\mathcal O(r) has determinant character equal to the sign of sheet monodromy off the branch value, and the three-cycle there is even. The mod-two index gives the same product sign around the vanishing circle. The exceptional spin pair has equal parity, so the base parity contributes +1+1. This proves the factor χ\chi for both types. At a triple point on an inserted target line the permutations about its two ends may have different cycle types. Their signs agree by the product relation with the three-cycle at its interior branch value. For the determinant signs and their expression in sheet monodromy, see Article III, Proposition 14.2, and Article V, Lemma 6.2.

2. Keeping the collision on the expanded target

First mark the collision value on the target. Normalize the ordinary source node on NN and mark the unordered pair over that value. On TT retain the triple ramification point. The resulting covers are admissible covers with fixed branch data and one additional marked target value. In the nodal case two smooth sheets of this auxiliary cover will be identified. Properness of admissible covers gives limits after finite base change, with finite choices for a fixed marked stable target. Disconnected auxiliary covers are handled by taking the corresponding products and finite quotients. Conversely the distinguished nodes can be smoothed by the usual contact equations and the cover away from them follows by étaleness off the branch sections. At the triple section the prescribed map is the constant local model z↦z3z\mapsto z^3. This gives smoothings of each of these marked covers. Cavalieri–Markwig–Ranganathan, §§2.2, 4.2.

As the sole marked value approaches the seam the stable marked target has one inserted rational line carrying it at W=1W=1, with ends 0,∞0,\infty. In the nodal case its normalized inverse image is a union of rational power covers. Identify the two chosen preimages of 1, on the same or on different components. In the triple case its inverse image is a cover branched only at 0,1,∞0,1,\infty, with one three-cycle over 1. The main cover is allowed different profiles at the two sides of the line. Forgetting auxiliary marks gives stable expanded maps because the distinguished collision fixes the target dilation. A level containing only two-ended power covers is unstable and contracts. There are finitely many choices with the value fixed at the seam. There is a unique ordinary node or a unique triple point away from the distinguished nodes, and its image recovers the forgotten mark. Thus these constructions describe all limits of both collision loci in the expanded-map stack. Their supports remain disjoint. The closure of the two-simple-point collision with a common value can be treated by retaining its two distinct relative ramification marks in this same construction. It keeps two simple points over the smooth marking on the inserted level.

Here are the actual transverse deformations. Use labeled étale charts for the following local computations. For completeness, in a hull AA choose distinguished parameters satisfying the power equations, absorbing unit factors by roots over the complete complex ring. Predeformability imposes these equations over Artin bases. The previous tangent calculation leaves at most one further parameter after their differentials vanish. At an ordinary node use the ordinary smoothing parameter. At a triple point take the discriminant of the length-two critical algebra over the base near the marked point. Each cut hull has pure dimension two, and is reduced and smooth on its dense interior. Near these curves the ordinary tangential virtual class agrees in top dimension with the fundamental cycle. The smooth Hurwitz surface, its branch components and their self-intersections were studied in the complex local theory by Bryan and Pandharipande. Article V, §§4–6 supplies the real spin weights on the smooth target. The nonseparating degeneration formula gives the ordinary tangential contact factors. The calculation here identifies the transverse lines of the two collision types on the compact expanded cut, including a change of seam profile, and evaluates the corresponding signed specialization. The twisted real realization proved here is local to the double-cover collision. A compact real normal theory for arbitrary relative profiles, its higher-excess boundary pairings and a universal comparison through individual walls remain open. Bryan–Pandharipande, §4 · Nonseparating gluing, Appendix A.

D6. The real spin obstruction bundle on paired expanded covers

Let a projective genus-gg curve degenerate transversely to an irreducible nodal curve, with g≥2g\ge2. Fix the two branches of its node and write (B,p,q)(B,p,q) for the normalization. On finite maps its positive real form is computed by ramification residues, even when a critical point lies on an inserted target component and even at an ordinary source node. At the first genus above the étale minimum this identifies the ordinary relative cycles of Calculation D5 with integrals of the actual real Euler classes.

Use either the two exceptional spin gluings with the same square root A0A_0 of KBK_B or a repeated exceptional spin. Source curves after pairing are connected of positive degree.

Theorem. At an ordinary source node with branch orders a,ba,b the local summand has dimension a+ba+b. Distinguished source nodes over target seams give no summands.

1. The target spin and its expansions

2. The Fredholm problem on the full family and on its cut

Compose each map to an expansion with contraction to the original balanced spin target. On the universal source pull back HaH_a and the ambient antilinear term of Calculation D6, §1. Near the original crossing its differential factor is 2(UdU‾−VdV‾)2(U\,d\bar U-V\,d\bar V) in the specified frame. It vanishes after contraction on YY and the cylinders. On a smooth fiber the resulting real operator DaD_a is the smooth spin operator up to positive metric deformation. Use matched sections at nodes, and orient its determinant by continuation along ∂‾+u(Da−∂‾)\bar\partial+u(D_a-\bar\partial), 0≤u≤10\le u\le1. This convention retains the signed Thom unit at index zero.

Here is the vanishing argument on any central map, including components occurring only in the special fiber. On a main component Stokes for the spin square gives the nonnegative energy of Calculation D6. Boundary residues are opposite signed multiples of the square of the end value, with multiplier the coarse order kk. Indeed the log derivative of the coarse coordinate has uniformizing order kk times the source stabilizer order, and stack integration divides by that order. A nontrivial fiber character forces the end value to vanish. On each connected part contracted to the original gerbe the mass vanishes, so the square of a kernel section is a constant in the same squared line. Orient the target chain from pp through YY to qq. The divisors of zeros and poles on every nonconstant cylinder or exceptional component have equal total coarse degree. The internal matched orders cancel on summing over the part. Ordinary contracted components add no orders. The signed residues therefore sum to zero, including for maps with different partitions at p,qp,q. Stokes forces vanishing on the positive-degree main components wherever their differential is nonzero. The holomorphic constant-square property on the remaining contracted pieces and matching across nodes propagate vanishing on the connected source. At an ordinary contracted component away from the gerbe its line is a fixed fiber and the same propagation holds.

The orbifold degree of HaH_a is m(g−1)m(g-1). At a balanced node with nontrivial sign fiber the two ages sum to one and the invariant evaluation fiber is zero. At a trivial fiber the ages vanish and one complex matching row occurs. Normalization and orbifold Riemann–Roch give real index −2n-2n. The family of cokernels VaV_a therefore has constant real rank 2n2n on the full transversal-map family. More explicitly, on a balanced plumbing one uses Dolbeault stabilization by forms off the nodes on the finite uniformizing charts. The ambient pullback term satisfies the shrinking-neck bound there as in Calculation D6, §2. Restriction by finite-group averaging preserves the inverse estimates and gives invariant stabilizations. After the surjectivity stabilization, the kernel and quotient charts give a continuous bundle, with the same determinant continuation. This argument works directly on the given source with its actual finite group, even when the spin action has a kernel. It uses no identification of smooth invariant functions with smooth functions in a powered coordinate. The ranks of the separate relative kernels may jump. Nodal stabilization, Siebert §§4.1–4.4.

Let KηK_\eta retain the split expansion, the root labels, and the identifications of the two source marking gerbes. Representability gives f=2/gcd⁡(2,k)f=2/\gcd(2,k) and c=k/gcd⁡(2,k)c=k/\gcd(2,k). For a common twist rr divisible by all cc, the source stabilizer is 2r/k2r/k. Its distinguished generator maps to the original sign character as (−1)k(-1)^k. Thus only even kk have invariant end values. Write Da,X,Da,YD_{a,X},D_{a,Y} for the operators on the two relative sources with independent section domains, retaining matching at their internal nodes. Write FjF_j for the invariant XX-end line at an even root, and τa,j\tau_{a,j} for the isomorphism from the other end given by the chosen gluing. Take W1,p0W^{1,p_0} sections with p0>2p_0>2 so point evaluations exist. The required augmented Fredholm map is (u,v)↦(Da,Xu,Da,Yv,(u(j)−τa,jv(j))j:2∣kj).(u,v)\longmapsto \left(D_{a,X}u, D_{a,Y}v, \big(u(j)-\tau_{a,j}v(j)\big)_{j:\,2\mid k_j}\right). \tag{2} The evaluation-difference map onto ⨁Fj\bigoplus F_j is surjective by local invariant cutoffs. Its kernel is the glued section domain, including the automatic zero equalities at odd roots. Inclusion of the two form spaces with zero last row consequently identifies the cokernel of the glued operator with the cokernel of (2), and identifies their kernels. The identification extends over families by finite-dimensional stabilization and the exact sequence for normalization. At the Dolbeault endpoint this sequence is complex-linear. 3. Virtual gluing and rational transfer

Let K→SK\to S be the proper transversal-map family. Its relative obstruction theory gives the fiber virtual classes by Gysin restriction. Pass to rational Borel–Moore homology and cap the total virtual class with e(Va)e(Vb)e(V_a)e(V_b). The virtual complex fiber dimension is 2n2n and the total Euler degree is 4n4n in real grading. Proper push to the smooth base therefore gives a multiple of its fundamental class. Compatibility of the fiber Gysin map with cap by a class on KK and with proper push identifies this multiple at a smooth fiber and at zero. There is one comparison of fiber degrees over the base with coordinate ss. The input from the algebraic theory is the relative virtual class and its splitting, so the argument includes its vertical components and requires only a topological real Euler class. Abramovich–Fantechi, §§4.6, 5.5–5.8.
