4. Which splittings distinguish the two spins?

The ratio H−/H+H_-/H_+ is a square-trivialized line. On each half of the normalized target choose square-compatible identifications of the two spins. They extend by contraction along the trees of cylinders on that half. Their transition ratio across DD is +1+1 at pp and −1-1 at qq, up to simultaneously changing the sign on one half. Choose the same metric on the identified restrictions. Pullback to the source multiplies both spin clutches by the same identifications of marking gerbes, hence their ratio stays the indicated sign at every even root.

On a finite labeling cover for the relative vertices let γj\gamma_j denote these edge signs. If signs ϵv\epsilon_v on the vertices satisfy γj=ϵvX(j)ϵvY(j)(2∣kj),\gamma_j=\epsilon_{v_X(j)}\epsilon_{v_Y(j)} \qquad(2\mid k_j), \tag{5} then multiplication by ϵv\epsilon_v on each connected piece intertwines the two versions of (2), with multiplication by ϵvX(j)\epsilon_{v_X(j)} on matching rows. The same holds along the Dolbeault orientation homotopy. At its complex endpoint these identifications preserve the determinant orientation. Hence the oriented Euler classes agree, including in rank zero. Transfer through the vertex-label cover gives equality in rational cohomology on the original splitting. On a spanning forest one can always solve (5) inductively. Extending the solution to the remaining edges is equivalent to positive product around every cycle. This proves the cycle criterion and shows why odd contacts can be omitted even when they connect distinct vertices of the source. With no even roots (2) is the direct sum of the relative operators. Their kernels then vanish, and their separately oriented cokernels on the compatible relative spaces give the product by complex normalization and continuation. The two relative operators are independent of the clutch in this sector. In particular every graph with only odd contacts at either color gives equal mixed and repeated contributions.

There is a further restriction on the exceptional side. On a connected relative YY-source the operator is Dolbeault on a line with structure group μ2\mu_2, since YY contracts to the original gerbe. A holomorphic section has constant square. It vanishes identically unless the associated double torsor is trivial, in which case a square-normalized nonzero section trivializes the line. This dichotomy is locally constant in the family. The torsor is proper and flat over the base with geometrically reduced nodal fibers, as is its coarse curve. For the latter assertion use exact finite-group invariants in characteristic zero in balanced charts, which commute with base change and are direct summands for flatness. Its Stein factor is finite étale after localizing on the base, so the number of geometric connected components is locally constant. A trivial double torsor on a connected curve has two components and a nontrivial one has one. Stein factorization for proper flat families with geometrically reduced fibers, Lemma 37.53.8.

On a sector where a YY-vertex has nontrivial torsor, multiply its evaluations v(j)v(j) in (2) by λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]. Any kernel element has zero section at that entire vertex by its Dolbeault equation. Its equations therefore agree with the original kernel equations at every λ\lambda and the augmented cokernel rank stays constant. At λ=0\lambda=0 its former rows are just u(j)=0u(j)=0 in the XX-end fibers. They carry no clutch. Orient this homotopy by continuing the determinant, or by scaling the evaluations also along the Dolbeault path, where the zero-mass comparison is complex-linear. These vertices and their incident edges can thus be deleted before testing (5). Apply the argument on the vertex-label cover and descend the Euler equality by transfer. This retains the vanishing conditions from the deleted rows in the operator. Only their edges are deleted from the sign test.

There is also a vanishing for the product itself. For a YY-vertex FF of genus jj let A=R1π*H|FA=R^1\pi_*H|_F be the Dolbeault cokernel there. It is a vector bundle on each of the locally constant torsor sectors, by cohomology and base change. If oo is the number of its external odd ends then orbifold Riemann–Roch and balanced internal normalization give rk⁡A=j−1+o/2+h0(F,H).\operatorname{rk} A=j-1+o/2+h^0(F,H). Projection of the form component in (2) to AA gives a surjection Va,η→AV_{a,\eta}\to A of real vector bundles. Indeed any class in AA can be represented by a forcing on FF alone, and images of (2) project to zero. The fixed square-compatible identification on the exceptional side gives the same complex quotient for the second spin. Both oriented real Euler classes are consequently divisible by ctop(A)c_\mathrm{top}(A), orienting their kernels by the exact sequences.

For the double torsor TF→FT_F\to F, the pushforward of the structure sheaf splits into its trivial and sign lines. Thus R1π*𝒪TF=R1π*𝒪F⊕AR^1\pi_*\mathcal O_{T_F}=R^1\pi_*\mathcal O_F\oplus A. The structure-sheaf cohomologies agree with those of the coarse nodal curves by tameness. Apply Mumford’s relation c(E)c(E∨)=1c(E)c(E^\vee)=1 for the Hodge bundle to those two families. On a labeling cover one can stabilize each positive-genus connected coarse curve with a marked point when necessary: FF has a relative marking, whose inverse images supply markings on each connected covering component. Rational components removed by stabilization preserve H1(𝒪)H^1(\mathcal O) and genus-zero Hodge factors are trivial. Duality and division of total Chern classes give c(A)c(A∨)=1c(A)c(A^\vee)=1. If AA has positive rank, the component of twice that complex codimension gives ctop(A)2=0c_\mathrm{top}(A)^2=0. Transfer removes the labels. The mixed and repeated products therefore both vanish on that sector. The three possible exceptional vertices surviving this test are a trivial torsor of genus zero, a nontrivial torsor of genus zero with exactly two odd ends, and a nontrivial torsor of genus one with only even ends. A trivial torsor necessarily has only even ends. Mumford’s Hodge relation, Faber–Pandharipande, §1.

5. A single relative integral in degree two

In degree two the only graph that can contribute to the difference has one connected vertex on each side and two parallel edges of order two, one of each color. Indeed a negative cycle uses both colors and a contact of order two exhausts that color. The exceptional vertex must have trivial torsor by the evaluation homotopy, and genus zero by the Hodge vanishing. The main relative genus is h−1h-1 since the graph has first Betti number one.

Use the minimal twisting choice, with r=1r=1 for both possible degree-two orders. The exceptional map contracts to a map to YY which lifts to ℙ1\mathbb P^1 by triviality of its torsor. The lift has coarse degree one. More precisely the relative map has no expansion or attached ghosts. Every nonconstant normalized coarse component of a putative expansion maps onto a two-ended rational target and has at least two preimages of its ends. If vv is the number of nonconstant components and ll the number of internal source nodes over target joins, the sum of these numbers of preimages is 2+2l2+2l. The genus-zero source graph is a tree, so l≤v−1l\le v-1. Equality follows and each component has exactly two ends. Each normalized coarse map is then a power map by Riemann–Hurwitz. The join edges span all nonconstant components, so any remaining tree of contracted rational components would have an unstable leaf. Any inserted target level with only these power maps admits a nontrivial common dilation lifting to the covers, contrary to expansion stability. The remaining relative map is the atlas ℙ1→Y\mathbb P^1\to Y. Its automorphism group is the deck group μ2\mu_2. The two relative markings are transverse on uniformizers, and the atlas is étale, so the relative deformation complex is acyclic. Equivalently the differential identifies the two logarithmic tangent lines on ℙ1\mathbb P^1. This component has virtual class [Bμ2][B\mu_2]. Abramovich–Fantechi, Appendix C.2.

For target genus two take distinct even smooth spins in the indicated degeneration. Write s(t)=2sin⁡(t/2)s(t)=2\sin(t/2). For every source genus simultaneously the total on this one graph type (summing its genus distributions and gluing choices) is ∑h≥3(L2,h+,−−L2,h+,+)t2h−2=−2s(t)2s(2t)2=−8t4+103t6+O(t8).\sum_{h\ge3}\big(L_{2,h}^{+,-}-L_{2,h}^{+,+}\big)t^{2h-2} =-2s(t)^2s(2t)^2=-8t^4+\frac{10}{3}t^6+O(t^8). \tag{6} Indeed the mixed series is −s(t)4/2-s(t)^4/2 by Calculation A2. The repeated-spin series is the connected degree-two balanced series: the two partitions each contribute s(t)2s(2t)2s(t)^2s(2t)^2, and passage to the logarithm subtracts s(t)4/2s(t)^4/2. This also recovers the leading difference for a genus-gg target directly: nonzero binary characters classify connected unramified double covers, each with deck order two. The repeated count is (22g−1)/2(2^{2g}-1)/2 and the mixed character sum is −1/2-1/2, by Article III, Appendix F. The difference −22g−1-2^{2g-1} is necessarily carried by the full-contact graph. Equation (6) localizes a series obtained independently on a smooth target. Its coefficients are not evaluations of separate relative vertices.

For any g≥2g\ge2, let KXK_X be the relative degree-two genus-(h−1)(h-1) stack on XX with one full marking at each color. Denote its two evaluation maps to Bμ2B\mu_2 by evp,evq\mathrm{ev}_p,\mathrm{ev}_q. After fixing the identifications on the exceptional target, the atlas deck transformation acts by sign at both fibers. Its evaluation map is the diagonal Bμ2→(Bμ2)2B\mu_2\to (B\mu_2)^2. Consequently the matched stack K̃X=KX×(Bμ2)2Bμ2\widetilde K_X=K_X\mathop{\times}_{(B\mu_2)^2}B\mu_2 is a representable degree-two étale cover of KXK_X, with pullback virtual class. In (3) the two orders of the colors cancel 2!2! and the split multiplicity is one. The relative kernel of the atlas is the line of constant flat sections, with zero cokernel. Its evaluations identify the two end lines on this cover. Eliminate its surjective Dolbeault block in (2) by any invariant right inverse, then eliminate the constant line against the first matching row. Both eliminations have the complex determinant orientation at zero mass and continue along the mass path. Equivalently the cokernels are identified by inclusion using representatives with zero exceptional forcing and zero first row. On the two sheets the remaining main operator is u↦(DXu,u(q)−Tu(p))u\mapsto(D_Xu,u(q)-T u(p)) with TT or −T-T as the end identification. Write eT,e−Te_T,e_{-T} for its two Euler classes on K̃X\widetilde K_X. The deck involution exchanges them and preserves the virtual class. On this stack the mixed term is eTe−Te_Te_{-T} and the repeated term is eT2e_T^2. Symmetrizing the latter gives L2,h+,−−L2,h+,+=−12∫[K̃X]vir(eT−e−T)2.L_{2,h}^{+,-}-L_{2,h}^{+,+} =-\tfrac12\int_{[\widetilde K_X]^\mathrm{vir}} (e_T-e_{-T})^2. \tag{7} Equivalently it is minus the integral on KXK_X of the square of the class in the sign local system whose pullback is eT−e−Te_T-e_{-T}. Formula (7) includes all stable maps on the main relative factor. For the genus-two degeneration it gives the series (6), hence integrals of the square on the double cover of 1616 and −20/3-20/3 in source genera three and four. In genus three the main covers are the four square roots on the elliptic normalization branched at p+qp+q, each of deck order two. The two clutches give opposite determinant signs at each by Calculation D1, so the square has value four on a stack of degree four, independently recovering 1616.

The two-component semistable model gives (1) in rational homology in all genera. Identifying a separate state on each half for general even profiles, computing individual higher-genus wall corrections, and lifting this comparison to universal cycle classes remain open. Calculation D6 treats a different compactification of the one-node cut. No termwise comparison of the two target models is used here.

Marked covers and polar crossings

E1. The normal twist at a ramified quartic tower

Let DtD_t be a smooth fixed-symbol path on the normal bundle NN of degree 2g−22g-2 over a genus-gg curve CC, g≥2g\ge2. Suppose D0D_0 is invertible on the base and f:Y→Cf:Y\to C is a smooth connected double cover with b>0b>0 distinct simple branch values, a one-dimensional odd pullback kernel, and an embedded graph γ=(f,ξ)\gamma=(f,\xi) of a generator. Assume the derivative WfW_f in the Hurwitz and time directions is an isomorphism, and write ηf\eta_f for its absolutely oriented sign. Use the homogeneous graph almost complex structure of D0D_0 on the total space of NN, with holomorphic projection, standard vertical complex structure, and holomorphic sections on covers precisely the solutions of the pulled-back linear equation. Denote the normal operator of this particular embedded γ\gamma by AA.

Take a connected étale double p:X→Yp:X\to Y of character λ≠0\lambda\ne0 and put h=fph=fp. Write AλA^\lambda for the twist of AA by the flat real sign line on YY. Its index is zero since the ambient first Chern number on γ\gamma is zero. The genus of XX is 2g(Y)−12g(Y)-1. The graph (h,p*ξ)(h,p^*\xi) has image γ\gamma with multiplicity two.

Proposition. At the smooth map hh, the pullback h*D0h^*D_0 has just the inherited kernel line and its full Hurwitz-and-time derivative is an isomorphism if and only if AλA^\lambda is invertible. In that case the point hh is isolated in the fixed-genus projectivized kernel incidence and its local contribution to the change of the ordinary Euler integral is 2ηfϵ(Aλ)|Aut⁡C(h)|.\frac{2\eta_f\,\epsilon(A^\lambda)} {|\operatorname{Aut}_C(h)|}. \tag{1} This is an individual smooth-point contribution at the given genus. The source moduli stack includes other ramified or nodal covers, and a tower can have higher-genus stable maps attached to its image.

Proof. Work on the chart with individually identified ramification disks and the complex orientation. For maps to the fixed curve with variable domain the deformation complex [TX→dhh*TC][TX\xrightarrow{dh}h^*TC] is quasi-isomorphic, with the usual tangent shift, to its torsion cokernel. Each simple critical point contributes one independent complex velocity in the tangent to CC at its image. There is no obstruction. Two critical points have the same branch value here but are distinct on XX and give different skyscraper summands. The upper deck involution swaps the two summands over each ramification point of ff. Its invariant tangent space is TfℋfT_f\mathcal H_f and its anti-invariant space T−T^- is the complex bb-plane of opposite branch velocities. Intrinsically its summands are Tf(r)C⊗ℝλrT_{f(r)}C\otimes_{\mathbb R}\lambda_r.

Consider the fixed-time linearized graph equation with variable domain at G=γpG=\gamma p. Projection to CC gives the preceding horizontal complex. Its vertical subcomplex has operator h*D0h^*D_0, since the graph equation is linear in height. Alternatively GG is an immersion and its tangent and domain variations cancel, leaving the normal operator p*Ap^*A. To see the cancellation, project vector-field variations along GG to the normal quotient and use that dG:TX→TG(TX)dG:TX\to TG(TX) is an isomorphism of complex lines. The remaining tangent variations have operator ∂‾TX\bar\partial_{TX}, with infinitesimal changes of complex structure as its full equation target modulo infinitesimal reparametrizations. Thus this tangent/domain complex is acyclic. The induced normal operator is the pullback of the one along γ\gamma because pp is locally biholomorphic. The description is equivariant for the upper involution. Bai–Swaminathan, §4.2.1 and Lemma 5.9 · Normal operator and infinitesimal deformations, Doan–Walpuski.

Taking the anti-invariant part of the first description and using the second gives the exact sequence, with Fλ=(f*D0)λF_\lambda=(f^*D_0)^\lambda, 0→ker⁡Fλ→ker⁡Aλ→T−→δξcoker⁡Fλ→coker⁡Aλ→0.0\longrightarrow\ker F_\lambda\longrightarrow\ker A^\lambda \longrightarrow T^-\xrightarrow{\delta_\xi}\operatorname{coker} F_\lambda \longrightarrow\operatorname{coker} A^\lambda\longrightarrow0. The connecting map differentiates the equation a*D0u=0a^*D_0u=0 in the horizontal direction at u=p*ξu=p^*\xi and projects to the vertical cokernel. A different lift or trivialization changes the derivative by an image vector. This is exactly the anti-invariant block of the intrinsic wall derivative evaluated on the inherited generator, up to the conventional simultaneous sign of a connecting map. Its source has even real dimension, so this latter sign has no effect on its degree. If AλA^\lambda is invertible then FλF_\lambda is injective and δξ\delta_\xi is an isomorphism. Conversely those two properties force both the kernel and cokernel of AλA^\lambda to vanish. The complementary invariant block is the entire lower wall derivative, including time. This proves the equivalence.

For orientations the graph complex has the absolute Cauchy–Riemann determinant. In the anti-invariant splitting its determinant is the product of the complex orientation of T−T^- with the absolute determinant of FλF_\lambda. Canceling the tangent and domain directions gives the absolute determinant of AλA^\lambda. These determinant identifications preserve the orientations: deform the triangular operators to their complex-linear parts, preserving their tangent, vertical and quotient symbols and the upper involution. At the complex endpoint the determinant sequence has the complex orientations. For an invertible AλA^\lambda, the sign of δξ\delta_\xi is consequently ϵ(Aλ)\epsilon(A^\lambda). The real dimension of the anti block is 2b2b, so changing ξ\xi to −ξ-\xi, reversing the convention for its connecting map, or moving time past this block does not change its sign. The signed degree of the full derivative is ηfϵ(Aλ)\eta_f\epsilon(A^\lambda).

On a chart of smooth maps the full cokernel at the crossing is real (4b+1)(4b+1)-dimensional, the kernel one-dimensional, and the Hurwitz-and-time chart has real dimension 4b+14b+1. On a small linking sphere the cokernel is the quotient by the line spanned by the column, with Euler integral twice its signed local degree since χ(S4b)=2\chi(S^{4b})=2. At these smooth fixed-target covers the unperturbed tangential virtual class is the ordinary fundamental class of the Hurwitz chart. Division by its stabilizer gives (1). This use of the linking sphere does not require the map GG itself to be simple. Bai–Swaminathan, Lemma 6.10.

There are exactly two maps from XX to the specified YY over CC, differing by its lower involution τ\tau: this follows on function fields since Y/CY/C is quadratic Galois. Hence |Aut⁡C(h)|=2|Stab⁡⟨τ⟩(λ)||\operatorname{Aut}_C(h)|=2|\operatorname{Stab}_{\langle\tau\rangle}(\lambda)|. When λ\lambda is fixed, a lift of τ\tau squares to the identity: on the two-point fiber over a ramification point of ff its square fixes both points, whereas the upper deck involution is free. The three nonidentity elements therefore give a Klein four group. Distinct λ\lambda exchanged by τ\tau give one tower over CC and equal twist signs; fiber negation carries γ\gamma to itself over τ\tau and preserves its absolute determinant. If all the indicated twists are regular, the sum of (1) over the inequivalent étale upper doubles of this fixed ff is ηf2∑0≠λ∈H1(Y;𝔽2)ϵ(Aλ).\frac{\eta_f}{2} \sum_{0\ne\lambda\in H^1(Y;\mathbb F_2)} \epsilon(A^\lambda).

Regular twists under perturbations preserving the lower wall

Theorem. Suppose at one simple ramification point the projected antilinear jet of the lower equation is nonzero, in the sense of Article IV, §§2–3 and Appendices A–B. By arbitrarily small smooth fixed-symbol perturbations of the operator on CC which preserve ff and its chosen kernel section ξ\xi, one can make all AλA^\lambda for 0≠λ∈H1(Y;𝔽2)0\ne\lambda\in H^1(Y;\mathbb F_2) invertible simultaneously. This property is open and dense in a small neighborhood in the perturbation space described below. The lower crossing remains transverse. Thus the sum from the smooth towers is an odd integer times 1/21/2 at such a wall; in particular it cannot vanish.

Allowed variations. At an unramified value use the normal identification of a graph sheet with the vertical bundle: a graph varying with its projection held fixed satisfies the original equation on this disk. In these coordinates AA on either sheet is D0D_0. The normal section ss obtained by differentiating real fiber dilations is represented by the sheet height ξ\xi and is nonzero here. The lower involution τ\tau is induced on the graph by fiber negation; its derivative identifies the normal equations on the two sheets and preserves the global radial section.

Write locally D0=∂‾N+BD_0=\bar\partial_{N}+B, with BB conjugate-linear, in a frame holomorphic for the complex-linear part. Near the chosen ramification point w=z2w=z^2 and ξ(z)=zv+O(|z|2)\xi(z)=zv+O(|z|^2) with v≠0v\ne0. The assumed [B(0)v]≠0[B(0)v]\ne0 modulo ℂv\mathbb Cv implies B(w)ξ(z)∉ℂξ(z)B(w)\xi(z)\notin\mathbb C\xi(z) in a punctured neighborhood. They annihilate −ξ-\xi on the other sheet as well. On a smaller disk these variations can realize any smooth tensor on N/ℝξN/\mathbb R\xi; multiplication by a bump extends it by zero. They preserve the graph exactly and, on these sheets, produce those same zeroth-order variations of the normal operator. Take a small neighborhood of zero in this perturbation space so that [Bξ]≠0[B\xi]\ne0 still holds on a fixed smaller disk and the simple transverse lower crossing persists. A bump in time, equal to one at the crossing, incorporates the perturbation in the original path.

Noninvariant characters. Let μ≠0\mu\ne0 with τ*μ≠μ\tau^*\mu\ne\mu, and suppose AμA^\mu has a nonzero solution uu. On the selected sheet use flat real sign frames for μ\mu and τ*μ\tau^*\mu. Transport the other-sheet value of uu to this sheet by the differential of fiber negation and write it as u′u'. Thus u′u' globally solves the twist by τ*μ\tau^*\mu on YY, and on the disk s,u,u′s,u,u' solve the same equation. On the common connected étale cover of YY trivializing the two characters they give solutions with three distinct deck characters 1,μ,τ*μ1,\mu,\tau^*\mu. Each is nonzero and they are linearly independent as global real sections.

If u=asu=a s with complex aa on a disk, the equation modulo ℂs\mathbb Cs gives (a‾−a)[Bs]=0(\bar a-a)[Bs]=0. Thus aa is real where [Bs]≠0[Bs]\ne0, and the ordinary Leibniz rule gives ∂‾a=0\bar\partial a=0. It is constant. Unique continuation would make uu a constant multiple of ss on the common cover, contrary to their distinct characters. Consequently s,us,u are complex independent on a subdisk. If u′u' lay in their real span throughout that subdisk, we could write u′=as+duu'=a s+d u with smooth real coefficients. Applying the equation and using complex independence yields ∂‾a=∂‾d=0\bar\partial a=\bar\partial d=0. Constant coefficients again contradict the deck characters after continuation. Hence s,u,u′s,u,u' are real independent on an open disk.

Consider the universal equation on nonzero sections for the allowed operator variations. An adjoint annihilator of its derivative solves the homogeneous adjoint equation by variation of the section. On the last disk, tensors killing ss can prescribe arbitrary independent values on uu and u′u'. Testing with such tensors forces the adjoint to vanish on both sheets, then everywhere by unique continuation on the connected curve. This proves surjectivity. Fiberwise the source operator is Fredholm of index zero. Dividing by the real scaling of a nonzero solution gives index −1-1 for projection of the universal projective incidence to the perturbation space. Sard–Smale gives generic absence of such solutions.

Invariant characters. If τ*μ=μ\tau^*\mu=\mu, lift τ\tau to the flat sign line. It squares to one, since the square is a parallel automorphism and acts as one on a real sign fiber over a fixed point. The twisted normal operator splits into two real eigensystems. Each has index zero. Indeed at a fixed point of τ\tau the ambient action has a positive horizontal line and two negative vertical lines; quotient by the vertical tangent of the graph leaves one of each. Twisting by the sign fiber preserves the unordered pair. Deform the normal operator to an invariant Dolbeault operator and take invariant and anti-invariant direct images separately on CC. For the invariant direct image the pullback evaluation to the twisted normal bundle is an isomorphism away from ramification and has length-one cokernel at each ramification point: in equivariant holomorphic frames with signs +,−+,- its generating sections are e+e_+ and ze−z e_-. The anti-invariant case interchanges the roles of the two frames. Each rank-two direct image therefore has degree (2g(Y)−2−b)/2=2g−2(2g(Y)-2-b)/2=2g-2 and index zero by Riemann–Roch.

For a nonzero solution in one eigensystem, the same complex-collinearity argument for s,us,u uses the nontrivial character μ\mu on YY. There is a disk where variations killing ss have arbitrary value on uu. On the other sheet the kernel and the adjoint in the same eigensystem transform by the same sign and the same normal symmetry. With equivariant metrics the two integrals in the annihilator test are equal. Thus the adjoint vanishes by the same argument. Projectivized index −1-1 separately in the two eigensystems gives generic absence of both kernels.

These transversality tests can be made in a sufficiently high finite differentiability completion, using W1,pW^{1,p} sections for p>2p>2 and localized bump variations. Surjectivity follows from the Fredholm range and the adjoint test. Open invertibility permits smooth approximation of the resulting perturbations in the real subbundle of tensors killing ss. Starting at any smooth admissible perturbation with any prescribed finite collection of smooth seminorm bounds gives density in the smooth topology. There are only 22g(Y)−12^{2g(Y)}-1 nontrivial characters, so simultaneous invertibility is still open and dense. The sum in (1) over those characters uses this odd number of signs with the common factor ηf/2\eta_f/2. It is a local sum in the proper stable-map space at genus 2g(Y)−12g(Y)-1.

For generic paths the simultaneous regularity also follows on the universal lower-wall incidence. Take the regular marked lower-cover chart with a normalized generator of its kernel line. Its projection to the fixed-symbol operator space is Fredholm of index −1-1 (the bb complex branch parameters offset the real operator index −2b-2b, and projectivization removes one real dimension). Work locally so the upper character, and in the invariant case its eigenspace, are identified throughout the family. The smooth-cover equations give smooth Fredholm families on these charts, using coefficients of sufficiently high differentiability for the normal linearization along the graph. For the universal equation of a second marked kernel line, the fixed-graph variations just tested are already tangent to the lower incidence. They supply the same surjectivity there. Its projection to the lower incidence therefore has index −1-1, and its composite to operator space has index −2-2. Relative parametric transversality for a path avoids this image. Countably many smooth Hurwitz charts, branch profiles and choices of finite character suffice; each simple lower incidence has the projected jet for a generic path by Article IV, §§2–3 and Appendices A–B. This gives the tower formula at every ramified ordinary double crossing on such a path. It does not require separate transversality of primitive quartic kernel graphs.

The other quartic loci, calculated in Groups E and F, include a double graph joined to degree-two curves at zero height and pairs of nonzero double graphs joined at ramification. There the odd section vanishes at the joins and independent real scalings can match. The direct-node argument for a single line and the smooth-tower comparison above do not yet evaluate those loci.

Separating the sheets over the zero section

Fix the height of Γ\Gamma by a real normalization of the generator. A small neighborhood U⊂NU\subset N of Γ∪C\Gamma\cup C admits an mm-sheeted covering p:Ũ→Up:\widetilde U\to U that is trivial along Γ\Gamma and restricts to uu along CC. To construct it, use tubular neighborhoods of the two embedded curves meeting in disjoint small contractible neighborhoods of their bb crossing points. The two tangent complex lines at such a point are distinct. They span a real four-plane, and local coordinates straighten the two embedded disks to coordinate disks. Equivalently a regular neighborhood retracts to the two surfaces glued at the bb points. Glue the trivial cover of the graph tube and the pullback of uu on the zero-section tube by a bijection on each overlap. At rir_i send a distinguished copy Γ0\Gamma^0 to sis_i; the bijections can be chosen independently. Transitivity on the fiber over CC gives connectedness. The lifted zero section is an embedded TT. It meets Γ0\Gamma^0 in precisely one point above each ramification point, with distinct tangent lines, even though mm different source sheets in the original zero section coincide in NN. The construction uses a neighborhood of the union. A lift of ff to the target curve TT is unnecessary.

The central graph map and every contracted decoration have a unique lift whose nonzero component lies on Γ0\Gamma^0. On the zero component this lift is the identity parametrization of the chosen copy of TT. At the first join its value is prescribed, and path lifting fixes it everywhere. Constant connected blocks lift constantly with the values prescribed at their ends. This gives one choice also around the cycles made by several joins. A deck automorphism of uu fixing any one point is the identity. Thus replacing the tuple (si)(s_i) by its simultaneous deck translate gives an isomorphic finite map, and different orbits give distinct maps. The lower deck involution fixes all rir_i and acts by sign on the central line.

We use this lift locally on the space of normalized sections. On a chart of stabilized maps with universal domain E→BE\to B, take the graph of the chosen lifted map in E×ŨE\times\widetilde U. The projection 1×p1\times p is a local diffeomorphism in the target variable and is injective on this compact graph, since the domain point is retained. It is injective on a neighborhood of the graph: otherwise two different points with equal images approach the compact graph and converge, up to a subsequence, to the same point, contradicting local injectivity. In the relative graph topology a nearby map, including one with smoothed nodes, has graph in the image of this neighborhood, hence it has a unique nearby lift. One can also lift the short-pointwise geodesic homotopy from the central map composed with a domain collapse. Both descriptions preserve the original map to CC. Forgetful maps, automorphisms preserving the normalized lift, and transition maps act on the lifts by uniqueness. This identifies local mapping charts, including their stabilized equations when the slices and forms are transported by dpdp. It is not an integration over all lifts of an unpointed map. A nonregular mm-sheeted cover need not give mm such lifts. Swaminathan, definitions of the relative topology and local chart construction.

Contracted components and the virtual comparison

Fix kk. Properness of GI,s,kG_{I,s,k} follows by gluing evaluation fibers of the degree-one maps to YY and TT, with the prescribed marks, and proper spaces of two-pointed contracted curves of positive arithmetic genus at any bridged join. The remaining components are included in the two degree-one map spaces. Distribute k−Hk-H among the factors and take their finite union. In the lifted graph the two positive images are embedded with multiplicity one. A connected constant block with two positive ends can only join the two different components. Its image determines its joining point. The same holds for direct nodes. These facts recover II and the tuple modulo deck equivalence, also at colliding attachment marks. Restricting sections to the normalized components and matching on each constant block gives exactly the original real kernel line.

Here are the modifications to the displacement and virtual argument in Article IV, §§2–3 and Appendices A–B. Choose a disk of regular values away from the bb branch values, and label the two sheets of YY there up to the lower involution. These assertions also hold at an operator with kernel by adding finite-dimensional supplements first. Bai–Swaminathan, Appendix B, (B.5)–(B.9).

The invariant part has the oriented determinant of the base operator. To check this, a homogeneous invariant solution descends off the branch values and extends by bounded removability. The same holds with forcing pulled back from smooth base forms away from the special values, by subtracting local solutions there. On a nodal double use the normalization and matching, and on the trivalent component use constant invariant sections. The invariant index is the base index, by deformation to the complex-linear finite pushforward, with the constants on the inserted bridge imposing the same matching. Stabilize the base by forms on regular disks: the stabilized invariant and base kernels coincide, and this identifies their determinant lines. The isomorphism is complex-oriented at a complex operator and continues along all real operators. The polar column is odd. Thus the two odd families have real indices −4-4 and −2-2. At a regular endpoint their cokernels carry the orientations of FF and F/P(S)F/P(S) multiplied by ϵ(D)\epsilon(D). All exchanged even-dimensional factors preserve orientation.

Perturbations preserving a lower wall

Let f:Y→Cf:Y\to C be the lower double, with chosen odd generator ξ\xi. Fix a disk of regular target values on which a sheet of its embedded graph has nonzero height. Perturb DD by smooth real zeroth-order tensors supported there and annihilating ξ\xi on this sheet. They also annihilate the opposite height. A small perturbation preserves the lower kernel exactly as a line, its branch/time transversality and any open jet hypotheses imposed on the original crossing.

Consider a nonzero odd upper solution, ordinary or augmented, denoted by HH on the punctured source. In the augmented problem it equals a principal part plus a smooth section and solves the homogeneous equation away from the mark. After deleting all branch values and poles, the upper and lower sign characters are different: the lower has more than two branch values and the upper has two or zero. On the connected common cover their lifts transform by distinct characters. On some regular subdisk of the testing disk HH and ξ\xi are real-linearly independent. Otherwise H=aξH=a\xi there on one sheet, where the scalar aa is real and smooth. The equation yields ∂‾a=0\bar\partial a=0 and aa is constant. Unique continuation on the common cover contradicts the character distinction. This argument includes any connected étale upper double.

For the universal kernel equation, an annihilator of its differential in the odd target solves the odd adjoint equation away from the special points, by variation of the smooth domain section. On the subdisk the allowed operator perturbations can prescribe any value on HH while killing ξ\xi. The adjoint pairings on the two upper sheets coincide by oddness. Localized testing forces the adjoint to vanish, first on that disk and then throughout. The dual is represented by an Lp/(p−1)L^{p/(p-1)} form for the W1,p→LpW^{1,p}\to L^p equation with p>2p>2, so no functional supported only at the marked point remains. Together with the Fredholm range this proves transversality. For smooth stable covers use local smooth trivializations of the sources and of the pole column to apply Sard–Smale on countably many charts. For connected étale doubles there are finitely many characters. Subtracting one real dimension for the choice of a kernel line, the respective projection indices are −4+4−1=−1,−2+2−1=−1,0+0−1=−1.-4+4-1=-1,\qquad -2+2-1=-1,\qquad 0+0-1=-1. Thus generically all these smooth families have zero kernel. At a nodal finite cover upper injectivity follows from invertibility on its étale normalization, including the base operator in the split case. At a trivalent component the principal part contributes the difference of the two endpoint values, a nonzero scalar multiple of its prescribed residue vector, as in Calculation E4. Compactness and the continuous stabilized families now give openness on the whole surface and ramification curve. One can work in sufficiently high finite differentiability, then approximate within the real subbundle of tensors annihilating the lower section. This gives density in the smooth topology, simultaneously for finitely many lower flags. A time cutoff inserts the perturbation at the original lower crossing. More than two branch values is essential to the ordinary assertion: with two, the unmarked upper family contains the lower cover itself.

The signed counts

For a generic complex-linear operator on NN, the base and all its étale sign twists have no kernel. The odd unmarked operators and the augmented ones are also generically injective. On smooth covers their complex indices are −2-2 and −1-1, offset by the respective complex parameter dimensions two and one before removing complex scaling. Complex-linear endomorphism variations supported on a regular target disk act arbitrarily on any nonzero value of one odd solution. The preceding adjoint test therefore applies with complex projectivization, even with fixed c,ℓc,\ell. The nodal tests follow from the regular étale normalizations. This constructs a reference on the given smooth complex bundle.

Along a generic real path with the prescribed regular endpoints, use the odd systems alone. In the smooth loci the same universal projective argument, now with unrestricted real variations supported also in time, has index zero. A transverse zero is a simple kernel since a kernel of real dimension at least two gives a positive-dimensional projective fiber. A solution of the augmented problem with zero residue would be an ordinary kernel with a branch fixed at cc. That incidence has path index −4+2+1−1=−2-4+2+1-1=-2 and is avoided.

At an unmarked nodal cover with collision point pp, an odd kernel is a nonzero solution vv of DαD^\alpha on the flat sign twist of NN satisfying v(p)=0v(p)=0. The trivial character covers the split case. At a trivalent marked limit p=cp=c, an odd augmented kernel requires v(c)∈ℓv(c)\in\ell in a sign frame. Indeed an odd meromorphic section on the bridge with at most one simple pole is determined by its opposite endpoint values, which lie in the residue line. A solution vanishing on the normalization is zero by this description. For an operator path, adding pp and imposing the former condition gives index 0+1−1+2−4=−20+1-1+2-4=-2. Fixing cc and imposing the latter gives 0+1−1−2=−20+1-1-2=-2. For transversality test away from the evaluation point with arbitrary operator variations where the solution is nonzero. This kills the adjoint as before, and arbitrary variations of the smooth section at the evaluation point kill any remaining evaluation functional. Thus generic paths avoid both strata for every character, even when a base or étale operator becomes singular elsewhere. Continuous stabilized reduction and properness of the compact parameter spaces preclude accumulation. This gives finite smooth crossing sets.

For index −d-d with d=4,2d=4,2, orient the smooth cover parameters complexly and the time by increasing time. At a simple kernel the derivative into Hom⁡(ker⁡,coker⁡)\operatorname{Hom}(\ker,\operatorname{coker}) is an isomorphism. Orient this space using the odd Fredholm determinant and any generator of the kernel. Reversing the generator changes both its evaluation and the induced cokernel orientation, giving the same sign for even dd. Equivalently choose the sign so that the Euler integral on the boundary of a small oriented ball is positive for the identity derivative. Indeed the reduced linear map sends a generator to its radial parameter vector, and its quotient on the link is the tangent bundle of SdS^d. The link integral is twice the local sign. Both parameter stacks have stabilizer μ2\mu_2 acting by sign on odd sections and trivially on parameters. Stack integration divides the link by two, including at the marked ramification point. Excision gives an increase of one signed unit per crossing in the odd Euler integral. This proves the variation in (1) and the independence of the signed counts from the comparison path. Bai–Swaminathan, local sphere calculation (6.36)–(6.37).

For completeness, the charts exhaust the fixed-target deformations near this locus. The normalized obstruction

These supplements are jointly minimal on ZZ. The matching equation off the ramification divisor

On a compact subset of Z\RZ\setminus R the upper branch values stay a positive distance from cc. A fixed smaller disk at cc contains a cubic joining factor and a separate ordinary sheet. Choose y′=wu−c′y'=w_u-c' there. The interpolation calculation of Article IV, §§2–3 and Appendices A–B gives a mass proportional to q′¯log⁡(1/|q′|)B(c)v\overline{q'}\log(1/|q'|) B(c)v in the matching fiber. Its singular primitive is the one on the lower branch of the cubic factor extended by zero on both upper sheets. Thus it projects to neither normalized component’s cokernel. In particular the presence of the nonzero upper cokernel FF introduces no additional logarithmic column.

We detail uniformity when the upper double is already nodal elsewhere. For the normal calculation hold the underlying unmarked upper cover fixed on q=0q=0. Its mark moves by the inverse unramified branch as the matched value c0+p2c_0+p^2 varies. The finite algebra near the selected value is the cubic polynomial algebra of Article IV, §§2–3 and Appendices A–B times a free sheet. Over the complement the lower and upper finite maps remain separate, with independent polynomial frames if their branch disks have the same target center. On an upper collision disk the quadratic frame 1,e1,e has conjugation coefficient e‾/e\bar e/e, uniformly bounded with convergence in every finite LaL^a when the nodal double varies. Varying lower branch centers off that disk uses lower-sheet translations as in Article IV, §§2–3 and Appendices A–B, leaving the upper factor fixed. Translations and identifications on the collars of the joining disk are smooth because both upper sheets there are unramified. The tt-variation is smooth in operator norm, uniformly on the disjoint upper factors.

Evaluation of the fixed-target stabilized line agrees with the actual line. At a central nodal map its polynomial coefficient solution is the ordinary lower odd generator and zero on all upper sheets, and the two indices agree by the finite projection formula. Evaluation of a coefficient solution with thick forcing is injective by interpolation, boundedness and removability on the normalization; a common root at a node has a single value. The two cokernels at the central map are therefore of equal dimension. The matching, lower and upper thick supplements span both: for the matching forces this follows also by using the lower cutoff section with prescribed mismatch, and for upper forces by the preceding odd-coefficient test. To justify the matching cutoff in the polynomial presentation, with w=z2w=z^2 and a free upper root at z=0z=0, a constant-valued mismatch is represented distributionally by z2H(w)a/wz^2 H(w)a/w as in Article IV, §§2–3 and Appendices A–B; its off-pole cutoff derivative is exactly the matching class. These forms may be chosen on regular sheet disks or annuli, and their extensions may be taken in common there. Surjectivity persists and both stabilized lines have rank one, so evaluation and the common normalization identify their obstruction coefficients. This is the stabilization comparison of Article IV, §§2–3 and Appendices A–B with a further quadratic summand away from the selected disk.

For each upper center take its own central normalized generator and dual obstruction tests. They range in continuous finite-dimensional bundles over the compact subset. On the joining disk the central multiplier is bounded in the polynomial frame and the tests have uniform Hölder norms by interior elliptic estimates. The joining matrix difference has L1L^1 norm O(|p|+|Q′|)O(|p|+|Q'|) with Q′=q′log⁡(1/|q′|)Q'=q'\log(1/|q'|); against such tests its only q′q' term of this order is the mass above, with remainder o(|p|+|Q′|)o(|p|+|Q'|). These are the disk estimates of Article IV, §§2–3 and Appendices A–B, independent of any off-disk collision. The stabilized generator difference tends uniformly to zero in C0C^0 by fixed-target W1,aW^{1,a} continuity, so its product with this L1L^1 variation has the same little-oh bound. The smooth principal-part differences on collars use convergence in W1,aW^{1,a}. In the central adjoint testing the image of the unchanged operator drops out. Thick forms whose lifts vary contribute their variation times obstruction coefficients tending to zero; equivalently a continuous change of supplement multiplies the reduced germ by its central invertible matrix plus o(1)o(1) in this comparison. For the full normal difference the other terms are the ordinary lower branch/time derivatives. The normalized central generator is supported on the lower component, so there is no first-order operator variation on the upper zero section from these directions. These arguments are uniform along sequences with varying upper central parameter: the relative comparison is made with the central operator for that same upper cover, not with an operator at a different point of the upper discriminant.

For clarity about coordinates in (7), local charts can first be used in the coordinates of the cubic computation. Comparison of the localized classes

The ambient fixed-target stack is smooth along ZZ. The nodal stratum has the compact smooth subfamily ZZ at λ=p=0\lambda=p=0; variation of c′c' preserves the smooth marked charts, including (4). Choose smooth orbifold tubular coordinates respecting the distinguished nodal divisor. For example first take a tubular neighborhood of ZZ inside that divisor, splitting its normal directions by the lower parameters and attaching mark, then take a tubular disk normal to the divisor. The derivatives identify the last line with SS as above. Bundle rows can be pulled back to these neighborhoods along the same retractions. The determinant orientations are obtained by deformation to complex normalization. The lower Hurwitz/time row has sign ηf\eta_f, p↦±vpp\mapsto\pm vp has positive real sign, and the remaining factors have the absolute orientation of FF and the complex orientations of WW and SS. All complex evaluation and gluing factors have even real dimension.

Choose concentric neighborhoods V0⋐V1V_0\Subset V_1 of the compact divisor RR, with V1V_1 small enough for (5), and an extension P′P' there whose least singular value is bounded below. Such an extension exists on an orbifold tubular neighborhood by bundle retraction and a metric. Arrange, by reducing V1V_1 and the normal radius, that the upper error divided by |q||q| is less than half this lower bound throughout V1V_1. Independently (7) holds uniformly on Z\V0Z\setminus V_0 with an injective leading block in the first three rows, bounded below there by a positive multiple of |λ|+|p|+|q|L(q)|\lambda|+|p|+|q|L(q). The two choices are compatible since the normal radius can be reduced after the base neighborhoods have been chosen. At q=0q=0 the nodal lower and attaching blocks are transverse uniformly on all of ZZ. These bounds already show that ZZ is the entire projective zero set in a neighborhood at the prescribed genus.

Here is a homotopy of the obstruction on that neighborhood relative to its zero-free boundary. One path for all the genera

For any finite kk the regular reference structures and the paths just used form open dense sets in the corresponding smooth spaces. Openness follows from the compact projectivized finite-dimensional reductions for kk fixed, absence of zeros on excluded strata and smooth transversality near the remaining finitely many points. For density in the smooth topology, the adjoint tests provide finitely many smooth perturbation directions spanning the missing equations in local reductions around any compact zero locus. First arrange avoidance on the compact nodal locus, then work on a compact complement of its zero-free neighborhood, doing the same for omitted poles before the full smooth incidence. Arbitrarily small linear combinations give the required regular values by finite-dimensional parametric transversality. Equivalently one can use Sard–Smale in sufficiently high finite regularity followed by smooth approximation; the regularity order can be taken above any finite set of seminorms specified in a smooth neighborhood.

The smooth Dolbeault connections form an affine Fréchet Baire space. Intersecting the regular sets gives one complex reference for any prescribed countable list of finite tests. The space of smooth fixed-symbol paths with two specified regular endpoints is also Baire, and interior perturbations suffice. Given an infinite sequence of distinct cic_i in one disk, identify the isotropic frame pairs of the repeated and distinct spin bundles there. The identification extends as a smooth bundle isomorphism, since the two rank-two bundles have the same first Chern class and a disk change of frame is nullhomotopic on its boundary. Thus the same flags give regular endpoints in every genus. The intersection of the countably many regularity sets supplies a single path. Apply (1) with all κi=1\kappa_i=1 to obtain the final assertion of the theorem. No uniform lower bound on the distance between successive singular times is needed. The calculation concerns the augmented odd Fredholm equation of the covers for the prescribed poles; a multiple-join contribution to the quartic virtual class would require its own local comparison.

Isolation and the projected degree

At the equal-height end the determinant just used vanishes and the split tower boundary moves; at the zero-height end division by the second amplitude fails and the marked zero-double family enters. The compact support is accordingly not the disjoint union of the two endpoint families and separately countable interior heights. Neither a division of this projected degree by a point stabilizer nor an integration of it over the open interval yields the full quartic Euler change.

F2. Contracted expansions of a regular unramified tower

Let CC be a closed curve of genus g≥2g\ge2 and DtD_t a smooth fixed-symbol path on a complex rank-two bundle NN of degree 2g−22g-2. Let f:Y→Cf:Y\to C be a smooth connected cover with simple ramification and let ξ∈ker⁡f*D0\xi\in\ker f^*D_0 have embedded graph γ=(f,ξ)\gamma=(f,\xi) in the homogeneous graph almost complex structure. Assume u*D0u^*D_0 has kernel ℝκ\mathbb R\kappa and the derivative WuW_u on the smooth fixed-target Hurwitz chart and increasing time, evaluated on this line, is an isomorphism onto its vertical cokernel. Denote its absolutely oriented sign by ηu\eta_u as in Calculation E1.

For k≥Hk\ge H let Gu,kG_{u,k} be the image of ℳ¯k(X,1)\overline{\mathcal M}_k(X,1) by composition with uu, together with the projective line of the pullback of κ\kappa at t=0t=0. Its nonconstant normalization is the specified uu. Every maximal connected contracted subcurve attaches at one point of this normalization, since a degree-one map to XX is an isomorphism on its nonconstant normalization. This includes collisions of attachment points and every stable specialization on a contracted block.

Proposition. In each fixed genus Gu,kG_{u,k} is compact and isolated in the projective kernel incidence. Its contribution to the connected absolute normal Euler change is 2ηu|Aut⁡C(u)|[v2k−2]xH−1,x=(2sin⁡(v/2))2.\frac{2\eta_u}{|\operatorname{Aut}_C(u)|}\,[v^{2k-2}]x^{H-1}, \qquad x=(2\sin(v/2))^2. \tag{1} The isolating neighborhood and time interval may depend on kk. A contracted block joining different sheets of pp is outside Gu,kG_{u,k}.

Lifting the graph and removing the contracted components

Take a relatively compact tubular neighborhood UU of γ\gamma in NN. Pull pp back along a smooth retraction to obtain a finite covering q:Ũ→Uq:\widetilde U\to U. The inverse image of γ\gamma is one embedded copy of XX, and the composite π∘q\pi\circ q with the bundle projection is holomorphic on the entire tube for the pulled-back graph structures. The tube retracts onto XX, so projection to CC sends its integral homology generator to degree dd. Every nonconstant closed holomorphic component in the tube has positive projection degree divisible by dd. Indeed a component with constant projection maps by qq to a single complex vector fiber, where it is constant. These assertions persist for the projection-preserving perturbation below, which keeps the standard vertical complex structure.

Properness of the degree-one stable-map stack gives compactness of the central image. Its vertical kernel is exactly the indicated line by restriction to XX and matching of constants on each contracted block. Write G=Aut⁡C(u)G=\operatorname{Aut}_C(u). The map to the projective incidence identifies central objects precisely by the action of GG on their degree-one target XX. An identification of two underlying stable maps induces an automorphism of the fixed positive normalization over CC and conversely. The automorphism preserves the projective kernel by its uniqueness. Thus the central stack is [ℳ¯k(X,1)/G][\overline{\mathcal M}_k(X,1)/G], retaining all automorphisms of the contracted curves.

Choose a small disk of regular values of uu where κ\kappa is nonzero on a chosen sheet, and order the dd degree-one pieces over this disk by their sheets. A point fiber may also contain a contracted subcurve. Over a smaller disk each labeled component still has degree one near the central family. Contracted curves mapping into the disk belong to the same labeled piece as their attaching point, as follows by domain collapse over a larger disk and degree at a regular value. One can use the whole d!d!-sheeted ordering cover. Its restriction to the central stack has d!/|G|d!/|G| copies of the degree-one family, since the deck action on orderings is free. On each copy the positive normalization has a fixed identification with XX. Fix a real linear normalization ℓa\ell_a by integrating a smooth real covector on the first selected sheet against pullback area, with ℓu(κ)=1\ell_u(\kappa)=1. Contracted attachments contribute zero to this integral. Use the same sheet under the identification on every copy, transporting choices by the corresponding labels.

For a central normalized graph the fixed identification gives a lift to X⊂ŨX\subset\widetilde U, with each contracted block lifted constantly at its attachment. On a local universal marked domain EE the map 1×q1\times q is injective on a neighborhood of the graph of this chosen lift in E×ŨE\times\widetilde U. This follows by compactness of the graph and local injectivity in the target variable. In the relative graph topology the graphs of nearby maps, including maps on smoothed domains, lie in the image and hence have a unique nearby lift. The construction commutes with chart identifications by uniqueness. It uses no count of all lifts of a map into a nonnormal cover. Stable-map relative topology · Calculation E3.

Consider a sequence of projective solutions approaching a point of the compact central locus. Normalize by ℓa=1\ell_a=1 and lift locally. There is precisely one positive normalization in each nearby map, by projection degree and the total degree dd. Forget its nodal flags and consider the unmarked maps from its smooth normalization. They have bounded genus and energy. On a bounded disk bundle containing the tube, a Hermitian connection gives a closed form restricting to the standard fiber form, and addition of a sufficiently large multiple of a base area form tames the graph structures on its closure. Its class comes from CC and the pullback area on every closed map is determined by the projection degree. The same form tames the small perturbations below on a fixed smaller lifted tube.

Pass to an unmarked stable limit. Its only nonconstant component maps with degree one onto the embedded XX, since the original marked sequence converges to the chosen central decoration and its homology class in the tube is [X][X]. A ghost in this unmarked limit would require a critical external branch, two external branches with the same complex tangent, or at least three external branches at a common target point. The embedding excludes each alternative. A self-node is excluded by injectivity at its two preimages. Thus the unmarked positive normalizations converge smoothly to XX and have genus HH. The ghost criterion also applies to a smooth family of target structures by placing the maps at constant parameter in a product with a complex parameter disk, with a block-diagonal almost complex structure. Ekholm–Shende, Theorem 1.1.

The nearby positive graphs are consequently embedded upstairs. Each connected contracted block has a single positive attachment, as all its attaching points have the same lifted target value. Deleting the blocks leaves a smooth normalized solution on the finite-map chart. Over a smoothed source the horizontal deformation complex [TX→u*TC][TX\to u^*TC] has torsion cokernel at the ramification points and no higher obstruction. Ramification points with the same value give independent summands. The hypothesis on WuW_u isolates the normalized bare solution on this chart. This proves isolation of the compact central family and excludes any sequence from a differently attached sector. Upper semicontinuity excludes a two-dimensional kernel throughout a sufficiently small neighborhood.

A displacement fixing the embedded graph

The fixed-time graph deformation sequence upstairs is 0→ker⁡L→ker⁡p*A→Tu→∂κcoker⁡L→coker⁡p*A→0,L=u*D0.0\longrightarrow\ker L\longrightarrow\ker p^*A\longrightarrow T_u \xrightarrow{\partial_\kappa}\operatorname{coker}L \longrightarrow\operatorname{coker}p^*A\longrightarrow0, \qquad L=u^*D_0. Shrink the test disk about a regular point where this normal field and a nonzero adjoint field are both nonzero. Such points exist by unique continuation. Its normal linearization has nonzero kernel-to-cokernel derivative, since at the graph the derivative factors via vertical projection along the graph tangent and gives the chosen BB. The finite-map normalized zero stays at (u,0,κ)(u,0,\kappa) and stays transverse by openness of the original derivative. The preceding unmarked-limit argument, applied with parameter δ\delta, and this unique bare zero isolate its contracted expansions throughout a sufficiently short homotopy. In particular no boundary contribution is introduced by the displacement.

Write La,tδ=La,t+δBaL^\delta_{a,t}=L_{a,t}+\delta B_a for the homogeneous operator of the displaced affine equation. At the central bare map it is injective. A fixed-horizontal kernel vector induces a kernel vector of AδA_\delta. Restriction and matching then give injectivity on all contracted expansions. The homogeneous operator and the nonzero forcing in the affine equation play different roles here.

For precision about the virtual comparison, take common stabilized horizontal charts for maps to CC and lifted graphs, pulling back the same slicing hypersurfaces by π∘q\pi\circ q. Their horizontal row and stabilization marks coincide. Lift the horizontal obstruction forms using the horizontal splitting of the affine graph equation. The target lift is a local diffeomorphism in these charts and keeps both horizontal and vertical rows.

The invertible AδA_\delta gives a unique smooth path of nearby embedded graphs for the unconstrained ordinary equation. The unmarked-limit argument above also applies before imposing the scalar constraint, uniformly on a short interval in this family. Every nearby positive normalization is the moving embedded curve, and each contracted block attaches to it at one point. Thus the ordinary zero locus consists precisely of its contracted expansions. Transversality of the normalized bare zero says that ℓa(v)−1\ell_a(v)-1 cuts this path simply. Contracted expansions have the same scalar value as their bare graph. On the ordinary zero locus the scalar is the smooth function of time obtained by evaluating it on this moving curve. Interpolating the scalar row to that function preserves the zero set on a small isolating neighborhood and its oriented class. Cutting by it therefore leaves the ordinary fixed-time degree-one local invariant of the embedded curve, times the oriented scalar intersection. Indeed its fixed-time normal is injective on all degree-one maps by restriction and matching. The ordinary comparison gives ϵ(Aδ)xH−1\epsilon(A_\delta)x^{H-1}, the determinant sign times the degree-one Hodge series. A smaller symplectic tube may be identified with a tube in the projectivization of the symplectic normal bundle plus a trivial line, and the tame structure extended from its closure. This supplies a compact ambient space for the comparison theorem, with unchanged local equations. Its normal bundle has degree 2H−22H-2 by adjunction, since the ambient first Chern number along the graph is zero. Zinger, Theorem 1.2 · Pandharipande, Theorem 2 · Article IV, Appendices A and D.

In genus HH the scalar sign times ϵ(Aδ)\epsilon(A_\delta) is the projective bare degree ηu\eta_u, by the transverse homotopy. The relative projective Euler class gives half the ordinary Euler change, since the real cokernel on the transverse link is the tangent of an even-dimensional sphere. The horizontal virtual dimension and the real normal index stay even in every genus, so this orientation calibration persists. Finally the calculation gives one copy of the ordinary series per framed central family. The factor (d!/|G|)/d!(d!/|G|)/d! is 1/|G|1/|G|. These observations prove (1).

F3. The two endpoint degrees at a ramified double wall

Use the transverse embedded odd double graph f:Y→Cf:Y\to C, γ=(f,ξ)\gamma=(f,\xi) and absolute crossing sign ηf\eta_f of Calculation F1. The lower double has two simple branch values. Assume the base operator is invertible and that the vertical derivative vv at each ramification point satisfies B(c)v∉ℂvB(c)v\notin\mathbb Cv, in a frame holomorphic for the complex-linear part of the lower operator. At the two ends of each projective interval there are concrete families of double covers. We compute local Euler changes in these families as their own operator parameters vary.

Zero height

Fix a ramification point rr, put c=f(r)c=f(r) and ℓ=ℂv\ell=\mathbb Cv, and freeze the lower sign and flag. Vary the upper operator through D0D_0 along the original increasing path. The local variation at the upper cover u=fu=f in the ordinary surface Euler number F2F_2 of Calculation E5 is ηf\eta_f. Its local variation in the prescribed-pole Euler number E(D;c,ℓ)E(D;c,\ell) is also ηf\eta_f. In particular the change of the regular upper expression in Calculation E6 due to this event is Δf[−ηf(2F2+E(D;c,ℓ))]=−3.\Delta_f\big[-\eta_f(2F_2+E(D;c,\ell))\big]=-3. \tag{1}

Indeed, write PfP_f for the ordinary cokernel and SS for the complex plane of permitted simple poles. The selected branch-velocity column of WfW_f sends δ\delta to the class of the principal part with coefficient −δv/2-\delta v/2 in the coordinate w=c+z2w=c+z^2. This follows by differentiating the lower solution at fixed target off the moving branch and extending the regular remainder, as in Calculation F1. Hence the pole map S→PfS\to P_f is injective. The augmented operator has the same one-dimensional kernel, represented by the smooth section with zero residue, and cokernel Pf/P(S)P_f/P(S). Varying the other branch and time gives the quotient isomorphism of WfW_f. Multiplication by −1/2-1/2 in a complex line and the removal of two real dimensions preserve the relative crossing sign. Both links have even sphere dimension and both have deck stabilizer of order two, so the ordinary and augmented Euler changes each equal one signed unit. The contribution after displacement

For a generic arbitrarily small real perturbation of D0D_0 preserving ff and its given section, the only ordinary upper incidence on the unmarked double surface and the only augmented one on either prescribed-flag curve are at the distinguished cover ff. The equation off the support is their common equation. The standard marked comparison of Calculation E6 applies: its two transverse lower rows give the original sign, its last two plane rows give the marked Euler integral, and the distinguished nonzero component orders the two roles even when the genera agree. The scale slice can be changed to the chart’s one lower thick test because the equation here is homogeneous with its coefficients on the plateaux. Thus no smoothed solutions can accumulate on the zero-height family as δ\delta tends to zero. The number in (4) concerns the displaced, excisable marked families. Recovering the full weight at the original wall still requires the equal-height family.

F6. Regularity of the finite double covers of the embedded graph

A subdisk can be chosen disjoint from those finitely many branch values and their translates. The real index of the odd operator is −4-4. Doubles admitting a lift of the lower involution. Equality of the characters gives a lift of τ\tau on the punctured double, extending uniquely across its punctures once chosen on one sheet. Independent times therefore prescribe a single operator on the smoothed domain, with the original equation on the neck. Interchange sends (e1,e2,M)(e_1,e_2,M) to (e2,e1,−M)(e_2,e_1,-M) exactly, with the central cokernels identified on the two copies.

Theorem. Fix a constant C0C_0. Near the split join, if all these frozen rows have norm at most C0|h0|L4C_0|h_0|L^4, then either the two amplitudes are equal or all the geometric and time parameters vanish. In the equal-amplitude case the resulting exact solution is a double cover of the original embedded lower graph at time zero. The same assertion holds with a,ba,b in a compact neighborhood of their common positive limiting amplitude. The theorem concerns the neighborhood of this split join; it makes no claim about regularity of upper covers elsewhere.

The symmetric tower

The involution interchanging z,yz,y has local quotient coordinate Z=z+y+mZ=z+y+m. With d=z−yd=z-y one has the exact identities d2=(Z−m)2−4q,w=(x−m2−2q)+Z2+2nd.d^2=(Z-m)^2-4q,\qquad w=(x-m^2-2q)+Z^2+2nd. \tag{1} When n=0n=0 and the other two branch positions coincide, the quotient extends over the complements, which are two copies of the same exterior. Indeed on the outer annuli the identification is the unique nearby lift of the target coordinate to the old exterior covering. Interchange preserves this identification, and the quotient disk in the coordinate ZZ is attached by the usual moving simple-branch construction. The quotient is the lower double with selected branch displacement x−m2−2qx-m^2-2q and the common other branch displacement. When these displacements and the common time are zero, pullback of kk gives a solution for each common amplitude, on both the smooth and nodal upper covers in (1). This supplies an exact family along which the matching and all antisymmetric component rows vanish. The matching row also vanishes for equal inputs before imposing the symmetric component equations by uniqueness of normalized stabilization.

Parameter derivatives with the node coordinate fixed

We give the parameter estimates in detail. Keep the complex plumbing parameter qq fixed while differentiating. Source identifications use the same zy=qzy=q cylinder, the fixed simple-branch source coordinates on the other disks, and moving identifications on collars of fixed size where the projections are unramified. These identifications and any fixed number of their derivatives in p,s,x,uip,s,x,u_i are bounded on the smaller collars, independently of qq. They are obtained by local lifts on a slightly larger collar, as in Calculation E6. Smooth cutoffs transport the comparison to the unchanged thick regions. The changing principal symbols in these identifications are supported on those fixed thick collars. The inner equation has the ordinary Dolbeault symbol. On the half with |z|≥R|z|\ge R, its multiplier is given by the smooth B(w)B(w) and dw/dz=2z+2p−2q2/z3−2sq/z2dw/dz=2z+2p-2q^2/z^3-2sq/z^2. Its derivatives in the indicated parameters are uniformly bounded there, since |q|/|z|2≤1|q|/|z|^2\le1; the same holds on the other half. This also bounds the derivative in multiplication norm from the first weighted Sobolev space to its equation space, by the uniform section sup bound and the bounded half-collar measure. The thick tests and supplements have uniformly bounded parameter derivatives. The normalized stabilized inverse is already uniformly bounded by continuity through the nodal fiber. For qq fixed, differentiating the inverse uses ∂T−1=−T−1(∂T)T−1\partial T^{-1}=-T^{-1}(\partial T)T^{-1} in these identifications. Consequently both the stabilized sections and their first derivatives in these parameters and the amplitudes are bounded, uniformly in sup norm and in first Sobolev norm. Higher interior estimates hold on fixed smooth collars. No derivative with respect to qq at the nodal fiber is used. Siebert, Proposition 4.15 · Bai–Swaminathan, Appendix B.

The undifferentiated o(Q)o(Q) in (2) is the two-sided Green projection of Calculation F1, (2). The conclusion identifies exact equal-height zeros and rules out approach by unequal frozen heights with nonzero geometry. Applying it to a nonlinear normalized displacement requires a comparison with the frozen rows at the tolerance used in the theorem. The normalization constraint, target perturbation, and the stabilizers in a compact Euler-class comparison are additional data.

F8. The quartic contribution one genus above the minimum at a two-branch wall

Fix a transverse embedded odd lower double graph f:Y→Cf:Y\to C with exactly two simple branch values, on a genus-gg target, g≥2g\ge2. Write h=2gh=2g for the genus of YY, ηf\eta_f for the absolute crossing sign and Dt=D0+tKD_t=D_0+tK for the transverse path of Calculation F4. The latter require that the only exceptional upper incidences be the ones forced at ff and at the two split doubles on its graph. They hold simultaneously after an arbitrarily small generic perturbation preserving the prescribed lower graph, as the respective tests use the same permitted lower variations.

Let DθD_\theta be the lower-target operator at θ=δ(χ(0)−χ(2))\theta=\delta(\chi(0)-\chi(2)) and AδA_\delta the graph-normal operator produced on YY by the normalized height perturbation of Calculation F4. Theorem. The supported class and its evaluation

The residual set consists of the two compact marked upper surfaces, the two closed height intervals, and the compact finite double surface on the embedded graph with its projective identifications. The genus budget and list of the disjoint contracted and unramified sectors are those of Calculation E3 and the proof. In particular a one-ended contracted expansion of an unramified tower belongs to the separate compact sector of Calculation F2. All points of the residual set have finite maps to CC, including the finite double collisions, apart from the marked trivalent bridges described in Calculation E6. The bridge charts there have unobstructed horizontal equations. Elsewhere finite maps have unobstructed relative deformations, including ordinary nodes: the normalized ramification jets move independently in the relative tangent complex, and at an unramified flag its marked motion can vary its target value. At two critical flags their distinct local branch deformations vary the two marked evaluations. The normalization sequence then supplies the independent node smoothings. Thus the horizontal virtual class near this set is the ordinary class in the fixed-target charts of complex dimension six.

At zero height Calculation F5 isolates the marked families uniformly through displacement, also when the limiting upper cover is ff. On the open interval Calculations F1 and F4 give isolation at zero displacement and removal for nonzero displacement on compact subintervals. At equal height the preceding comparison treats the two split radial joins, and the uniform normal comparison of Calculation F6 treats all other points of the compact finite surface. These statements concern every sequence approaching the respective points as δ→0\delta\to0, with original time allowed to vary. They give an isolating neighborhood of the compact residual set and, for all sufficiently small δ≠0\delta\ne0, excision into the marked and finite-tower families. Indeed a sequence of additional zeros approaching that set would have a convergent subsequence with limit in one of the charts just treated. The intervals were joined to both surfaces before applying the perturbation.

For clarity at a point with two-dimensional kernel, the local class for the absolute Euler change is twice the projectivized relative class. In a finite stabilization of index −12-12 the matrix ranks drop by at least two on a set of real codimension at least 2(12+2)=282(12+2)=28. In the universal space of real matrices removal of these strata does not change the relative cohomology in degree thirteen of the matrix space modulo its injective locus. This follows from the exact sequence for nested supports and the codimension bound on each smooth rank stratum. On the remaining simple-kernel stratum the connecting class of the oriented cokernel Euler class equals twice the pushed-forward Thom class of the tautological projective equation, by its even-sphere link. Hence the equality pulls back across the full stabilized family even where its rank drops by two. The same argument on local orientation systems, or over the oriented determinant cover, descends by the determinant convention. Stabilization preserves the Thom classes. Finite quotient charts use the usual rational equivariant weights. The homogeneous perturbation on projectivization defines a homotopy of this local class on the isolating neighborhood. It can be computed by solving the uniformly supplemented equation or on the signed I=1I=1 double cover. The tensor is supported over a fixed target disk. An upper node can lie over that disk. In a plumbing chart the differential of the total holomorphic map is bounded on each half in the larger source coordinate, with the same bound at the ends of a marked bridge by the charts of Calculation E6. The section sup estimate controls the nonlinear coefficient and its section derivative there. The two half-disks of shrinking radius have vanishing weighted target mass, and their pulled-back area tends uniformly to zero. Thus the integral II, its section derivative, and the zeroth-order equation term extend continuously in the stabilized norms across the node. On the support under consideration II stays bounded below. The resulting Lipschitz bound times |δ||\delta| gives contraction in the complementary section variable and the required finite-dimensional section homotopy. On overlaps common stabilization and the positive normalization give the same class. This is the local calculation of Article IV, §§2–3 and Appendices A–B with the higher rank-drop stratum retained.

After displacement Calculation F5 gives −ηf(4F2(Dθ)+∑rE(Dθ;r))-\eta_f(4F_2(D_\theta)+\sum_r E(D_\theta;r)) for the marked surfaces. Calculation F6 gives ηfϵ(Aδ)F2(Aδ)\eta_f\epsilon(A_\delta)F_2(A_\delta) for the compact finite-tower family with normalization and all stack factors. This proves (1). With increasing δ\delta the marked expression changes by +3+3 at each flag and the weighted tower changes by −6-6 in total. Thus the signed chamber differences cancel, also directly verifying agreement of the two expressions for the original residual.

Choice of the original time direction. Let D̃t\widetilde D_t be any smooth fixed-symbol path through this D0D_0 whose time column completes the lower branch map with the same sign. Interpolate the path to D0+tKD_0+tK by their convex combination, keeping the central operator fixed. It suffices to isolate the undisplaced central incidence throughout this compact homotopy of paths. This check uses only one time on the two components. In Calculations F1 and F5 the coefficient on both sides of the neck is the same smooth Bt(w)B_t(w); all centered estimates, including (3) of Calculation F5, apply with uniform smooth bounds in the homotopy parameter. In the frozen proof of Calculation F7 the exchange interpolation keeps a common time fixed, so no difference of neck coefficients from independent times arises. One may include the interpolation parameter as another constant complex-disk coordinate tangent to the fixed submanifold in that argument. F9. Smooth double-cover crossings near a ramified graph

Let f:Y→Cf:Y\to C be a connected double cover of a genus-gg curve, g≥2g\ge2, with b>0b>0 simple branch values and h=g(Y)=2g−1+b/2h=g(Y)=2g-1+b/2. Theorem. After an arbitrarily small generic perturbation of the lower operator preserving f,ξf,\xi, take any transverse fixed-symbol path AtA_t through AA on YY, with crossing sign ηA\eta_A. On a sufficiently short interval its endpoints are regular for the upper odd two-branch family.
